#8417. The 9 Ways That Mature Bucks Are Different Than Other Deer

Published Oct 27, 2026 4:29 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Almost every deer on the farm is on its feet. Bucks and does of all ages are hammering food sources. They’re hungry after the rut, but there’s also a snowstorm incoming. Temps are dropping, and there’s a flurry of snowfall — and activity.

Even though the entire herd appears to be on its feet, one buck is still holed up in his fortress. It’s broad daylight, frigid, and snowing. The 5-year-old you want to kill refuses to leave his bedding sanctuary. He’ll move in daylight — all deer must move eventually — but not until it gets closer to dark.

It’s been said many times, but a deer and a mature buck are two different animals.  Older bucks don’t just have more inches of antler on average — they have more wits, senses, and experience. You don’t get to be a five-year-old deer without learning how to survive in the wild, and that’s why these deer not only look different but behave in ways that don’t often align with the does and younger bucks we’re used to seeing. Here’s how.

Hunters can use many physical signs to estimate a buck’s age, but the key I often look for is a buck’s muscle definition. Older whitetails look vastly different than their younger cohorts. Mature bucks have a muscled-up body structure that younger deer just don’t have. As deer progress through each age bracket, they exhibit different body structures.

For example, yearling bucks look like small does with antlers. Two-year-old bucks look like large does with antlers. Three-year-old bucks exhibit a more muscular frame but aren’t filled out just yet. Four-year-old bucks show significant swelling, with heavy shoulders and an enlarged brisket and neck. Five-year-old bucks and older exhibit even more body weight with heavy swelling of the neck, shoulders, and brisket. They might even begin displaying a pot belly and swayed back. Practice judging age in the field, and you’ll be able to better recognize an old buck when he shows up.

Every set of antlers is unique, regardless of the buck’s age. Still, as bucks reach older age classes, they express their genetic code and capabilities. Often, this leads to antler character traits that are usually present in older deer, regardless of the overall score or size of a deer. Examples include kickers, stickers, drop tines, and other unique antler points. It can even lead to greater numbers of points and other interesting non-typical characteristics. Even as they age and their antler size may decrease, older deer still tend to have more mass than younger bucks, particularly around the bases of their antlers.

Deer don’t have personalities in the human sense, but researchers have identified behavioral preferences that we can think of as personalities — particularly when it comes to their movements across the landscape. Some bucks are homebodies or wanderers. (One study found that 33 percent of bucks had a mobile personality.) And as bucks reach older age classes, these personalities can become even more apparent. For example, bucks might be more aggressive or passive. They might be more or less engaged in the rut. Perhaps they even express preferences for specific food sources. If you can start to identify those tendencies and preferences, you have a better shot of patterning your buck.

A common myth suggests that bucks increase their home ranges as they age. For the vast majority of whitetails, this isn’t true. Numerous studies have determined that whitetail buck home ranges and core areas actually decrease in size as they get older. As they become more familiar with their surroundings, they learn the safest areas, best bedding, premier food sources, and more. This leads to a more distinct and deliberate use of the landscape. Hunting older bucks requires finding these smaller areas and home ranges and hunting them accordingly.

As bucks get older, they become more in tune with their environment. They learn where hunters focus their efforts (we humans can become patternable and predictable) and how to avoid us. Older bucks use the landscape to their advantage, especially from a safety perspective.

For instance, bucks use thermal hubs, the low points in the topography where scent collects from the surrounding area. In other words, they don’t necessarily have to walk just downwind of your stand to know there’s a hunter in the area.

Another example includes bucks bedding in ways that give them a security advantage. For instance, mature bucks often bed on leeward ridges, ridge endings, bench edges, and more. Bedding in certain ways allows them to see danger coming from a distance while also smelling any threats upwind that could approach from behind them.

Bucks are also good at finding trails and travel routes that elude stand locations, blinds, and other hunting setups.

Let’s dig even deeper into a buck’s bedding habits, all of which are proven methods that help mature deer detect danger before it detects them. From a scenting perspective, deer find many ways to benefit from prevailing winds and daily thermals.

Using Advantageous Terrain: Bucks tend to bed in areas with advantageous terrain. These locations give them better visibility but also provide winding advantages. As noted above, hilly and mountainous terrain allows deer to use topography to their advantage, but even flatland whitetails find ways to do this. Often, deer that bed in flatter creek or river bottomlands bed close to the water.

For example, deer routinely bed in oxbows. A location with water on three sides helps diminish the odds of a predator approaching from those directions. And if they do, deer can hear them coming through the water. Meanwhile, they can see danger that comes by way of land. If something does approach, deer can bolt out the back door and across the water to safety.

As mentioned above, bucks tend to express a unique personality type. Within those individual preferences comes varied responses to hunting pressure. Human intrusion impacts every deer differently, but most mature bucks don’t tolerate much of it. If they do, they’ve likely been conditioned to certain activities on the property. In other words, some mature bucks may tolerate more pressure than others, but in general, mature bucks won’t tolerate all of it.

Though all bucks are biologically motivated to participate in the rut, some individual bucks can be more active than others. Depending on an individual buck’s tendencies, they might be very active and move a lot during daylight, or they might be reclusive, searching for does at night and bedding back down before daylight.

Read Next: Best Hunting Rifles, Tested and Reviewed

Numerous expert hunters I’ve talked to agree on one particular thing — bucks are hardest to hunt from ages four to six. Often when a buck hits seven, eight, or older, they seem to become more active during the daylight. Perhaps they become overconfident, get delusional and senile, or maybe they just care less. Regardless, they move more and get easier to kill again, almost as a 3-year-old buck would.

Hunting old bucks requires different approaches and tactics than hunting deer in general (does and younger bucks). So, put together a good plan this season, and tag that old buck that’s been haunting your dreams.

#8413. Piolets d'Or Insider: How the Jury Works, Style Debates, and Future Plans

The recent 2026 edition of the Piolets d’Or awards, held last week in a remote corner of the French Alps, felt like an organization trying to adapt to fast-changing times and attract larger audiences while keeping its prestige and spirit intact.

ExplorersWeb was there to meet old acquaintances and to put a face to some of the names we wrote about in the last 12 months. We also wanted to participate in the collective exercise of reflection about the future.

Views of Les Ecrins Massif from Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides

Piolet d’Or recipients enjoyed a relaxed atmosphere at the tiny village of Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans and a ceremony at Burg d’Oisans, a 30-minute drive down the valley. Yet, the most interesting event took place the following day, as an elite group of climbers sat around a table in a small hall with large glass windows facing autumn-colored forests and the ragged peaks of the Ecrins Massif, covered in the first snow dust of the season.

Representing the awardees were Nicolas Jean (awarded for climbing Jannu East with Benjamin Vedrines); the complete teams from Ultar Shar, Aikache Chokk, and Jerupaja Grande; a hyper-energetic, widely smiling Peter Habeler, 84, who received a lifetime achievement Piolet d’Or; Simon Welfringer, who gave a talk; organizers Christian Trommsdorf and David Chambre; geographer and chronicler Rodolphe Popier, and two members of the jury: Jordi Corminas of Spain and Paul Ramsden of the UK. At a press conference, these experts debated some of the hot issues in today’s mountaineering.

Simon Welfringer of France speaks at the post-Piolets d’Or experts’ panel. Photo: Angela Benavides

Trommsdorf noted that the jury had an easy time selecting the awarded climbs this year. He explained how these expert jurists choose the best alpine-style activities of the year.

The members work remotely, choosing from a Big List of outstanding activities. This list is previously compiled by Lindsay Griffin, long-time editor of the American Alpine Journal, and the UK’s Alpine Club. Jurors study the climbs and narrow it down to a short list of candidates, which is not made public. The awards go to those activities chosen by the majority of jury members. In this case, decisions were finalized on the first vote, with no need for a tie-break.

Left to right, Rodolphe Popier, Jordi Corominas, Paul Ramsden (speaking), and David Chambre. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

That led to the first topic of debate: It was noted that some climbing teams happily announce themselves as “Piolet d’Or nominates” on social media when their climbs appear on the Big List — although organizers make it clear that not all activities on that list are suitable for a Piolet d’Or. Yet, no one supported the idea of making the short lists public. The general agreement was to keep the small “best of the year” finalists available only to the jury.

The second topic for debate was the presence of a relatively new piece of technology now ubiquitous on expeditions: drones. These have become essential on rescues, but climbing teams also use them to scout the route ahead. In the near future, drones could also carry supplies, emergency kits, or extra equipment. Commercial outfitters are already using them in this way.

Benjamin Vedrines and Nicolas Jean of France used drones to check the state of their planned route on Jannu. However, they explained that the drone was useless in relaying information about a section that they couldn’t see from Base Camp. It had a different angle of view, and the drone lost connection when it tried to approach that area.

Drones piloted by their base camp film crew also hovered overhead as they traversed the long summit ridge. Finally, before the summit push, they used drones to clearly identify the highest point, to make sure they reached the true summit.

The Ultar Sar team also had a drone, they noted. All the awarded climbers agreed that drones are okay as long as the climbers are completely transparent about what they used them for. Jordi Corominas said the drones are a technological innovation that has come to stay, no different than InReach devices, satphones, or even ice axes and crampons.

Jordi Corominas, left, discusses past climbs with Benjamin Vedrines. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

Interestingly, one jurist stood against the tide: Paul Ramsden is an advocate for the pure alpine-style criteria of the UK climbing school, and with five Piolets d’Or, he is the overall record holder of these prestigious awards. In his opinion, drones spoil the adventure and uncertainty inherent in pure alpine style. Ramsden himself uses neither drones, trackers, nor even satphones.

Finally, Trommsdor suggested possibly expanding the awards to create a special Piolet d’Or for the best rock climb and perhaps even the best ski descent. The idea expand on the new performance category introduced this year in the big list as a test. The category featured, among others, the two Everest ski descents in 2025. Both were heavily supported, and Jim Morrison‘s descent of the Hornbein Couloir was oxygen-assisted.

In the end, one of the performance ski descents received the female award: Typhaine Duperier‘s alpine-style climb+ski descent of Nanga Parbat’s Schell route, with Boris Langenstein.

It is unclear whether the new additions will become official in the near future, but some attendees expressed concern about the context in which these take place. Would they award ski expeditions for their boldness or technical excellence without bearing in mind how the skiers reached the start of their descent (supported climbs, fixed routes, even helicopters)?

As for rock climbs: where to set the difference between a rock climb and an alpine climb on high, but dry, faces? The debate was left open. We will find out what, if anything, changes in the next edition of the Piolets d’Or.

Buried houses at the now abandoned village of La Berarde. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

The physical award is no longer an actual piolet (ice axe). In the last few years, it has been a hand-crafted trophy that changes with the venue. This time, it was a plaque with a reproduction of Ecrins National Park’s most distinctive peak, La Meige. It rested on a piece of rock from the remains of La Berarde, a nearby village destroyed in a flood two years ago.

At the Piolets d’Or ceremony in Burg d’Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides

Next year, the Piolets d’Or will be staged in the same location, perhaps in late summer. The event will commemorate the 150th anniversary of the first ascent of La Meige. The long-term plan is to turn the Piolet d’Or ceremony into a bigger, international mountain festival.

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

#8412. 19. Floating to the Moon

We stood at the edge of the river canyon, looking down into the unknown. The rain had quit two days ago but still the water level would be high. All part of the fun.

Up on the desert plateau we had been in the open, walking in grass and volcanic rocks pitted like the bark of trees. Now we walked over a thousand feet down, almost straight down, down to the river at the heart of the canyon.

Huge trees stood above us, rooted into the banks or holding to the cliffside. The sun slanted in over the rim on the eastern side. The flowing surface steamed in the cold. We checked ourselves and each other. Every pocket was zipped. Our shorts were rolled up or taken off entirely, exposing the lines on our thighs where pale skin had been browned by months of sun. Everything in our packs was wrapped up tightly in plastic and cinched down tight. Time to get wet.

Stepping in hurt, but stepping out hurt more. The cold made us yip like coyotes, and when we squelched out onto the sand on the far side, the blood rushed through our legs and ached terribly. The trail crosses in and out of the Gila river hundreds of times. We were only getting started.

On either side of the river there were boulders and logs, downed trees and debris crushed together into walls and barricades by the pressure of the floods. Since the waters had receded they had dried out, and although some had broken down a bit, they remained. The floodrack created an obstacle course that seemed to never end. Sometimes the cliffs rose straight up out of the water in a bend, forcing us to the inside of the curve. The flowing river was mostly clear of debris, but the silty waters were impossible to see through, and with the loose rocks and invisible drop offs – not to mention the cold- we were pushed to make our crossings as quickly as we could. We found ourselves slogging through quicksand, crashing through willows, crawling under downed trees or traversing them like balance beams, and bracing against the torrent when it was time to cross again.

“Man, this reminds me of the Bob!” “Oof, don’t remind me.”

Way back in Montana we had all had a time of it traveling through the Bob Marshall Wilderness. Although we hadn’t met each other yet, we had all been there at around the same time and had all had to deal with the fallen trees, flooded waters and general cold.

I lifted the heavy curved stick above my head and brought it down in a crushing stroke, breaking an opening through a natural fence of dead tree branches. They broke easily, sending dust and fine bits of bark flying. I gave the air a moment to clear and pushed through. Wonder and Gunslinger followed. I had accidentally left my trekking poles in the backseat of a hitch the day before, but had found this stick on the bank just before the first crossing. Long enough to act as a support for the water crossings, strong enough to break through the environment when needed, and not cool enough to be heartbreaking when it was inevitably lost, broken or left behind: in other words, the perfect stick for my needs.

We stepped out onto a gravel beach and looked up at the cliff wall across the river where the ancients had left their mark. The roofs of caves and overhangs were scored black by generations of cookfires, and the little paths up and down could be seen from most angles. We crossed the deeply gouged meadow on the inside of the river’s wide, shallow curve. The long grass was all flattened and drawn out towards the downstream flow.

“You think this was all from this past week? Or the September floods?” “I don’t know. Probably September, but I’m sure this week didn’t help much.”

The soft mud and sand had already shown us the tracks of plenty of animals: black bear and fox, mule deer and ringtail cat, iron-shod horses but no people on foot, not since the flood at least.  Something dark and sleek slipped into the river and followed its nose upstream

Yesterday I had seen two wild dogs up in the grass, about as different from one another as could be. The first was a dachshund that had run out from behind a set of cattle loading pens, barked once at me and then run back. Nobody around, no collar that I could see, so strange an interaction that it took me a moment to be sure it had actually happened. The second had been a lobo, a Mexican gray wolf of the prairie, rangy and lean, loping along through the tall grass. Desert dogs both, but neither down here at the river.

We crossed again. After noon now, the water was still cold but no longer painfully so. Wonder went first. She faced upstream and used her trekking poles, always keeping three points of contact as she went. Not very far to go, only ten feet across here, but the water reached her hip and the current made the poles in her hands thrum like picked guitar strings. As she ascended the far bank, Gunslinger went. He’s a good bit taller, but he still had to pick his way carefully. He stepped up onto the sand and then it was my turn to make the crossing. I held my stick in both hands and faced upstream, crabbing sideways as they had, moving slowly. A bad step, a rock turned and rolled over my foot on its way downstream. Ow. My feet weren’t numb, not quite, but they were club-like from the cold. Still, I felt that. Just a little blood from one cut on my ankle. Oh well, keep moving.

Dead willows slashing at our legs and left white scratches on the skin. The live ones caught our feet like cables and held us until we could untangle ourselves. Deep black mud under the flowing current, grabbing and holding anything it could.

We reached the junction. We had gone a bit over six miles in almost six hours. We looked at the map and made the call. If we’d had enough food, we could’ve kept going through the river canyon. If we had more time, more food, if the water wasn’t so high, if we knew there wasn’t going to be more rain soon…

We had only done the first of the four segments of the river that the trail ran through. I had wanted to do all four, we had all wanted to do more than just the one, but we were beat. Our feet were waterlogged and raw and our legs were slashed and bruised. We went uphill.

The high route follows the river from the top of the canyon. Sparse forest and dry meadows. An eagle dove into the tall yellow grass and swept away victoriously. We followed the rim of the canyon as it wound in and out, and as the sun declined it provided us with stunning colors. We found our spot, right at the edge of the drop. Nobody set up a tent: we put our energy into a fire instead. The stars came out, then the moon. Full, piercing spotlight of the night, bathing us in silver light. We meditated upon the burning red embers and the echoing calls of the lives of the canyon.

Golden light drenched the walls of the edge. We loaded our gear and swung our packs up and ate the last of our food as we went. A long slow descent as the plateau broke open into the great river valley, the way down decorated by the late blooms of cholla and high red pillars of stone. We reached pavement and dropped our packs, then set out to explore the homes that had been built into the naked caves more than 700 years ago.

We met up with other hikers, friends old and new. We bought food and ate it and bought more. Fresh pizza and homemade ice cream, hard to beat. When we were full and happy, we went down to the hot springs beside the river. Hot water and clear skies. We set up for the night the best that we could – only a few tent stakes found purchase in the hard ground.

I woke in the dark. Cold, shivering, damp. No, wet. I sat up. What the hell?

Everything was covered in condensation. Of course. We’d heard how bad it was from people who had slept by the river last night. Now here we were only a few yards away from it, and it was too late. 2:38am, and not a chance I’d dry out enough to warm up enough to fall asleep again. Damn.

I fought against it for a while but it was no use, so I made the call. I shucked off my quilt and liner and rocked to my feet. Another shiver ran through me as I walked to the steaming pool. I wore every layer of clothing I had but it wasn’t enough, and every one of them landed in a pile on the wooden bench. I stepped down into the hot water.

The surface passed my calves, my thighs, and the water splashed gently as I crouched, as my ribs slipped below, as my shoulders dropped back into the heat, and finally my head went under.

Quiet. The odd clicking in my ears from escaping air. The slight burn in my nostrils from the hot water. The gravel bottom pressing into my tired muscles. Exhale. Bubbles from the nose. Chest falling deeper into the pool. Head tipping back. Water tipping in, force it out – exhale – too late. The burn in the sinuses. Slow rise. Forehead breaking the surface. Water running down my face. Breathe in through the mouth, out through the nose, clear the passageway. Wipe water from the eyes, open them.

The blazing moon above, now a day past full. The stones and trees of the riverbank stand motionless in the bright light. The chuckling of the Gila, the pools smoking like volcanic lakes. I lie suspended in the hot water, almost motionless. Silver steam in the cold air, rising from my skin where my chest breaks the waterline.

Almost four in the morning, still hours until dawn. Exhale. My body sinks below the surface again. Not far to go now, to Mexico.

I do not open my eyes, but I can feel the bright moonlight penetrating the waters of the hot spring. What has been a distant future for so long now is just…the future. The near future, even.

I breathe out slowly, deliberately, keeping my nose tilted forward, keeping my airway protected. The trail is drawing to a close, we can all feel it. There is a slowing down of sorts, a carefulness, like the last movements of a painter finishing their masterpiece. An involuntary resistance to the inevitable end.

I feel the tightness in my chest as my lungs reach complete emptiness. I feel the tightness harden as my oxygen depletion reaches maturity. I feel the twitching of my muscles as they cry to be released from stasis, to drive my living being up into the world of air. An involuntary resistance to the inevitable end.

Up. Cold air. Deep breath. Good oxygen. Steady heartbeat. Steady mind. Deep breath. Cold air. Good oxygen. Good life. Good living. An involuntary resistance to the inevitable end, but a worthy one. Good life. Good living.

#8411. Elk Hunting from ATVs Has Gotten Out of Hand

Published Oct 27, 2026 5:24 PM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

I’ve always been a pretty “go with the flow” type of hunter with a general mindset that if it’s legal, there’s nothing wrong with it. But then I went elk hunting on public ground during Colorado’s first rifle season.

I made the 28-hour drive from my home in Pennsylvania to Colorado with my cousins for their first-ever elk hunt. I had warned them of the side-by-side presence I’d experienced on a previous archery hunt in this very unit. It was manageable then. Plus, we’re from PA so we’re used to hunting pressure.

But as our elk hunt progressed, I felt no small amount of anger and sadness as the backcountry we were trying to hunt became a side-by-side racetrack.

We arrived several days before the opener to set up camp, scout the nearby creek drainages and finger ridges, and find the elevation band the elk desired. After a long hike up and into some national forest ground, to my elation, we found a pile of elk. We spotted a few raghorns, a couple smaller satellite bulls, a bugling herd bull, and his harem of cows. They were all using a knob near a meadow for their mid-day bedding area.

We watched them for a bit, then backed out of the area to continue our scouting mission. After zeroing in on the terrain features and elevation a few more times over two days of scouting and finding new elk in each location, we were feeling good about our opening day plan. When the alarm went off in my tent at 3:00 a.m. that morning, we were ready to get started on our 4-mile hike into the target area. As daylight set in, we were already at the bottom of the creek, letting the thermals pull our scent down and away from where we expected the elk to be.

We spent the next three hours meticulously crawling through the creek bottom, checking the north and south facing slopes on each side of us. To our surprise, we never laid eyes on an elk by the time we crested the knob mid-morning. I was a bit confused, until we rounded the corner and a mere 300 yards from where we had seen the large herd was a guide camp with generators, side-by-sides, a large tent with woodsmoke rolling out of the stovepipe, and several easy-ups.

I was frustrated, but I kept my composure and assured my cousin that what those guides were doing was legal and this kind of thing happens. They had accessed the spot via a legal access road that snakes up and around the basin we were hunting. My guess is, they had no idea they had effectively spooked an entire herd of elk by setting up their camp in that location. We hiked away from their camp in search of the elk, but were unable to locate them that day. I counted it as a learning experience for us — if a place is legally accessible by vehicle, we should expect vehicles to be in there.

The next morning, we executed a plan I’d devised lying in my sleeping bag the prior evening. After some obsessive map study, I felt as though I might know where that herd of elk was pushed to. We made our approach and found the herd. Unfortunately, my cousin’s scope had been knocked off zero and he ended up making a non-fatal hit on a nice bull at only 125 yards. His shot resulted in only a few drops of blood and broken spirits. We later found out that his rifle was shooting a foot low.

After re-sighting the gun and mentally recovering, we made our way to a nearby trail to begin our hike to the next pin on my map. The trail had a big sign that read, “Administrative Route — Motorized use allowed only by Forest Service Authorization.” As our trekking poles squelched down into the fresh, muddy UTV tracks, I gave a quizzical look to my cousins. Moments later, a side-by-side came ripping up the trail behind us with two hunters hauling a dead bull. We congratulated them, and they regaled us with their hunt.

“We were just driving around when all of the sudden a whole herd took off in front of us, I threw the gun out the front window and ‘BOOM’, dropped this guy on the run!”

I’m sure my face said a whole lot more than I could muster in that moment, because after that, they quickly said goodbye, good luck, and drove off. Aside from shooting out of a vehicle being illegal in Colorado, it’s just unethical and lacks any respect for wild bull elk, which is a critter that I hold in high regard.

As we continued down the trail shaking our heads in disbelief, three more side-by-sides ripped past us. Our boots became caked in mud as we walked out of the basin, contemplating our next move. That afternoon, we loaded our truck to find a new area. To our dismay, we counted more than 50 side-by-sides either out and about, or parked near tents or campers along the main road through our unit. Every trail was rutted up, and the national forest had seemingly become a UTV mudders’ paradise, except these mudders were pursuing elk.

We also encountered certain trails that were closed only to certain motor vehicles, with a width restriction in place. In essence, any vehicle under 50” was allowed through, and any wider would be stopped by two large metal poles on each side of the path. Unsurprisingly, the poles were bent out to high hell, allowing vehicles much wider than 50” to baja their way through the forest.

By the end of the third day of our hunt, we were disheartened. We had been in elk every day, and able to evade the side-by-side pressure. At times we were even able to use it to our advantage. But we were not enjoying anything representative of a wilderness hunt. The lack of respect for the place and the animals that lived there really started to eat at me.

Read Next: Roadless Areas Provide 10 Times Better Elk Hunting and Support the Best Trout Streams in the West, Study Shows

As someone who grew up in the most hunter-dense state in the United States, I’ve experienced a lot of folks taking shortcuts and not wanting to put in the physical effort to go hunting “the old fashioned way.” However, driving their four-wheelers to their stands on private land is a whole lot different than ripping side-by-sides for miles on supposedly closed national forest roads in pursuit of an elk near the trail.

What draws Eastern hunters like me to the West and to elk hunting is the wilderness. The untouched, unkempt backcountry where humans don’t frequent. Where you can walk up on blue grouse and where the creeks are devoid of cairns and boot prints, where you can witness animals in their natural habitat and their natural state. We dream about silence that almost hurts your ears, the yellow aspen leaves trickling down in a slight breeze, and the snow-capped peaks looming on the horizon. Most of us want our Western hunt to be wild and we want elk hunting to be hard.

Elk deserve to be hunted by woodsmen who read the terrain, watch their wind and thermals, and stalk carefully into range. Elk should not be relegated to some trailside target practice.

I look forward to, train for, and dream about my annual elk hunt for 11 months and 3 weeks every year. Maybe I’ve over-romanticized the beauty and wildness of elk hunting in my mind. But I also know I’m not alone.

There are many of us who welcome the hardships that come with a lack of sleep, long miles, steep climbs, and heavy packs. After all, that’s what makes filling an elk tag so rewarding.

So take the perspective of one Eastern elk hunter for what it’s worth. We should be prioritizing enforcement of off-road rules in our national forests and not letting the off-roaders run amok. We should not be cutting new roads into the little remaining backcountry that we have left, simply because we can. And we need to refocus on what elk hunting, real elk hunting, is supposed to be about.

Derek Horner is the manager of audience development for Outdoor Life where he manages OL’s social accounts and email campaigns, and shares our stories with the world. He was born and raised in central Pennsylvania where his father and grandfather taught him to hunt and fish. He graduated from Pennsylvania State University in 2018 and still lives in central Pennsylvania.

#8407. Adventurer to Climb 100 Peaks on 2,000Km Taiwan Traverse

Tomorrow, November 1, Japanese adventurer Yoki Tanaka begins a four-month, 2,000km trek north to south down the length of Taiwan. Along the way, he will summit all 100 of Taiwan’s celebrated Baiyue peaks.

Taiwan has about 268 peaks exceeding 3,000m, but only 100 of them made this special list, which is based not only on height but beauty, difficulty, prominence, and character. Prominent Taiwanese mountaineers compiled the list in the early 1970s, partly inspired by Japan’s own list of 100 revered mountains.

Yoki Tanaka arrives in Taiwan earlier this week. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

The 43-year-old Tanaka has specialized in this unusual combination of long-distance trekking and mountaineering. In 2014, he summited Japan’s 100 famous mountains while walking 7,800km over 208 days. (Japan, though far bigger than Taiwan, has only 23 mountains over 3,000m.) A year later, he extended that by climbing 200 mountains and walking 8,000km in 222 days. Finally, he increased that again to 300 mountains. This time, it took him three years and about 20,000km of walking.

Tanaka will begin on Sunday from the northernmost tip of Taiwan, at the Cape Fugui lighthouse, and finish sometime in March at Eluanbi, the country’s southernmost point. The first 150km will be along roads before he reaches his first trailhead. He’ll spend the next week trekking. His first five peaks will be Xueshan (3,886m), Nanhudashan (3,742m), Hehuanshan (3,417m), Qilaishan (3,560m), and Nenggaoshan 3,262m).

Although he won’t use motorized transport for the entire journey, he will have ample opportunity to resupply along the way. His expedition plan includes a charmingly precise breakdown of how he plans to spend his evenings: town stays, 48 days; mountain huts, 38 days; tent camping, 39 days. He has also budgeted 16 rest days and 20 contingency days.

Tanaka trains in Taiwan earlier this year. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

His most difficult section, scheduled for early January, will take him through the remote interior of the Central Mountain Range for over two weeks. During this time, he’ll have to carry his own food, search for trails that may no longer exist, and gamble that he will be able to find enough water.

During a December 2025 reconnaissance trip to Xueshan, Taiwan’s second-highest mountain, Tanaka discovered how difficult it can be to obtain water. Two water sources marked on his map were completely dry.

On a previous hike. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

By late January, the Japanese trekker should reach the historic Batongguan Trail, eventually leading to 3,952m Yushan, Taiwan’s highest mountain. The Batongguan Trail was originally constructed in 1875 under the Qing dynasty to establish a route across the mountainous interior. Decades later, Japanese colonial authorities constructed a separate crossing through the region. Sections of the route survive as remote hiking trails and provide access to some of Taiwan’s highest mountains.

Tanaka first visited Taiwan in the spring of 2025 and has made several reconnaissance visits since, including an east-west crossing of the island earlier this year. He had intended to begin his Taiwan 100 Peaks Traverse project this past spring, but local mountaineers advised him to avoid the rainy season and typhoon risks. Their advice prompted him to shift his starting date to November.

Yoki Tanaka on a training hike in Taiwan. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

Interestingly, of Taiwan’s 100 Baiyue peaks, only 99 are now recognized as surpassing 3,000m. The exception is Lushan at 2,981m. It was originally measured at 3,043m but subsequent measurements reduced its elevation. Nevertheless, it remains on the list.

Taiwan’s representative in Japan told Japanese media that the fastest prior completion of the Baiyue by a foreign climber took three years and eight months, spread over multiple trips.

Once Tanaka begins, his expedition website will provide live tracking of his progress across Taiwan.

Jerry Kobalenko is the editor of ExplorersWeb. One of Canada’s premier arctic travelers, he is the author of The Horizontal Everest and Arctic Eden, and has just finished a book about adventures in Labrador. In 2018, he was awarded the Polar Medal by the Governor General of Canada and in 2022, he received the Queen’s Platinum Jubilee Medal for services to exploration.

#8405. I Caught the World-Record Striped Bass During the Eclipse of a Full Moon

Published Oct 28, 2026 10:00 AM EDT

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

Somehow I knew that the full-moon night of July 16, 1981, was going to be special when I left my berth at Lake Montauk, New York, at the eastern extremity of Long Island. My only company on the 24-foot inboard-outboard was 13-year-old Eddie Turpek, who was on his first nighttime bass trip. We left at 9:30 p.m. My friend John Alberda and I had gotten word that a few big stripers had been trolled up the night before, and we felt sure that we could pick up a few fish by drifting live eels. John was fishing from his own boat, so we could cover all the likely areas and call each other on the radio if either of us hit fish.

The southwest breeze died after dark, and we were able to work our drifts perfectly at the end of the flood tide, but there was no action. However, I was marking bass on my recording depthfinder, and I was sure that they would turn on and feed sometime during the night.

It was a great night on the water. The sky was clear, and the full moon made it seem as bright as day until the eclipse started after midnight. The bass were still turned off at the beginning of the ebb. The waiting was too much for young Eddie, and he racked out in the small cabin.

Time after time I worked several spots I had fished for years. Then I tried several narrow ledges near the Great Eastern Buoy. Because bass have been getting scarcer, it has become ever more important to focus on tiny productive areas. Most of these ledges are in deeper water than we used to fish for bass. The drift usually starts over a 40-foot ledge that quickly slopes down to about a 50-foot depth. The big bass seem to hang in very specific slots where they can feed on baitfish coming over the ledge and still stay out of the full force of the moving tide.

When we first started this fishing, it was necessary to use visual ranges on buoys and objects ashore to locate a good area. Then we’d scout around the drop-off with the graph depth recorder and throw out a buoy if we marked fish on the paper. Today the miracle of Loran C has made it all a lot simpler. With the new pinpoint navigation gear, I can go back to an exact spot time after time, after which the graph recorder helps to pinpoint the proper drift for that particular stage of the tide and the wind velocity.

My tackle is simple. I use an Ambassadeur 8600 conventional reel. All the local bass experts favor reels of this type because the push-button release makes it easy to keep the terminal rig just above the bottom as the depth changes. All that’s required to put the reel back into gear is a flip of the reel handle. My rod is a custom-built job on an Ugly Stik blank. The reel had just been filled with some new 40-pound-test Ande blue mono that a friend had given me. My terminal rig consisted of a three-way swivel with a sinker (the size varies with the tide) attached on a short piece of mono, and a long leader to a 6/0 No. 92554 Mustad hollow-point hook. I’ve found that style to be ideal for this fishing. At one time I used stainless steel hooks, but I felt guilty because stainless steel hooks don’t rust out of bass that break off.

The eclipse was still going on at about 3:30 a.m. when my live eel got tapped. Usually big bass tap the eel first, and then it’s necessary to free-spool and drop back instantly so the bass can really grab the eel. I free-spooled and dropped back all right, but just as I got ready to set the hook, the bass bolted with the eel. The result was a massive backlash and a burnt thumb!

I was in big trouble, though I suspected that the fish was only a 30-pounder. The bass pulled out about 130 feet of line, right down to the knotty backlash. I couldn’t give any more line, so I walked forward from stern to bow using the bend in the rod to absorb the surges against the snarled mono. After a while I backed up and retrieved a few yards. By retrieving line this way several times I was able to get the fish within 20 feet of the boat. Then she (all trophy stripers are females) ran all the line out again, right down to the knots.

Once again I was able to stop her at the snarl and used the same procedure to get back some line. I realized now that I was dealing with a bass of respectable size, perhaps in the forties. Soon the fish was near the surface and swimming around the boat. Just as I was looking for my gaff she dived to the bottom with a great surge of power that brought me back to the backlash again. By that time I had the drag screwed down hard, but I couldn’t do anything with the fish. Perhaps, just perhaps, I thought, I’ve hooked a big fifty!

I kept turning the handle of the Ambassadeur, taking in an inch whenever it was available. I’d been fighting the fish for 10 minutes and was worried that the new rod (I’d previously used a somewhat stiffer blank) was too light. However, I worked the bass up again, and I had my four-foot aluminum-handled gaff in hand when the big cow bore down and stripped me right back to the knots again! Now I knew the fish had to be my first sixty. The only other possibility was that I had foul-hooked a medium-size bass in the body or tail. Never before had I experienced four such powerful runs against a stiff drag.

I applied maximum pressure again, and the fish rose on her own. She came up about 100 feet from the boat. I got my first real look at her finning in the moonlight. I reeled carefully, and she came in on her side. There was such a huge expanse of white showing that she didn’t even look like a bass! This was the chance I’d been working for, but when I hit her with the gaff, both rubber grips slipped off the handle and the gaff fell in the water!

The gaff’s hook was still in the fish. I grabbed the handle of the floating gaff, dropped my rod, and used both hands and my back to lift the fish into the boat. I’m six feet tall, weigh about 205 pounds, and pride myself on keeping in good condition, but it took everything I had to swing that fish aboard. As she came over the side I was knocked backward. After 15 minutes of playing her and about 600 yards of drifting, the fish was mine. She made one slap with her tail—a real boom—and she was through. I couldn’t even fit her in my 44-inch cooler. I finally realized that I had the sixty I’d yearned for!

Eddie Turpek was awake now and completely shocked by the size of the first live striper he’d ever seen. I called John Alberda on my CB radio and told him about the huge fish, but John urged me to go on fishing and catch another while they were still hitting. That’s exactly what I did, and on the next drift over the same spot Eddie’s first bass ever hit a 35-pounder. We missed a couple of others before going in at daylight for breakfast.

I was so nervous by that time that I was actually afraid to find out what the fish weighed. At Inlet Marina I showed my bass to veteran night striper charter skipper Frank Braddick, and he could only shake his head. Another night charter captain, Jack Passie, and John Alberda lifted the bass out of my boat with a boom used to unload commercial catches. At that point I had set my heart on 68 pounds, but I was afraid that I was too optimistic. The fish was weighed, and everyone on the dock shouted seventy-five pounds!

The next move was to take the fish to Montauk Marine Basin for weighing on a certified scale. Though I now have a wonderful job running a police patrol boat, I served my apprenticeship as a law-enforcement officer in the toughest areas of my county, and I was involved in many dangerous situations. But nothing shook me up more than the weighing of that bass. What if the Inlet Marina scales were off? Well, they were off, but in the right direction. The bass actually weighed 76 pounds. At 53 inches, the cow was relatively short for such great weight, but the 35½-inch girth made up for that.

Read Next: The Best Lures and Live Baits for Striped Bass

That’s the story of Bob Rocchetta’s fantastic catch in his own words as he told it to me shortly after he brought in the bass that will almost surely be the new all-tackle world-record striped bass. Though the International Game Fish Association hadn’t approved Bob Rocchetta’s record at the time this article went to press (August 1981), it is hard to imagine a refusal.

All of the tackle used in live-eel fishing complies with IGFA regulations, and there are plenty of witnesses to the legitimacy of the catch. Obviously, in this case, identification of the species is not in doubt. Most legitimate catches on sporting tackle are accepted by IGFA if the fish is fought by a single angler. If you’re interested in the rules and procedures, write to IGFA, 3000 East Las Olas Boulevard, Fort Lauderdale, FL 33316.

In 1913 an angler named C. B. Church trolled a 73-pound striped bass up from the hallowed bassing grounds in Vineyard Sound, Massachusetts, to establish an all-tackle record that has been recognized by striper fishermen ever since. To be sure, the IGFA withdrew recognition of Church’s catch in recent years during one of its periodic reviews of records. The reason was that Church’s claim had never been properly documented in accordance with current IGFA procedures. Nevertheless, that’s the record that every striper angler had been shooting at. Until July 17, they all failed.

Actually, there have been a few close calls over the years. The 73-pound record was tied during the 60s by Charlie Cinto while fishing on Capt. Frank Sabatowski’s charterboat off Cuttyhunk Island, Massachusetts. However, the IGFA didn’t recognize that fish because it was caught on wire line and hit a big plug bristling with treble hooks. Then, on October 10, 1969, Edward J. Kirker boated a 72-pounder on an eel at Cuttyhunk, a catch that received official IGFA recognition as the all-tackle and 50-pound-test class world records.

Considering that striped bass in the 60-pound class are caught every year, it’s hard to believe that the popularly accepted 73-pound record endured so long. In addition to the saltwater fisheries on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, stripers are now thriving in fresh water, and there is a real possibility that a landlocked striper may one day top all the records. As it is, the National Fresh Water Hall of Fame currently recognizes a 59-pound 12-ounce bass taken from the Colorado River in Arizona as the landlocked record.

Breaking a record set in 1913 is a remarkable feat, but that’s no reason to think that it can’t be broken again. Very big fish seem to run in cycles and are often particularly abundant as the species declines. No one caught a bluefin tuna weighing 1,000 pounds until 1970. Now quite a few well over that mark are caught every year, though the species is in big trouble. Certainly the Atlantic coastal run of striped bass is in bad shape, but trophy fish seem more abundant than ever—possibly because of lessened competition for food. There are records of stripers that weighed up to 125 pounds caught by commercial fishermen.

To striper enthusiasts, it’s a pleasure to know that the new record fish was caught by an experienced, very skilled fisherman and not by someone who relied on a charterboat captain and mate to do most of the thinking and work. Bob Rocchetta, now 32 years old, caught his first striper in the Narrows area of Conscience Bay, Long Island, when he was 13 years old. Bob had to learn the ropes from old-timers and many magazine articles and books. After graduating from college, he went to work for the Suffolk County police department, and he bought a four-wheel-drive vehicle so that he could surf cast at Montauk. He had to learn that art from scratch but did quite well with bass and bluefish by casting live eels. However, watching boats working areas well beyond his reach, Bob decided that he’d never be satisfied without a boat of his own.

Just as he was getting into a financial position to buy a decent boat, Bob got married, and instead of a boat he had to invest in a home. Nevertheless, he found an old garvey and rebuilt it and an old engine for a total investment of about $250.

To become a better fisherman Bob knew that he needed a bigger boat. He was eyeing one at a local boat dealer’s but couldn’t justify spending the family’s money on it. Then the engine in the old garvey seized up, and it looked as if he’d be beached for quite a while. Returning home dejected, Bob was met by his wife who told him that she’d just made a down payment on the boat with money she’d saved from her own salary.

The boat was soon in the water, and the fisherman was free to expand his horizons until he finally hit the giant cow bass off Great Eastern Rock during an eclipse of the moon.

This story was originally published in the November 1981 issue of Outdoor Life.

#8404. Kili Day 7 – Kosovo Camp to Summit to Mweka Camp

Sun Oct 25 11.7m Climb 3528 From Kosovo Camp (elev 16,000 ft, 4876m) Via Uhuru Peak (elev 19,341 ft, 5895m) To Mweka Camp (elev ~10,000 ft) 6.1m and climb 3514 ft to summit and back 5.6m 14 ft from Kosovo Camp to Mweka Camp

I woke up a little before 11pm. There was definitely ice on the tent. I was wearing my thicker wool socks and less breathable (warmer) gore-tex trail runners. On my legs, I was wearing mid-weight cycling tights, winter fleece cycling tights, my pants, rain pants, and over-the-calf gaiters. On my upper body, I had a long sleeve thermal shirt, my sun hoodie, a fairly lightweight fleece, and my rain jacket. On my head I had my fleece balaclava, and the hood from my sun hoodie. I was wearing my will glove liners with hand warmers in them. Additionally, I had my down puffy jacket and a pair of ski gloves in my backpack.

We headed out at 12:12 on our hike to the summit. It didn’t take long for me to trade my glove liners for ski gloves, moving the handwarmers from one set of gloves to the other. When we started climbing, that ended up being a little much, but was rectified by slipping my balaclava off my head, leaving it around my neck for ready access.

As the night went on, it got much colder. I felt a struggle. I wanted to hike faster to generate more heat to keep warm. And while I was never winded, I wasn’t sure if I could process enough oxygen to speed up. In any case, it was clear that others in the group couldn’t. I really wasn’t that cold, with the exception of my toes. I wished I had brought toe warmers.

It was only a day before full moon, so we had lots of light until the moon set behind Kili, allowing me to follow Herment without either of us using it headlamps.

A nice surprise was when the guides gave us hot tea a couple times. The warmth and sweetness was a real treat.

Stella Point – Finally done the steep climbing

Once we reached Stella point (elev 18,884 ft) on the rim of the crater, the steep climbing was over. It was still a little while before sunrise, but it didn’t look like the whole group would make it to Uhuru Peak (the actual summit) by sunrise. Herment let Florian escort James and me to the summit, hopefully in time for sunrise. We saw sunrise from a couple hundred yards from the summit. The rest of the crew arrived about 10 minutes later.

It was really cold and windy up there. My water bottles had turned to slushie, even though I filled them with warm water before we left camp. All we ended up doing at the peak was take several photos. No Thriller dance.

As I was walking around the rim on the way down, I saw lots of people being assisted by guides. I even saw someone getting a piggy back ride. The guides will do amazing things to help hikers achieve their summit dreams.

Looking down on a glacier and Mt. Meru from the summit

The trip down beat people up. Joel and Dave both had. Joel’s stomach hadn’t felt right for the last couple days. Both of them were able to hike – they still seemed pretty strong – but the guides escorting them provided a little extra stability. Jake and James both complained about their knees hurting. I used my trekking poles to cushion every downhill step. That was one advantage of hiking a couple thousand PCT miles with them.

Long line of people descending from the summit

Back at camp, the staff has brought the chairs out from the dining tent for us to sit in. They served us fresh juice and sang and danced congratulations for us.

Previously on the trip, there had been numerous call and response cheers/yells.

Call: Kilimanjaro Hakuna Response: Matata Call: One team Response: One dream Call: Non-stop Response: To the top

But from this point on, “To the top” was replaced with “To the shower.” I thought that was fun.

We went into our tents to pack up and rest – no time to rest for me after packing up – before being served a brunch.

It was a 5.6 mile hike from Kosovo to Mweka in which we also descended about 6000 feet. With the descent back to camp, that would amount to about 9000 feet of descent in 9 miles, averaging about a 20% grade.

As we passed through Barafu Camp, I was amazed by the number of trekking groups camped there. Talking to our guides, they said that the sites at each camp were usually determined on a first-come first-served basis. They also said that this was as low season, so Barafu was actually much empty than usual. They pointed out more empty sites quite a ways away from all the occupied sites.

It became cloudy/foggy almost as soon as we left Kosovo and stayed that way the entire hike. For a couple friendly sections in the middle (gradual downhill on smooth trail), it felt like we were moving quite slowly.

We actually seemed to do better later on, with worse, steeper trails. Having not been able to eat enough the last couple days, Joel was struggling, not feeling completely steady on his feet. When Herment have him some extra support (hand under the arm), Joel was strong enough to fly down the mountain. Most of the crew wasn’t keeping up with him.

The rock scramble between Barafu and Kosovo camps

Working our way through a rather featureless stretch of moorland

Mweka Camp was in the moorland zone, with lots of small trees. When we got to camp the tents were all set up between the abundant trees. There weren’t any large flat treeless areas.

After getting things set up in my tent and resting for a few minutes, in went to the dining tent for some hot drinks, snacks, and company. But I was the only one there. It want into a few minutes before dinner that anyone else showed up. They were really tired.

I was amazed by how much I saw guides doing for hikers on the mountain. That was especially true watching Herment helping Joel. Granted, Joel is very strong. He also willingly accepted the help and worked with Herment, talking about things like where he was placing his feet on some of the rocky steps. But I was truly impressed to see how effective it was.

#8401. Everest 1971: Ambition, Death, and Dispute

In the spring of 1971, only one party attempted to climb Everest. Led by Norman Dyhrenfurth and Jimmy Roberts, this ambitious expedition planned to split into two groups. One party would go for the steep Southwest Face, while the other would attempt the West Ridge.

It was meant to be as much a test of international cooperation as an extraordinary climbing effort. But what happened turned out to be more complicated and controversial than anyone had expected.

Before the team even arrived in Nepal, the venture was heavily commercialized and advertised to the public. The BBC secured exclusive television rights and embedded a nine-person film crew directly into the expedition. At the same time, the British newspaper rights were sold to The Sunday Times, which sent along prominent journalists like Murray Sayle. The media machinery relentlessly hyped the expedition beforehand, boldly framing the climb as a mere formality and setting public expectations for a historic success.

The expedition itself came from a merger of two plans. A British-Norwegian group asked Roberts to lead a Southwest Face attempt. Dyhrenfurth was already organizing the same route, so they joined forces. As the combined team was large, they decided to try two routes at once.

The Southwest Face was the main goal, specifically aiming for a direct, vertical line (a direttissima), while the other group targeted the complete, aesthetic West Ridge route. Both goals were very difficult, and climbers chose their preferred route.

Jimmy Roberts in Nepal. Photo: The Nepal Times

The Southwest Face team included British climbers Dougal Haston and Don Whillans, Japanese climbers Naomi Uemura and Reizo Ito, and others. The West Ridge team included Austrian Wolfgang Axt, Swiss climbers Michel and Yvette Vaucher, Norwegian climbers Odd Eliassen and Jon Teigland, American David Isles, and Indian Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna. Frenchman Pierre Mazeaud and Italian Carlo Mauri later joined the West Ridge side.

In total, the whole expedition had 31 foreign climbers from a dozen countries, as well as several Sherpas, including Ang Phurba and Sonam Girme. According to early planning notes, neither leader had personal summit ambitions. Both described themselves as the older men of the team.

The Southwest Face of Everest. Photo: Wikimedia

Base Camp was established on March 22, 1971, at 5,425m. Both teams worked through the Khumbu Icefall. Dyhrenfurth later said it was in the most difficult and dangerous state he had ever seen it. They set up Advance Base Camp on the Western Cwm, then separated.

The Southwest Face team pushed higher. The West Ridge team, with Axt as coordinator, began setting up their own camps, although supplies arrived slowly. Some of the West Ridge climbers didn’t want to carry heavy loads. A long storm in late April made conditions worse for both teams and delayed everything by two to three weeks. Dyhrenfurth’s own account in the American Alpine Journal confirms the early harmony among the team and the exceptional difficulties of the Icefall that spring.

The 1971 Everest expedition. Photo: ‘Surrender to Everest’/imdb.com

On April 18, Bahuguna and Axt of the West Ridge team were descending from a high camp in a storm at about 7,000m. They were not tied to each other. Axt had left his harness and climbing rope higher up to save weight, knowing fixed ropes were already in place. He crossed a long fixed-rope traverse by hand, waited for Bahuguna, saw him wave, then continued down because he was exhausted. He later heard screams and raised the alarm.

A rescue party reached Bahuguna still clipped to the fixed rope, about 25m from easier ground. He had lost a mitten and a crampon, and his face was covered by ice. Attempts to lower him failed in the storm and darkness, and he finally died of cold and exhaustion. Bahuguna’s fingers and face were crusted with ice, his eyes were wide, and he could not recognize Whillans or speak.

Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna on the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal

According to Roberts’ report in the Himalayan Database, the rescuers had to leave Bahuguna because it would be completely dark in 10 minutes, and the others would freeze too. Roberts later described the death as the result of a series of mistakes by Bahuguna and Axt themselves, and noted that allowing them to go so high alone had been a factor.

Bahuguna’s body was later recovered and cremated near Base Camp.

Dyhrenfurth held an inquiry after the fatal incident. Axt said that the fixed ropes made roping up unnecessary and that he didn’t realize how serious things were until the screams. He later explained that if he had stayed longer, he risked losing his own fingers and toes.

“What should I do? One hour later and I am frozen,” he said. He added that he couldn’t pull Bahuguna himself and had to go down for fresh men.

Mazeaud called it murder through negligence. Dyhrenfurth agreed that Axt should have gone back to look, but said that it was easy to judge after the event. Roberts noted that Bahuguna’s death was very sad but didn’t determine the expedition’s final outcome.

Norman Dyhrenfurth, Carlo Mauri, Yvette Vaucher, Reizo Ito, Pierre Mazeaud, and Michale Vaucher in ‘Surrender to Everest’ (1971). Photo: imdb.com

After the death and the storm, most of the remaining West Ridge climbers (especially Mazeaud, Mauri and the Vauchers) wanted to abandon both hard routes and switch to the normal South Col route. They said that it was more practical and gave a better chance of reaching the summit.

Many others, including most of the Southwest Face group and the leading Sherpas, believed that those climbers mainly wanted personal success: first Frenchman, first Italian, or first woman. A vote that included the Sherpas went strongly in favor of putting all remaining effort into the Southwest Face. The West Ridge group said the decision was a plot to keep them off the summit, so the press would stay focused on the Southwest Face.

Camp 2. Pumori on the left, with snow-and-ice slopes leading to the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal

Mazeaud’s radio message said that they expected him — a French member of parliament — to work like a Sherpa for Anglo-Saxons and Japanese. He said France had been insulted. Yvette Vaucher called the decision monstrous and said she had lost Everest and her friends at the same time.

According to one account, Roberts told Mazeaud to leave during a loud argument. The four went home in early May, ending further work on the West Ridge. Isles and Teigland later said that the decision to cancel the West Ridge climb, made in a highly emotional moment after Bahuguna’s death, was a great mistake. Teigland said he had dreamed of the West Ridge for two years.

A virus, diagnosed by some as mononucleosis, spread through the camps and forced many climbers down, including Dyhrenfurth. Bad weather continued to block supplies. With the West Ridge group gone and fewer people left, Haston and Whillans kept pushing on the Southwest Face. Japanese climbers and Sherpas carried heavy loads high on the mountain. Camps were placed up to approx. 8,290m.

Haston and Whillans fixed ropes partway into a chimney in the Rock Band but ran out of rope, oxygen, and food. According to Roberts, they placed Camp 6 at 8,290m and were making progress every day. He said they could have traversed onto the South Buttress and reached the summit that way in one day, but that was not the route they had come to climb. Extreme cold hampered them. They needed another camp higher up. They turned back 450m short of the summit on May 21.

Roberts later said weather was the basic cause of failure: Once it goes bad, it affects everything else. He described the expedition as 50 percent successful. They failed to summit, but those who stayed worked well together.

Roberts said that he was bitterly disappointed after three years of work, but apart from Bahuguna’s death, he had nothing to regret. He criticized Schloemmer for contributing almost nothing and said that Axt was asked to come up and help on the Southwest Face but thought it over and went down instead.

Haston called claims that the Austrians were ready to help “complete balls.” He said that when they asked for support at Camp 5, Schloemmer replied that he needed a Sherpa to carry his personal gear. Haston added that he and Whillans were the only ones who could push hard enough to get the route going, and that the Japanese were the only others with real high-Himalayan experience.

Uemura said that he and Ito helped by carrying loads because that was their obligation, and that if the weather had been good, the expedition could have succeeded. After the 1971 expedition, Uemura decided to always climb solo thereafter.

Axt and Schloemmer complained there was no real authority above Advance Base Camp. Axt said the two British stayed high for three weeks and monopolized the lead, and that without a coordinator to rotate people, there was no room for others. He said if there had been good organization on the Face, he could have succeeded. Isles and Teigland said the international aspect had nothing to do with the failure.

The problems came from personalities and the emotional decision after the death. Mazeaud and the Vauchers maintained that the leaders had broken the original plan of two routes and prevented them from reaching the summit for publicity reasons. Dyhrenfurth said the experiment in international climbing was only partially successful, but cooperation had been good until the argument over the route. He noted that the United Nations had tried international cooperation for a long time and had not done too well, either.

In their interesting and detailed post-climb article titled Post-Mortem of an International Expedition for Mountain magazine (later reprinted by The Himalayan Club), authors Ken Wilson and Mike Pearson traced exactly how the initial merger and massive team size doomed the expedition from the start. They concluded that the 1971 expedition’s collapse was primarily driven by severe natural forces, specifically adverse weather and illness, rather than interpersonal friction. They also attributed systemic blame to organizers for combining distinct climbing factions into an unmanageable, oversized team.

Memorial at Everest in 1971 for Harsh Bahuguna. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal

The questions remain: Was Bahuguna’s death mainly the result of mistakes by the two men involved, or something the leaders should have prevented? Did the decision to drop the West Ridge and focus on the Southwest Face save the expedition or destroy it? And was the international idea itself the problem, or simply the mix of strong personalities, bad weather, and the pressure of being on Everest?

KrisAnnapurna is a writer with ExplorersWeb.

Kris has been writing about history and tales in alpinism, news, mountaineering, and news updates in the Himalaya, Karakoram, etc., for with ExplorersWeb since 2021. Prior to that, Kris worked as a real estate agent, interpreter, and translator in criminal law. Now based in Madrid, Spain, she was born and raised in Hungary.

ExplorersWeb is part of AllGear Digital's portfolio of media brands.
