#8330. How to Beat the Worst Case of Buck Fever, According to This Archery Pro

Published Nov 2, 2026 11:29 AM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

When John Dudley was a kid, still learning how to hunt in Illinois, he had an encounter with a big buck that changed the trajectory of his bowhunting life. Dudley was hunting with a compound bow that was set too heavy—though he was able to draw the bow fine during practice.

When a stud buck casually walked into range, Dudley pulled with all of his might but he couldn’t get the bowstring back.

“He literally walks like 10 feet underneath my treestand … and I freakin’ pulled and tugged on that bow while my knees were clacking together,” Dudley says. “I had that thing pointed straight up in the air trying to pull it back. My heartbeat was hitting so hard I honestly thought I was going to need some stents or something by the time it was done.”

At first Dudley thought there was some sort of malfunction with his bow. As the buck walked off he examined the cams and the string. Then, with the deer (and the nerves) long gone, he simply grabbed the bow and drew it back without issue.

“You know when you have that nightmare that you can’t scream, well this was a living nightmare of John Dudley not being able to pull his bow back because he had buck fever that bad,” he says.

Fast forward a couple decades and Dudley is now an accomplished pro archer, a veteran whitetail hunter, and perhaps the most popular archery instructor in the country. Since that fateful Illinois bowhunt Dudley has learned a lot about shooting well under pressure during hunts and competitions. His hard-earned knowledge (which you can hear all about in the podcast episode below) will help you shoot your best when that big buck steps into your setup this fall.

When Dudley is sitting in his treestand he visualizes all the good scenarios that he hopes will happen. But this is far more than daydreaming about a giant buck turning broadside. Just like an athlete preparing for all the motions of a game, he visualizes each specific movement he’ll make under each possible scenario.

“I visualize myself getting a couple good ranges on him [as the buck comes in],” Dudley says. “I visualize making sure I grab my release the right way. I’m pivoting my feet the right way. And [the buck] is doing his thing as I’m able to slowly draw. And then I think about my shot process.”

With all the waiting we do in a treestand, there’s plenty of time to visualize and plan for a variety of shot scenarios.

“Sometimes I’m in a stand for two weeks before I have an opportunity and I’m constructing these things in my mind,” Dudley says. “You literally end up creating a vision. And when that happens, your conscious mind is already thinking about all the processes [you need to execute].”

In other words, when that giant buck finally does show, you won’t feel shocked, because you’ve already visualized it hundreds or thousands of times.

It’s almost a guarantee that every professional shooter in any shooting discipline has a shot process. As Dudley describes it, this is simply a series of words he says in his mind that coincide with actions he executes in order to make a perfect shot. Dudley’s shot process is this: 1) Stance; 2) Grip; 3) Shoulder; 4) Anchor; 5) Peep; 6) Pull and Finish.

Dudley learned the importance of having a process from Olympic medalist Lanny Bassham who wrote the book “With Winning in Mind” (which Dudley recommends for any shooter). The key is that saying the words and executing the movements is the work of the conscious mind. Activating the conscious mind helps prevent a shooter from “going on autopilot,” rushing the shot, punching the trigger, or simply blacking out.

You can and should adapt a shot process for your own needs. For example, OL gear editor and competitive archer Scott Einsmann’s process is: 1) Anchor; 2) Get it there (his cue to just get the aiming portion done with); 3) Feel alignment; 4) Okay, my shot can break anytime.

If you have a bad habit of getting excited and drawing back wildly, you might want to add a word like “smooth” to your shot process. If you have a tendency to get anxious about your pin floating around the target then you might want to add the word “float” to your process—reassuring yourself that it’s ok to let that pin float. The key is to have a shot process that works for you and to follow it on every single shot. Especially that shot on a giant buck.

Reciting a mantra is similarly useful. Just like running through a shot process, a mantra gives control to your conscious mind. You must choose to say your mantra.

For competitions, Dudley’s mantra is: “I shoot Xs because they make me feel good.”

When an animal comes in during a hunting scenario Dudley says the word “checkmate” to himself.

“When the animal presents that shot … I’m thinking ‘checkmate’, you know, game over,” he says. “Because that’s a positive affirmation that really reinforces your conscious thought process rather than sitting there thinking ‘Oh man this is the biggest buck I’ve ever seen.’”

But these tactics don’t eliminate the excitement and subsequent pressure you’ll likely feel when you see a shooter buck. The real key is training yourself to get comfortable while shooting under pressure.

“Think of buck fever like a hot bathtub,” Dudley says. “It might be scalding hot when you first put your toe into it. But if you just breathe and ease into it, eventually you’re going to acclimate and that water is going to feel OK.”

This is why Dudley recommends shooting in archery tournaments so you can “put yourself in a situation where you feel like you’ve been in the boiling pot before.”

If you have a high deer population where you hunt, or you just need to fill the freezer, shooting a few does with your bow is also a great way to get used to shooting under pressure. Your potential case of buck fever will likely be less extreme if you’ve cleanly killed a few does earlier in the season.

On the flipside don’t crank up the pressure on yourself during a hunt. In the treestand you want to feel positive, confident, and mellow.

“Don’t apply self-induced pressure,” Dudley says. “That’s the only pressure you really have control over. Most of the time buck fever or target anticipation is from pressure that you’re applying to yourself. It’s not like the animal is shooting [pressure] up at you. The best thing you can do is just positive self affirmation.”

In the days leading up to a big deer hunt Dudley makes sure to get in some practice sessions from a seated position and from an elevated position. This is because most whitetail shots will be from a ground blind or a treestand.

It’s important to know that shooting downhill or shooting from a seated position will induce more pin movement while you’re holding on target. But that’s OK if you’re used to it.

“It’s about mentally getting over that [pin movement],” Dudley says.

But there’s also value in practicing at long range even if you won’t be shooting at long range during a hunt. This is because flaws in your shooting will be more apparent at longer distances, and recognizing those flaws will help you correct them.

“I actually practice more at 80 than any distance I shoot at,” Dudley says.

Dudley believes in Chuck Adam’s theory that your effective range as a bowhunter is half the distance of your effective range in the backyard. In other words, if you’re able to shoot 8-inch groups at 80 yards in the backyard, you’ll be able to shoot 8-inch groups at 40 yards under a hunting scenario.

Plus, practicing at long range will boost your confidence when you move in for those realistic 20- and 30-yard shots. And really, at this point in the season, all practice is about building confidence for that moment of truth.

“Always practice at distances where you have confidence,” Dudley says. “Especially when you’re trying to instill confidence.”

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.

In the fall of 2025, under banner-blue skies, I backpacked into a remote Utah canyon to help celebrate my friend Ace’s birthday. #8328. ‘There Was No Controlling that Fish.’ Two Buddies Land One of the Largest Blue Marlin Ever Caught in Southern California

Published Nov 2, 2026 12:56 PM EST

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

California fishing buddies Mike Mackenback and Matt Mackinga headed their 20-foot fishing boat into the Pacific at about daybreak on October 25. They were targeting wahoo, which had been hitting off the coast of southern California, but they were about to catch something much bigger.

“We ran south, looking for water temperature breaks where we believed wahoo would be found,” Mackenback tells Outdoor Life. “We were trolling by about 8 a.m., with three lines out – one a deep diving plug, a surface-skipping ‘Black Bart’ lure on another line, and a far back shotgun line with a lure.

“We were about 12 miles from San Pedro, trolling on a beautiful slick-ocean with clear water about 1,500-feet deep.”

Mackenback is a veteran marine boatman, having worked on tugboats and as a merchant marine. He knows boats and fishing and trolled fast at 8 knots for wahoo along a water temperature break from 73 to 75 degrees.

“The fish came up and smashed the surface skipping Black Bart lure about 30 minutes after we started,” says Mackenback, 29, who is now a real estate agent in Redondo Beach. “I thought at first it was a striped marlin until it jumped, then I knew it was huge – there was no controlling that fish as it ran 400 yards of line off a reel in one minute.”

Mackenback held the trolling rod which was set with a Shimano 30 Tiagra reel. It was spooled with 80-pound test Spectra braided line, with a top-shot of 50-pound test monofilament, and a 25-foot 200-pound test fluorocarbon leader.

Mackenback quickly realized they had hooked a huge blue marlin that was rapidly taking all the line off his reel, which was rigged for wahoo and much smaller striped marlin.

“I gave the rod to Matt, he went to the bow to fight the fish, and I turned the boat to chase after it,” Mackenback says. “The marlin was jumping and racing away, and I chased it with the boat for a few minutes while Matt tried to gain some of the line it took on those blistering runs.”

Matt kept the line tight on the marlin, and Mackenback got closer to the fish with his boat.

Then the marlin dove deep as it got a second wind during the fight.

“It almost spooled us twice,” says Mackenback. “Matt would gain line fighting the fish. I’d stay over it with the boat, and then it would dive deep again, and again, and again.

“We traded back and forth fighting the fish with the rod. We had no fighting belt or harness – just a small slide on the rod butt cushion. I didn’t think there was a 10 percent chance we’d catch and release it. My wahoo tackle wasn’t built for a giant blue marlin.”

One hour into the epic battle, the anglers decided to just follow the blue with their boat, trying to tire it out over time.

Almost two hours into the marlin battle they gained enough line on the fish that they could see its shiny blue color deep below in clear water. Then it dove deep again, and it was another 45 minutes before they spotted the fish near their boat.

“Suddenly the line went slack, and I thought it was gone,” Mackenback says. “We saw the swivel to the leader, grabbed it, and hauled on the leader to get it close.

“The fish was whipped, I knew it was gone as I was holding 600-pounds of blue marlin beside my 20-foot boat.”

They tried multiple times to revive the marlin for release. But the big blue fought until it was dead. There was no way they could get the marlin pulled up into their Grady-White boat. So, they lashed it to the side of their boat and ran slowly back to San Pedro’s Cabrillo Way Marina where they’d left that morning.

They notified the marina they were coming in with a huge marlin, and a crane was waiting for the anglers to haul the fish up and weigh it.

Their blue marlin measured more than 13 feet and weighed 595 pounds. It’s one of the largest blues ever caught off Southern California. Giant blues are believed to have moved into the region due to unusual water and weather conditions in this El Nino year.

In September 2015, a 648-pound blue marlin was caught 40 miles off San Diego by anglers aboard the boat Pegasus. A 692-pound blue was caught also during an El Nino year off the coast of Southern California.

Read Next: My Outboard Died — Just as We Hooked Up with a Giant Marlin

Mackenback and Mackinga cleaned and processed their marlin, and had some of it for dinner that night.

“We spent hours processing the marlin into steaks, and gave a lot of it to neighbors and friends,” says Mackenback. “We grilled marlin steaks that night and had a great cookout.”

Bob McNally has been an outdoor writer since shortly after the earth’s crust cooled. He has written 12 outdoor books, more than 5,000 outdoor magazine stories (including many for Outdoor Life) and more newspaper outdoor columns and features than there are hairs on a grizzly bear.

#8327. Why 5 Days of Heat Training May Be Enough

In a perfect world, we’d spend the month (or more) leading up to toasty races like the Javelina Jundred training to handle the heat. Actually, in a perfect world, we would heat train all year round to reap the potential physiological rewards, such as increased plasma volume, and maybe even improved Vo2 max and lactate threshold.

But we’re not all pros with flexible schedules and not everyone lives in the Arizona desert, where the average high is around 82 degrees Fahrenheit.

The last thing any of us want is to succumb to hot conditions, much less end up in the med tent, because we were too busy for heat training. But many heat training protocols call for weeks and even months of heat sessions to induce positive physiological adaptations; time we don’t often have to spare while juggling work, sleep, family obligations, and the ever-important logging of miles.

So when I found out that endurance gravel cyclist Metheven Bond claimed he managed to acclimate to the heat in only 5 days, I was curious: Can runners implement a similar protocol?

Off his 5-day protocol, Bond rode for 43 hours and 6 minutes with no sleep through the sweltering desert of Eastern Andalusia to finish sixth overall in The Badlands. If you’re unfamiliar with the gravel cycling race, Badlands runs some 507 miles across the Gorafe and Tabernas deserts in Spain,where temperatures regularly exceed 104 F.

To find out exactly what he did and how it may apply to runners, I spoke with Bond himself, as well as Aline Barre, a competitive ultra-cyclist and triathlete with a master’s degree in Sports Performance Analysis, and Daniel Snape, Ph.D., a performance physiologist, accredited sport and exercise scientist, and researcher in endurance and environmental physiology.

Earlier this year, Bond, who races for Ribble Outliers gravel cycling team, competed in some hot races in Spain and Switzerland. Temperatures reached nearly 97 degrees.

“I fell apart even though I thought I did everything right,” he told Trail Runner. “I froze all of my bottles and was drinking over a liter an hour for hydration, but my power still dropped off a cliff, my heart rate was through the roof, and I couldn’t think properly. I knew it was from the heat.”

Racing in hot conditions can compromise endurance capacity, and, as Bond discovered the hard way, it’s not always enough to rely on mid-race cooling. “I needed to find ways to adapt so the heat bothers me less, so I looked into heat acclimation.”

The goal of heat acclimation is to cause adaptations that allow the body to more effectively function in high temps. That process involves exposing the body to hot conditions that cause core body temperature to rise. Done long and consistently enough adaptations can include a lowered heart rate and body temperature, a higher sweat rate, improved performance, and better heat resilience.

“Before Badlands, I looked at the weather forecast and knew the heat was going to be bad. I’m in the North of England where it’s colder and somehow needed to get ready to be thrown into the heat,” Bond said. He visited the lab of Precision Fuel and Hydration, a sponsor of Ribble Outliers, for a focused heat training block. There, the Precision team implemented a protocol before Badlands consisting of five one-hour heat training sessions of cycling in a heat chamber set to 102 degrees over five consecutive days.

The team monitored Bond’s performance markers—such as heat transfer and skin temperature—throughout the block via sensors like the Core 2 Thermal Sensor, which mounts to any heart rate strap and transmits data in real-time to an app or wearable.

As the sessions progressed, Bond was able to push harder without a corresponding increase in cardiovascular effort. The result: Higher power output, lower average heart rate, and improved resistance to the fatigue of heat stress.

Aline Barre is a cyclist, triathlete, and endurance performance lead at Core. Like Bond, Barre had an equally unpleasant experience racing in the heat.

“My first endurance race was Ironman Frankfurt. For training, I didn’t do any running in the heat,” Barre said. “Race day was super hot and I was cooked. I was drinking a lot, but I felt horrible during the run. I was so afraid of the heat that I went to Finland for my second Ironman.”

Barre concluded the heat was holding her back—until she focused on acclimation. “Heat training is even more important for ultrarunners than endurance cyclists. In most cases, it’s easier to cycle in the heat than to run in the heat,” she said. “That’s because you move forward at a faster pace when riding a bike than running, creating substantially more airflow to help cool your skin through sweat evaporation.”

Combine this with the fact that running creates higher metabolic heat than cycling and it’s no wonder that medical teams see more cases of heat stroke at endurance running events than at cycling races. Additionally, some studies suggest that female athletes may require a slightly longer heat exposure period (10-14 days) or stronger heat stimulus relative to male athletes (seven days) to fully develop certain adaptations, particularly those related to sweating

“Most athletes see the majority of gains after 4-5 heat sessions and the full adaptation after doing 10 to 12 sessions within two to six weeks,” Barre said.

But for Bond, five days was enough. Performance physiologist and researcher Daniel Snape explains why.

“When you heat train, the main response you get is an increase in your blood plasma volume. For Bond to increase his plasma volume across those five days is a very normal and achievable response,” Snape said. Snape is part of a team of experts at the Health and Performance Hub at Leeds Beckett University. He works with professional ultrarunners like 2025 UTMB winners Tom Evans and Ruth Croft to develop specific heat acclimation strategies.

“Also you’re becoming more familiar with the heat, so your body doesn’t have that: ‘Oh no, I’ve got to increase my heart rate to cope with this stressor’ fight or flight response. That’s why five days straight was enough time for Bond to adapt and be able to hold a higher power output at a lower heart rate.”

While five days may be enough for a professional male endurance athlete who has a stellar baseline and access to a heat chamber, core body temperature sensor, and a team of experts, it might not be for many ultrarunners.

“Even I had to continue with three sessions per week of heat acclimation at home to maintain the adaptation, riding wrapped up in layers. I kept this up until a week before Badlands, when it was time to taper,” Bond said. He also points out that while significant adaptations can occur in five days, a few weeks is preferable for the mental preparation.

“The more times you train in the heat, the more confidence you have when you face it on race day,” he said. “You think: ‘Okay, it’s uncomfortable, but not as uncomfortable because I’ve been exposed to it. I’m used to this’.”

If you’re short on time and you want to have some semblance of conditioning going into Javelina or another toasty ultra, Core has a simple but mighty indoor heat training plan to build heat into your workouts with five sessions over 2 weeks. (See below.) It includes a long run where you start cool, then dress in warm layers for the last 75 minutes, as well as an easy 50-minute run where you run cool, but add a 30-minute passive heat session after.

The long run  is best done inside on a treadmill, but a smart trainer, stationary bike, or even a rowing machine will work as well. For your layers, you’ll need clothing that is non-permeable and traps heat against your body,  such as a heat suit, thermal top, down jacket, rain jacket, fleecy sweat suit, and/or wool hat. As a last resort, Bond recommends using a trash bag with holes cut out for your head and arms.

The passive heat session consists of time in a sauna, steam room, hot tub, or even the bathtub. If you’re preparing for a hot desert race, a sauna is the way to go if you can access one. Research shows that repeated post-exercise sauna sessions can enhance key components of heat adaptation, such as blood plasma volume and thermoregulatory efficiency. To prepare for a trail run in the tropics, a steam room or steamy bath are the best options.

Alternatively, you can do a micro heat training block that includes five days of only passive heat sessions immediately after your normal training runs, when your heart rate and core temperature are still elevated. According to Dr. Snape, even this can be effective at improving performance come race day.

The benefits of heat training extend beyond simply ramping up for a 100-miler under the desert sun, however.

“With the sauna for example, we know that if you do a hill workout, then go into the sauna, it has some muscle hypertrophy benefits, helping with recovery,” Snape said. “We also know that saunas improve your immune function. And if you do a sauna session late at night, it can actually improve sleep quality.”

Before starting a heat training plan, you should already be used to training for a minimum of four days per week and at least four hours of total weekly volume. You should also be able to complete a 60-to 75-minute run workout.

“You can do heat training right up until taper week. But don’t start heat training too close to your race. If you start two weeks before your race, the chance is quite high that you’ll expose your body to unnecessary fatigue because it’s not used to the heat,” Barre said. “We recommend starting four to five weeks out. During heat sessions, monitor your skin temperature, sweat rate, and heart rate so you don’t overdo it or get a heat illness, which can be life-threatening if you’re not careful. And hydrate before, during, and after heat sessions.”

It’s important to note that even if you use a Core sensor as part of your heat acclimation protocol, you can’t wear it into saunas or your bathtub at home, so there’s no way of knowing your internal body temperature during those passive sessions. As such, active and passive heat training should only be done when someone else is with you or in a nearby room.

“Any heat acclimation protocol will induce a training stress. Respect it as an additional thing to recover from,” Snape said. “That means you will have to take some training off the table elsewhere when undergoing a heat training block. That could mean cutting nine hours of running down to eight hours.”

Heat acclimation doesn’t have to be a part-time job. If you have time for 7-14 heat sessions during or after the run workouts on your training plan, you should experience full adaptations. But if you only have time for a 5-day heat adaptation block, it’s still more beneficial than not training for the heat at all, helping you develop a base adaptation that can make it mentally and physically easier to stay on pace when the heat is on.

#8326. Traversing the Saiga Silk Road

As we skidded off the main road and onto a mud path maintained only by tire treads, lines began to blur.

Flanking our two-track trail were a series of parallel lanes no more than a foot wide, which forked, merged, and crisscrossed our own. In the distance, I saw what looked like a ghost train, faintly visible and thrust forward by howling Siberian winds.

Through borrowed binoculars, I soon got my first glimpse of an ancient tableau, seemingly untouched since Neanderthals roamed the earth. On the far horizon, hundreds of nomadic travelers pierced the frigid air with their ringed horns, inhaling the brittle shards through Snuffleupagus snouts as they sprinted across the desolate steppe.

Watching them charge through the treeless plain at full bore, I was reminded of a saying I’d heard shortly before arriving in this remote corner of Kazakhstan: “The saiga is a freedom-loving animal.”

Since time immemorial, saiga antelope have blazed trails across Central Asia while other civilizations rose and fell around them. They once inhabited a world dominated by woolly mammoths, saber-toothed cats, and giant deer with antlers 12 feet across—and outlived them all. When pioneering human caravans first attempted to navigate this unforgiving land, they considered the saigas to be their guides.

Ahead of my arrival, seasonal rains transformed once-green grasslands into sludge punctuated by tufts of withering brush. Driving through such muck is, I would soon discover, akin to controlled hydroplaning. The steering wheel bucked wildly as our tires swerved, shredding deep into the gunk and desperately gripping anything remotely solid enough to push off from.

In the front seats were Alexandr and Albert, two team members from the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan, or ACBK. Between them, they have more than twenty-five years of experience following saigas across the steppe, and I’d arranged to join them for the western leg of one of their field audits.

Our visit was timed to coincide with the rutting season, a critical part of the year for saigas. This is a gathering time, when antelope from across the region sprint together in massive single-file lines, before congregating for a series of competitive battles and subsequent mating rituals.

For males, it’s a time for strutting and headbutting to demonstrate one’s physical prowess to female onlookers—an activity so energy-intensive that many will forget to eat and keel over from extreme physical exhaustion. For females, this is a time of choosing. In addition to assessing fitness, they pay particular attention to one distinctive feature: a potential mate’s floppy, elongated nose. The saigas’ sniffers are essential for filtering out dust in the semidesert plains and for warming frigid winter air before it reaches their lungs. A large nose is the ultimate sign of virility, so as the males marched into these annual gatherings, they were doing everything they could to accentuate their schnozzes.

Because of the saigas’ preference for large-scale migrations across a landscape almost entirely devoid of trees, they have long been a favorite of global wildlife trackers. The isolation and starkness of the saiga world is a strength when it comes to GPS collars, which deliver a reliable stream of daily pings without risk of visual obstruction. Prior to such breakthroughs, conservationists would sometimes spend weeks roaming the boundless steppe unsuccessfully trying to locate the nomadic herds.

The wildlife sanctuary we were traveling through was created only a year prior, with its boundaries informed by tracking data that Albert and his team personally collected. He seemed pleased that the animals were continuing to use the newly designated space as intended. Standing along the roadside, Alexandr spotted a stream of the famously skittish ungulates wrapping around the contours of the earth. As he did, ripping wind and snow started blowing in sideways—the outer ring of an encroaching storm.

These were no fluffy flakes. This was the harsh, crunchy ice of a walk-in freezer, which instantly hardened our truck’s caked-on mud like liquid nitrogen.

Seemingly unperturbed by the dropping barometer, Albert chirped, “Who’s hungry?” Setting up an impromptu picnic, he and Alexandr dug into a prepared meal of fresh bread, tea, and dried meats of unknown provenance. In a muted attempt to thaw my face, I opted to guzzle spicy instant noodles.

A tradition of nomadism has loomed large in this corner of the world since at least the Early Iron Age. The very word kazakh is thought to be derived from the Turkic word qaz, which means “wanderer” or “vagabond.” For millennia, small human groups routinely migrated to higher altitudes in the hot summer months, where melting snow made for abundant water and greenery, before returning to sheltered valleys ahead of winter’s whipping winds. At various times of the year, disparate nomads would also congregate for formal meetings and large cultural festivals, complete with physical challenges like wrestling and tug-of-war. When the gatherings were finished, the nomads dispersed once again.

Historical analysis has shown that nomads’ seasonal migrations and time-honed transit corridors may have helped pave the way for portions of the Great Silk Road, which was less a singular route than an ever-evolving web of pathways and bypasses that linked together reliable stopovers. At the Silk Road’s peak, this corner of western Kazakhstan along the fertile banks of the Ural River became a vital transcontinental crossroads. To this day, the river still serves as a natural boundary between Asia and Europe, meaning this part of Kazakhstan is, quite literally, where East meets West.

The land above the Caspian Sea also served as a main artery that linked together key transit points. Strategic settlements along the riverbank allowed weary caravans to rest their heads, unwind in large public baths, exchange knowledge, stock up on essential supplies, and regroup before moving onward.

Among overland voyagers traversing the continental divide, saigas have long been spoken of with an almost mythical reverence. Cave paintings of the antelope created as far back as the seventh century BCE depict them as resilient, elusive, and charismatic. Expert navigators who embody the true spirit of a most inhospitable terrain.

In human society, traditional nomadic practices persisted even as the land itself was variously claimed and reclaimed by Turkic tribes, Genghis Khan, and the Russian Empire. Only with the rise of the Soviet Union in the twentieth century did mandatory sedentarization efforts successfully manage to lock nomadic people in place, force them to farm, and extinguish a cultural flame that had burned brightly for millennia. Denied the ability to live in perpetual motion, people’s navigational muscles began to atrophy.

This transition was viewed by many as an inevitable shift toward “modernization,” but it also represented a significant diversion from our own history as a species. Of the roughly 300,000 years that Homo sapiens have existed, we spent the first 288,000 of them living in small, mobile groups that followed the migratory patterns of other animals. Forcing nomads into agricultural plots was also a colossal failure because much of the steppe soil was unsuitable for growing crops, which is why so many people were nomadic in the first place. Iconic filmmaker Werner Herzog once remarked that “whatever went wrong and makes our civilization something doomed is the departure from the nomadic life.”

Whether by choice or necessity, most Kazakh people now lead stationary lives in urban centers. The world that nomads once freely roamed has also been feverishly transformed, not only by agriculture but through the construction of new roads and railways.

For the saigas, whose nomadic days never ceased, these new layers now represent an existential threat.

With the weather taking a turn for the worse, Albert and Alexandr ultimately decided to call it a day and start fresh in the morning. After a blistering drive through whiteout conditions, we hunkered down in a tiny village less than 10 miles from the Russian border, where Albert pulled out his laptop and showed me how saiga movements have changed over the years.

“They would routinely trek hundreds of miles as part of an expansive migratory route across the Eurasian steppe,” he said. “Saigas could be found from the Caucasus Mountains to Mongolia, and everywhere in between.”

For millennia, they lived with few barriers and obstructions on the landscape. Then, seemingly overnight, rattling railways and roaring roads began to crisscross the region, fragmenting the saigas into smaller, more isolated groups. As the interior steppe got more accessible to vehicles and passengers, development begat more development.

On his screen, Albert clicked open a recent map that showed how a population of GPS-collared saigas once routinely traveled deep into Uzbekistan before being unceremoniously clipped off by a new rail line in 2014. The data from the years prior to the railway’s construction showed a flurry of squiggly lines representing individual animals zipping back and forth with the seasons. The post-construction slide showed those same animals spinning around despondently on the northern side of the tracks, while the fresh grasses and water they had come to rely on withered away to the south.

Such interruptions can lead to a complete collapse in spatial knowledge—a loss that science writer Ben Goldfarb once wrote is “as thorough as the erasure of a language.” Just as human nomads forced to stay in one place eventually lost connection to the physical landmarks of their ancestors’ journeys, young saigas learn where they can reliably find food and shelter, as well as places to stay away from, through active participation and observation. This cultural exchange keeps their world in orbit and is one of the reasons they have been successful at navigating a terrain fatal to so many before them. As the land they know is cleaved and partitioned, whole stretches of the Saiga Silk Road begin to fade from memory.

To unwind this damage, Albert’s team has partnered with the Kazakh government to construct dozens of saiga-friendly crossing points, where slightly sloping dirt ramps rise up to match the height of the train tracks, making it appear from a distance as though there’s a natural gap in the rail line. Cattle-guard fences positioned far away from the crossings ensure that trains and saigas never actually run into each other at these intersections, which would shatter the illusion of safety.

ACBK has also worked with the Uzbek government to reshape its border fences from a barbed-wire wall to an X-shaped barricade that blocks vehicles from driving through but leaves just enough space for saigas to pass. Over time, Albert hopes such efforts can rebuild the trust necessary for them to confidently return to a plateau they once relied on.

The next morning, I was astonished by how austere the steppe looked compared with the day before. Gone was the slippery muck and browning grasses of shifting seasons, replaced by a blanket of crunchy snow. Against this stark black-and-white backdrop, the fresh crystals functioned like fingerprint dust, illuminating the only remaining pops of color: the rust-red streaks of human and nonhuman pathways in the dirt.

Parked in an otherwise empty tract of prairie land, we watched in stunned silence as thousands of saigas seized the day, flying like banshees across the periphery, their hooves gouging the frozen crust and stamping pigment into an earthen canvas.

As I gazed east toward the colorless horizon, I tried to envision how it might have looked in the thirteenth century, when this corner of the world boasted a vast network of caravanserai, or road inns, where exhausted travelers could rest and recover before continuing onward into the great unknown.

I pondered what it must have felt like for an intrepid merchant to know that they would not see another human being for many days, maybe weeks. To be fearful of what you may soon encounter, but take solace that the space between is not wholly empty. For there is life beyond humanity’s margins, and among nonhuman communities, that in-between space is the center of everything. That, I imagined, must have offered some measure of assurance that the road ahead, perilous though it may be, is well traveled.

This essay was adapted from the new nonfiction travelogue The Hidden Nations of Animals and is published here exclusively for Adventure Journal, with permission from Penguin Random House.

#8325. Counter Drone Technology Has Come to Deer Hunting and Landowners Are Starting to Fight Back

Published Nov 2, 2026 3:39 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

You’re five minutes into legal shooting with high hopes for your morning sit, then you hear it. A faint buzzing overhead. Eyes to the sky, you spot the drone hovering over your property. Suddenly, you’re less optimistic about your hunt.

[Insert neighbor] is up to no good again, you think. But is it actually who you think it is? How can you be sure? Basic, consumer-level drones can fly for miles. They can also spook deer and other wildlife on both public and private land.

Talk to landowners and deer hunters in Big Deer country and you’ll hear that drone usage has skyrocketed in recent years. Sure, there are a lot of folks flying drones legally during deer season. In many places it’s legal to fly a drone while attempting to recover a hit deer. Thermal drones are incredibly effective at this. But more and more, folks are using drones to scan other people’s properties in order to locate (and sometimes harass) big bucks.

Enter the drone defense system — a technology that defends against unwanted drones flying over a hunting property for all the wrong reasons.

Modern deer hunting and land management look vastly different than they did just a few years ago. Today, drones weave through several aspects of whitetail management and sometimes hunting and poaching, too. Drones are used for population surveys, property management, and deer recovery. These are common reasons deer hunters and land managers consult drone operators or fly their own drones. So long as laws are followed and ethical hunting is prioritized, there’s nothing wrong with any of that. In fact, when used properly, drones can be a net positive for whitetail herds, especially when sound management is the driving force.

But like with any new technology, some people are hellbent on using thermal drones for unethical purposes, namely, spying on the neighbor’s deer — and possibly even poaching them. That has sparked the need for the drone defense systems being promoted by Jack Huston, owner and operator of Midwest Deer Surveys.

“Most of the problem is people flying over property they don’t own or have permission to be on,” Huston says. “It’s not so much local landowners flying every day trying to know how to hunt a buck. It’s more people scouting the whole township, if you will.

“That’s a huge problem, and in my eyes, it’s trespassing,” Huston says. “People work so hard to have land to hunt. They work to make it ready for hunting season. Then, if somebody wants to just go fly a drone and buzz your deer, they can. And I don’t think that should be OK.”

The fast-growing popularity of drones in the hunting world creates a whole barrage of questions: What are the regulations around drones? Is it legal to fly over someone else’s property? Will wildlife agencies be using drone tracking tech to prevent poaching? Huston says the laws are very different from state to state.

“You know, Ohio is completely wide open — probably too much so,” Huston says. “Then there are some states that are what I call anti-drone.”

For example, Pennsylvania prohibits drone usage for any type of hunting, including tracking wounded deer.

Huston’s system allows a landowner to identify when a drone flies their property, and who the drone is registered to.

“I go all around the country doing deer surveys for landowners,” Huston said. “I talk to all of these people, and they are complaining about drones flying over their farms. A lot of times, these people are bigger landowners in the area, and people get curious.

“A lot of people pushed me to find a product that could essentially serve as a radar for drones. That is this product. People are setting them up at their house or barn and it just sits there and monitors the drone activity on that property, and all around it.”

The system picks up the transmission between the remote controller and the drone itself. It’s able to read that transmission and get the location of the pilot, location of the drone, the make of the drone, its serial number, and more. It records all of that and stores it for the user.

The collected drone detection information feeds back to an app on the landowner’s phone. It lets them know who’s flying, where they’re flying, and everything that’s going on in their airspace. It’s essentially a monitoring tool to alert landowners when someone is flying their property.

“With these drone detectors, we have real data of how many people are flying, and it’s certainly far more than I thought,” Huston says.

Huston says you can buy one of several drone defense system sizes and choose from options that cover roughly a 5-mile, 20-mile, or 40-mile radius.

“A lot of my customers are just geo-fencing their farm,” Huston says. “So, they’re creating a bit of a bubble around their property where they want to cover the skies.”

But as you can probably guess, setting up one of these systems isn’t cheap. Smaller stations start at about $5,000 while the bigger station will set you back about $12,000. Still, for a large property owner who has spent millions of dollars on owning the ground and implementing habitat work, the cost of a drone surveillance system is only a drop in the bucket.

While Huston doesn’t manufacture these himself (he works with a company on the manufacturing side), he helped establish and design the drone defense system.

Huston’s installations are already making positive impacts for some landowners who invest. He says there have been several instances where drones were detected, confirmations of illegal use were made, and law enforcement was called to intercept. Essentially, drones were being used to aid in poaching, and the drone defense systems assisted in prevention, and maybe eventual prosecution.

It does not take too much imagination to see how wildlife agencies and their game wardens might one day use similar drone detection systems to catch poachers and illegal fliers.

“Drones are the Wild West, right now,” Huston says. “I think, when the word gets out on these… It will push drones to be used how they’re supposed to be used.

Read Next: Drones Could Revolutionize How Hunters Recover Lost Deer … If They’re Not Banned First

“When I go out on my land, or my family’s land, I don’t want a drone bothering me,” Huston says. “And if there is one, I want to know who it is and solve that problem. This is the solution to that problem. Without it, people can get away with whatever they want.”

#8324. Montana Man Banned From Hunting for 20 Years After Bowhunters Watch Him Poach a Trophy Bull

Published Nov 2, 2026 6:36 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

A father and son who pleaded guilty to poaching in central Montana have lost their hunting privileges for a combined 24 years. Their poaching activity goes back years, but the investigation into the men started last year based on a tip from two bowhunters, who reported a man shooting a bull elk with a rifle during archery season in September 2025.

“Lawful hunters are some of the most passionate outdoorsmen and women in existence. They’re very quick to report wildlife crimes and violations they see in the field,” Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks game warden and lead investigator Diego O’Brien tells Outdoor Life. “These two individuals, in my opinion, went above and beyond reporting the violation. They were very proactive with assistance in an area that I didn’t know very well. They proved to be incredible resources for me.”

Based on information provided by the two bowhunters, law enforcement located Billings resident Michael Letasky through a traffic stop. He matched the description of the man shooting the bull in the Little Belt Mountains, but he didn’t have the rack or any game meat. The bull was left to waste. (The two witnesses knew exactly where the dead animal was, but by then it was too late for wardens to salvage the meat.)

“The hunters that witnessed this trophy bull elk unlawfully shot during archery season were rightfully upset and immediately reported the crime to authorities,” O’Brien said in a statement. “Their quick and accurate reporting and assistance in locating evidence were crucial to this investigation. They sacrificed their own hunting trip to ensure justice was served.”

The poached 6×6 bull met the state’s trophy standards. By state code, restitution for the illegal killing and possession or waste of trophy elk is $8,000. The only animal with a higher restitution than a 6×6 bull is a bighorn ram with at least three-fourths curl, which earns a penalty of $30,000.

In addition to the poached bull, Letasky also shot a raghorn with a firearm during the 2023 archery season, and he had an unreported black bear. During the investigation, wardens also found evidence against Letasky’s son, Kolton, of Austin, Texas.

Kolton Letasky killed a Montana buck in 2024 and a Montana bull in 2022 without the proper permits. He pled guilty to two counts of unlawful possession of game and two counts of hunting without a license. His penalties include more than $3,000 in fines and no hunting for four years.

Read Next: YouTuber Poaching Bust Was a Case of ‘Wildlife Commercialization with a Modern Twist,’ Says Investigating Warden

The elder Letasky’s penalties are more severe. Michael Letasky plead guilty to two counts of unlawful possession of game, two counts of hunting during a closed season and one count of wasting game. He owes more than $12,000 in fines and can’t hunt for 20 years.

Kris Millgate is a multimedia journalist based in eastern Idaho. She’s a fly fisher, a bird hunter and an avid seeker of awkward moments. Read and watch more of her work at tightlinemedia.com

#8323. 10 Ways to Bag More Pheasants Now

Bag more pheasants by hunting the right cover at the right time of day. Birds move from roost to feed to loafing cover on a predictable schedule. Cold mornings push them to grain early. Wind and wet keep them on the roost. Hunt returning birds in the last 45 minutes of light. Don't write off pressured public land after opening day.

“We’ll flush about 150 birds today,” I told my new friend M.D. as we loaded our guns by his truck. A recent transplant to pheasant country, M.D. raptly surveyed the wide fields, trying to picture 150 flying pheasants where he could see only a wide expanse of snow. “But only one of them will get up within gun range,” I predicted. “Don’t miss.”

The pheasants looked like tiny black checkmarks against the whiteness as they scooted in and out under the sparse cover of bushes and brushpiles. With the long grasses buried under the snow, the birds had nowhere to hide. They flushed in large, nervous flocks before we could close within 100 yards. Finally, we found the one bird we were looking for, holding tight in a lone patch of grass tufting up through the white crust.

M.D. missed, proving that when it comes to pheasants, knowledge is power only if you shoot straight. Muffing deceptively difficult shots at close-flushing roosters is, perhaps, the most common error pheasant hunters make. But it’s not the only one. Here are ten lessons I’ve learned the hard way.

Pheasants roost in thick, heavy grasses, then walk or fly out to grainfields to feed in the morning. At midday, they hang around in light cover near food, then hit the fields again in the afternoon. Late in the day, birds will return to heavy roosting cover.

Many people believe pheasants linger on the roost on freezing cold winter days. Over the years, I wasted a lot of time getting up early on subzero mornings trying to kick-start sleepy pheasants out of their beds. In fact, when it’s 20 below zero and days are short, pheasants head for the fields at first light to load up on high-energy grain, so hunting their bedroom on a bitter cold morning is a waste of time. A nasty, windy, wet morning is a different story: Hunt the roost early when it’s spitting and blowing, and you may well catch pheasants reluctant to leave their warm, weedy roosts.

By the same token, hunting good roosting cover at midday when the birds are still feeding yields poor results. Be there in the last 45 minutes of daylight, however, as pheasants return from the grainfields, and the hunting can be absolutely spectacular.

Early in the season, when hunter after hunter tramples public land, birds move out to nearby private acres where the pressure isn’t as intense. Gunwise birds sometimes use the public area as a bedroom, returning around dark to roost, then leaving at the crack of dawn.

Hunt a public area the day the corn is picked on the private land across the road, and you’ll be amazed. Last fall, I walked a small, heavily used county area on a whim, thinking I’d give the dog a good run if nothing else. I didn’t know then that the corn had been picked across the road the day before, and without a roof of cornstalks over their heads, the pheasants had retreated in confusion to the marsh grasses of the public land. What I thought would be a quiet dog walk turned into one of the noisiest hunts of the year. Late in the season, when heavy snows have flattened sparser cover on private lands, public areas (especially wetlands) often hold birds again.

Pheasants don’t follow those neat rules of behavior printed on ammo boxes: “early season/close flushes” or “late season/wild flushes.” I’ve seen opening weekends where the wind blew and birds turned skittish, offering no shots closer than 35 yards. And wild-flushing late-season pheasants usually jump up a good 100 yards out of gun range; the birds you can actually shoot are the few that sit tight until you’re right on top of them.

Rather than guessing day by day what the birds will do, I shoot the same Improved Cylinder/Modified-choked 12-gauge double, or Modified-choked 12-gauge pump, from day one to season’s end.

This is one of the errors I commit regularly; I’m usually too eager to start chasing birds to wait while a blocker moves into position at the far end of a field. Every once in a while I hunt with someone who firmly believes in blocking, and I’m always impressed at how well it works. If you hunt any kind of strip cover, pheasants will run to the far end and flush. When pheasants know someone is watching the back door, they don’t run or flush wild; they hunker down and take their chances with the hunters working the cover. One solo hunter I know actually walks noisily to one end of a field and pretends to stand there blocking, then sneaks around to the other side and hunts towards, well, himself.

A slammed car door or a slide-action smacking shut can put pheasants to flight before the hunt even begins. Sometimes you’ll be treated to the impressive sight of pheasant flocks taking off in sympathetic waves across a field, each mass flush triggering the next, all the birds leaving the field you’d intended to walk.

Always approach pheasant cover quietly, especially late in the season when cover is sparse, and birds have grouped up. Once actually hunting, however, I’m not a stickler for silence. I believe pheasants can almost always hear you coming, no matter how quiet you try to be. They’re out there in the grass, monitoring your approach by the crunch of your footsteps and deciding to sit, run, or fly based on exactly where everyone in your party is at all times. Pause every once in a while; when ringnecks suddenly can’t hear you coming, they sometimes lose their nerve and flush.

Too many pheasant hunters bundle up in heavy clothes, then overheat after an hour of chasing the dogs chasing the birds. You want to feel a little chilly while you’re standing by the truck getting ready; you’ll warm up soon enough.

Pheasant hunting rarely requires heavy boots or brush pants. It’s better to wear something lightweight and easy to move around in. Wear several lighter, thinner layers up top rather than a heavy coat. You can add and subtract layers as you cool down and warm up, tucking unworn clothes into your gamebag. I choose a lightweight ballcap and keep a warm knit cap in my pocket should the weather turn colder.

Any color hunting clothes are fine, so long as they’re fluorescent orange. I glow like a Chernobyl pumpkin when pheasant hunting; I want the people I hunt with to do the same. Besides preventing accidents, this allows you to quickly verify everyone’s location when a bird’s on the wing and you want to be sure you’re taking a safe shot.

RELATED: The 10 Best Upland Shotguns Ever Made

If you travel to hunt pheasants, make your trip two or three weeks after opening day (unless of course you’ve already leased a section of South Dakota pheasant country or married into an Iowa farm family, in which case you don’t need my advice). Too many people think opening weekend, with its uneducated, unhunted birds of the year, is the best time to hunt pheasants. In fact, the weather can be hot, cutting your dog’s endurance and scenting ability. Many years, the fields aren’t harvested by opening day, either. Pheasants will hide among the standing crops where you can’t go after them. If you don’t have a place to hunt lined up long before opening day, you might not find one, and public lands will be very crowded.

Two or three weeks after the season begins, the crops will be in, the weather will be cooler, and the crowds will be gone. There will be lots of birds left, too.

We all know pheasants are birds of grasslands and marshes, not timber. Watch a rooster batter upwards through the branches on stubby wings, his long, graceful tail totally useless as a rudder in close quarters, and you’ll see why ringnecks usually avoid the woods.

Nonetheless, pheasants will hide in the woods if they can’t go anywhere else. When heavy snow flattens the grassy fields pheasants prefer, look for birds in the woodlots. The best pheasant woods have creek bottoms, bushes, or brush piles to hide in. Years ago, I read somewhere that when you find pheasants in the woods, they will usually be roosters. I’ve paid attention ever since and found it to be true, although I have no idea why.

Most pheasants are shot within 15 to 20 yards of the muzzle, and many more are missed at even closer range. Stifle the urge to shoot immediately. At 10 yards, your pattern is the size of a fist, and you don’t really know where the bird is going yet. Three feet of squawking, psychedelic gamebird blowing up at your feet is always startling; if you’re not paying attention, it’s downright scary. If you jump back and shoot in self-defense whenever a pheasant flushes, you’ll miss a lot. Take a second to read the pheasant’s angle, swing the gun at the white neck ring, and shoot. Trapshooting, with its varying, going-away angles, is wonderful training for pheasant-type shooting.

While you’re at it, give up trying to beat your buddies to the shot. Take turns; everyone will shoot better, you’ll lose fewer birds, and those you bag won’t be mangled.

The real trick to successful pheasant hunting isn’t bagging more birds, but getting more satisfaction from the ones you do shoot. Even those of us who live in the best pheasant country don’t get ’em every day, which is exactly as it should be. When my own focus narrows to encompass nothing more than the tail end of a bird dog in the weeds, I try to stop at the top of a hill, take a breather, look around, and ponder how lucky we are—after having plowed up the prairies and run off so many native birds—to have pheasants around. Think about it that way, and every single bird becomes cause for celebration.

Phil Bourjaily sold his very first outdoor story—a feature about snipe hunting—to Field & Stream in 1987. He became the brand’s Midwest regional editor in 1995, and the shotgun columnist shortly thereafter. Highlights Education Bourjaily graduated from the University of Virginia with a major in Art History. He also met his wife, Pamela, at college, so his years in Charlottesville weren’t entirely wasted. Experience Bourjaily has written for numerous shotgunning and wingshooting publications, and appeared on Field & Stream’s Gun Nuts TV show, as well as on DUTV and Clay Target Shootout, which received a Telly Award.He enjoys writing about shotguns and all forms of wing and clay target shooting and has traveled widely to hunt upland birds, waterfowl, doves, and wild turkeys. He also enjoys teaching people to shoot, and has coached scholastic sporting clays and trapshooting. #8322. Where Did the Midweight Ski Touring Boot Go?

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

The men's Tecnica Zero G Decoy Pro, staged and ready to go for a backcountry adventure in Cooke City, Montana. (Photo: Rick Sorensen)

Overview: Midweight ski touring boots, historically three buckles and 1,300 to 1,500 grams, can handle the whole range of backcountry skis, yet the class has stagnated while lightweight and crossover boots got most of the industry’s R&D. Writer Bergen Tjossem, a former ski-shop employee, argues the next big touring breakthrough should come from the midweight category.

It’s 4 a.m. and the biting cold plunges into the open garage as I stuff my partner’s idling Forester with gear. But I stall, hovering over my collection of ski touring boots. Big boots or little boots? Neither seems right for the day. I throw my thrashed 2023 Scarpa Maestrale RS boots over my shoulder, snap on my headlamp, and lug my skis to the car. I don’t know why I still hesitate at the start of every backcountry ski day—I end up picking the workhorse boot over the specialists most of the time.

Why, then, is the industry trying to squash this midweight ski touring boot class? Even the Maestrale RS, my beloved midweight archetype, is graduating toward the next class up this season, with a fourth buckle and more heft.

Owning a quiver of boots and skis is fun; it gives you options. But if you already own a pair of alpine boots like most skiers do, one dedicated touring boot could accomplish the vast majority of your needs. Yet where backcountry skis fall on a neat bell curve of dimension and weight, the boots we can buy to pilot them are bimodally distributed: ski shapes cluster in the middle, touring boots at the extremes. The evolution of midweight ski touring boots—the ones that best serve the majority of backcountry skiers—has stagnated compared to their cousins at the ends. It’s the “missing middle” problem every ski town knows from housing.

There’s no rule or buckle count dividing touring boot classes, but allow me to split them for the sake of the rant: lightweight boots typically have two buckles and top out around 1,200 grams, like the La Sportiva Kilo. Midweight boots historically use three buckles and weigh 1,300 to 1,500 grams. Then there are crossover boots that blend touring and alpine: four buckles, around 1,500 grams, typically with a GripWalk sole compatible with tech and alpine bindings, like the Dynafit Tigard.

Ski touring dogma says the optimum backcountry quiver is two pairs of ski touring boots and two pairs of skis: one lightweight and distance-oriented, the other beefy and fun. But here’s the catch—lightweight boots struggle with big skis, especially in poor snow, because they lack progressive flex and damping. And the opposite is also true. Crossover boots are a real drag on lightweight skis. Aside from the cumbersome ROM, the added stiffness, high cuff, and heft quickly overpower lightweight skis. Yet midweights can handle the whole ski spectrum.

When I worked in ski shops in the early 2010s as ski touring took off, midweight boots were the benchmark. Dynafit’s Vulcan and the Scarpa Maestrale were the choice for skiers who wanted to climb efficiently without giving up too much on the descent. What followed that workhorse boot era was an explosion of lightweight options, as almost every company in the business invested in svelter chassis while skis got lighter and less demanding. The rise of resort uphilling and Skimo racing only fueled the growth. Lately, lightweight boots such as La Sportiva’s Kilo XTR have been beefed up to claim more of that middle segment without overtaking it completely. But lightweight two-buckle designs with sturdier components still come up short on the leverage and suspension big skis demand.

Crossovers got the next round of R&D in the name of capturing the massive resort-hybrid buyer. Scarpa’s 1,500 gram 4-Quattro XT with a legit 61 degree range of motion (ROM) revolutionized the segment in 2022. All of a sudden, boots with alpine-like skiing capability unlocked a bigger ROM, while better materials and design brought weights down to 1,500 grams per boot or less. It also introduced freaky new levels of “quiver overlap” for skiers who already own alpine boots with a walk mode.

Smooshed between the crossover and the lightweight segments is that increasingly scant boot group, the midweights. It’s not that these midweight boots don’t exist—the Scott Cosmos Pro and Fischer Transalp prove they do—but rather that they’ve gotten the shaft on R&D over the last decade. Most of the remaining midweights are just stale, longing for a refresh, a trickle-down of new tech, and a burst of innovation.

A radical solution would be to have fewer skis, and I can’t believe you’d even suggest that. I’ve got a better idea: Give me one boot that can cover the entire ski quiver: three buckles, a camming power strap, over 65 degrees of ROM, under 1,400 grams, and minimal fiddle factor. Oops, I just mostly described the Scarpa Maestrale that’s been around for sixteen years. That’s because the industry is barely competing to refine that basic formula into its state-of-the-art form.

As a skier of many setups, I can say there’s a mismatch between the boots I want and those available. Lightweights and crossovers have had their run. My hunch is that the next big touring breakthrough will be, and should be, in the missing middle. Until then, you’ll catch me clinging to my 2023 Scarpa Maestrale RS boots like the gear troll I am.

#8321. Whatever You Think of Him, Mark Dowdle Is Built for the Backyard Ultra

At lap 87 of the Last Soul Backyard Ultra in Bornheim, Germany, this August, Mark Dowdle transformed (or regressed, he’s not entirely sure) into the football and lacrosse player he was in college.

To be fair, Ayyoub “Ello” El Osrouti pretty much started it. A backyard ultra, as you probably know by now, is a last-person-standing race not much different from “The Long Walk”—the movie about 100 boys who walk until there’s one left—except the runners in backyard races aren’t shot after they drop.

Now at 4 a.m. on August 18—three days and 15 hours into the race—it was just down to El Osrouti and Dowdle, who were engaged in a Hamilton-like duel to determine the winner. Ello busted out of the gate. The German had been trying to run faster laps to break Dowdle, but this was, by comparison, a sprint. Dowdle, deviating from his tactic of running his own race, decided to stay right with him.

Dowdle completed the lap in 38 minutes—his fastest of the race by over 5 minutes. El Osrouti got up and finished four minutes later, also his fastest lap.

But about half way through the lap, El Osrouti stopped and sat down. Dowdle stopped, too, and just stared at him in silence. It was both competitive and a little chilling, like Dowdle thought the Last Soul race was a literal invitation to collect his competitors’ souls along the way.

Dowdle’s behavior left many of his hundreds of thousands of followers on Instagram, Youtube, and TikTok a little stunned. The 29-year-old Minnesotan has become a wildly popular Internet figure through dishing out zen advice and positivity. Rich Roll, the addict turned endurance athlete who serves up mindfulness every week on his podcast, called Dowdle a “changemaker” when he had Dowdle on the show. There was a good reason for it: Basically every time Dowdle took a breath, he said something enlightening or inspiring about hard work, endurance, or self-improvement.

With two backyard ultra wins in 2026 alone, there’s little doubt that Dowdle is one of this year’s ultrarunning breakout stars, partly because of his success in the backyard format and partly because of his social media savvy. But he didn’t get that way by reading scripted platitudes on TikTok; Dowdle isn’t faking that zen.

When I told him about the Taco Bell 50K and how it attracted those who wouldn’t normally even consider running an ultra, he said, “people want to be challenged. Sometimes they just don’t know it yet.” Even when he was a football and lacrosse player at the University of St. Thomas in Saint Paul, Minnesota, drinking way too much and trying to please others at the expense of himself, he would think about the meaning of life and why people do the things they do. He attributes his personal growth to running, but also to journaling.

“These are the kinds of things I think about all the time,” Dowdle said. “I was constantly thinking about this connection between words and action and who I wanted to be.”

Dowdle works as a motivational speaker now. But deep down, he’s got an edge.

It’s that edge that makes him stand out (and ruffle feathers) in a sport known for its kumbaya positivity, especially the camaraderie-focused backyard ultra community. Dowdle likes being a little weird and competitive and even scary: He once made a YouTube video called “Ultrarunning Has A Mark Dowdle Problem.” He compares himself to Dennis Rodman, the wildly divisive and brilliant NBA player.

“I’m sure that some of these other guys who are competitive will want to put that competition right back on me,” Dowdle said. “I welcome that.”

His friend and rival Harvey Lewis seems like a golden retriever to Dowdle’s heeler. Dowdle sort of agrees with that comparison and sort of doesn’t. He points out that he and Lewis aren’t that different. (Lewis agrees with him, for what it’s worth.)

“I think Harvey Lewis is competitive in a way that’s much tricker to identify,” Dowdle said. “But I don’t hide it. There are times I don’t care. I’ll show everything on my sleeve.”

Lewis believes that Dowdle’s zen, more than his competitiveness, is what’s carried him to so much recent success. On October 17, 2026, they came together as teammates: Lewis, 50, and Dowdle lined up as part of a U.S. team of 15 against the world’s best at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship. Team USA competed on the Big’s Backyard Ultra course in Beltbuckle, Tennessee, the original backyard ultra devised by Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell. Dowdle went on to run 107 laps, or 446 miles—a personal best—to lead Team USA to victory over Australia. Lewis ran 83 laps.

The Backyard Ultra World Team Championship is held every two years, alternating with the individual world championship. The 2026 race began at 6 a.m. Mountain Time on Saturday, October 17, with 69 national teams competing simultaneously around the world.

The format is simple: Each team of 15 runners runs a 4.167-mile loop every hour, on the hour. The country with cumulatively the most loops completed across all 15 runners wins the team title. Team USA races on the original backyard ultra course in Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell’s backyard in Bell Buckle, Tennessee.

Mark Dowdle led Team USA to the win with a cumulative 1,120 laps (yards) to defeat Australia by 51 yards. He was the last American standing with 107 laps, or 446 miles—a personal best. Belgium’s Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts broke the individual backyard ultra world record by each running 124 yards (512 miles) before deciding to call it quits due to boredom, on-the-ground photographer Jacob Zocherman reports.

Since its inauguration in 2020, Belgium and the U.S. have each won two team titles.

Lewis said Dowdle’s “why” is perhaps the strongest he’s ever seen. It “cements his discipline and his unwavering desire to not give up.”

“Mark has a great energy force,” Lewis said. “He has a level of enthusiasm that’s immeasurable.”

But what, exactly, is an energy force? Is it zen or competitiveness? Dowdle likes to ask it another way: Why can’t it be both?

Take a wild guess who inspired Dowdle as a collegiate football and lacrosse player to turn his life around and start running. It wasn’t Joe Rogan, but if that was your first guess, you’re on the right track.

Feeling sorry for himself on the bus ride home after losing two of three lacrosse games his senior year, he listened to David Goggins on Joe Rogan’s podcast. Goggins talked about how running carved him into the person he was today. The way he bragged about pissing blood, shitting himself, and eating only saltine crackers during his long runs spoke to Dowdle. Dowdle already knew he needed to change.

He went for a run when they got back to campus—even though it was 2 a.m.

If Goggins lit the fire, James Lawrence, the Iron Cowboy, stoked it. Lawrence had completed the 50/50/50 challenge, or 50 Ironman-length triathlons in 50 days across 50 states. The way he leaned on his family during that journey spoke to Dowdle. Dowdle, to this day, gives all the credit to his wife, Lucy, for centering him and scolding him whenever he acts, for lack of a better description, too much like a bro.

Dowdle tried for many years to make it as a running guru—some might say influencer—and ultrarunner. He found some limited success. Runner’s World interviewed him in 2023 for his calendar challenge, when he ran the number of miles corresponding to the day of the month, for a full month. (For example, 26 miles on the 26th.) By the beginning of 2026, he had 40,000 Instagram followers and a modest apparel sponsorship that netted him $200 a month. And then he entered the BPN Go One More backyard ultra this April.

Dowdle had already won the Arrowhead 135-miler in January, finishing in 35:48:00—a four-hour improvement over his 2025 fourth-place finish. But he chalked that up to his ability to withstand the Minnesota winter conditions that dropped to minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit.

The BPN Go One More was another story; he hadn’t even made it to 100 miles in a backyard ultra before. He could sense other peoples’ doubts—they didn’t drive him, but they did irritate him a little. He mumbled at one point that they “had no fucking idea.”

Dowdle ended up running 306 miles in 73 hours of rainy and muddy conditions, and the way he did it captivated people: He looked fresh and happy most of the time, like he was playing tag on the playground. In a few days, his Instagram following jumped to 108,000, and brand deals were knocking at his door. He also began booking keynote speaking events, sometimes for conferences that he helped set up the year before for one of his odd jobs to get by while he pursued running.

He proved that BPN was no fluke two months later, finishing second to Lewis at the Mid-State Mile, a last-person standing event in Franklin, Tennessee.

But Last Soul sent him into a new stratosphere. After their fateful showdown on lap 87, Dowdle and El Osrouti dueled for another six hours. And despite the German banking a cumulative five hours of extra rest over the course of the race, after that 93rd lap he gave out. Dowdle ran the final lap solo to win the race with 94 loops, or 391.7 miles. The race attracted 10 million viewers to the livestream and more than 100,000 at any one time, attention that Lewis called “freakishly different” than any other ultra in history, even Western States or Rachel Entrekin’s historic overall win at the Cocodona 250.

After Last Soul, Dowdle’s Instagram following jumped from 108,000 to over 400,000.

“It’s been everything I’ve been trying to build for several years now,” Dowdle said. “But nothing really has changed. It’s sort of weird because I’ve been saying the same thing now that I have over the past seven years. But people are willing to listen more when I go 94 hours in a backyard.”

Dowdle, a Christian who has described his goal in races to experience suffering in a way that brings him closer to Jesus Christ and to others, says he’s handled his newfound success because of his wife. Everyone, he said, should get a Lucy. On the way home from the BPN race, Lucy saw his phone blowing up and reminded him that many of those people were loving him because of what he just did, but that she and his friends loved him for who he was.

Dowdle’s breakthrough would not be possible without the backyard ultra format, and not just because he’s one of the best in the world at it. The race, as Lewis alluded to, is insanely popular: What started as another one of Laz’s harebrained ideas with the Big’s Backyard Ultra in 2011 has ballooned to over 1,000 independent backyard ultras across the globe.

Lewis was perhaps the event’s first breakout star. He was known, he said, after winning Badwater in 2014, but the attention was far different after he won Big’s Backyard in 2023, his second victory, and set a backyard world record by running more than 450 miles. The format changed the high school teacher’s life.

“I was doing other cool stuff but never got noticed,” Lewis said. “But after the backyard, I was invited to all these running events, at no cost, places I’d never get to go to as a teacher. Australia, Botswana, all over the place. In Botswana, people knew who I was, and I was like, ‘really’? It just created so many more doors opening.”

Backyard ultras favor a unique skillset. Neither Lewis or Dowdle have the legspeed to compete for a top spot at a “fast” ultra like Western States. But, Lewis counters, a top contender at Western States may struggle at a backyard ultra.

“I’ve seen collegiate-type runners, and they get totally destroyed,” Lewis said. “It’s a different type of grit that’s required for running five straight days.”

Lewis and Dowdle possess that special mindset that doesn’t have much to do with a training plan. Lewis is writing a book on mindset, in fact, that will be released next fall. For Dowdle, the ultimate challenge (and intrigue) comes in the unknown.

“You have no opportunity to say ‘in 10 miles this race will be over,’” Dowdle said. “You just have to wrestle with the discomfort.”

Dowdle does that, he said, by using skills he learned from his parents. His relentless, even disturbing, will comes from his mother, and he got an addict’s penchant from his father. His dad, he said, has been sober for nearly 30 years by using his addictive personality for good, investing his energy in Alcoholics Anonymous and helping others overcome their itches.

But Dowdle also excels by finding out who he was as a person: “Running helped me figure out the person I was running away from and also running toward the person I wanted to be.”

There is a dual narrative in his head, one that every ultrarunner facing the highs and lows of a long race knows. The first tells him he’s not worthy. The other feels only elation. Neither, he said, is true.

“I know that the narrative playing in my head at that moment is not the full truth,” Dowdle said. “And the narrative that tells me I’m not good enough. As long as my feet are still moving forward, I can combat that thinking and know that’s not the full truth.”

Proving that imposter syndrome wrong is his part of his “why,” the magic power that he and Lewis seem to possess that helps them run much farther than just about anyone else. But that’s not his only motivation.

Dowdle was, at one point, a football coach. But when he examined his life, he didn’t think football was the right avenue for what he truly wanted to do. He wanted to connect with young men and try to help them crawl out of the same situation he was in years ago, before he began running and journaling. So he traveled across the country and hosted beer miles. He still does this, though he drinks non-alcoholic varieties now, or he simply challenges athletes to beat his beer mile time. (It’s 5:51.57.)

When the race is over, he sits down with athletes and talks with them about their lives. He tells them he was like them once, a little lost and full of doubt and pain, with only alcohol seeming to help. There are other ways, he tells them. Running could be one. A personal journey, like that of the Iron Cowboy, could be another.

“I watched the Iron Cowboy documentary, and it made me realize that I do have control, and that I can do hard things and I’m capable of more,” Dowdle said. “That’s the gift he gave me in that moment. Now I’ve been on a mission to try to give that gift to other people.”
