#8320. I Put This $1,500 Portable Power Station to the Test—Is It Worth It?

The Goal Zero Yeti 1500 is a capable, easy-to-use portable power station built for both camping and home backup. Its 2,000W continuous output, fast wall recharge, and solar compatibility make it a serious option. The one real tradeoff: at nearly 53 pounds, it takes effort to move. If you can live with the weight, the performance justifies the price.

Whether you spend your weekends camping or you just want to be prepared in case of a power outage, a portable generator is one of those things that you probably want—or maybe even need—to have on hand. There are plenty to choose from, but Goal Zero’s new-for-2026 Yeti 1500 caught our attention with its rugged build, fast charging, and battery designed to last for years. We spent weeks this summer testing the $1,500 power station to see how it performed, what we liked (and didn’t), and whether it’s worth the price.

I found the Goal Zero Yeti 1500 easy to use right out of the box. The display is simple to navigate and shows how much battery is left, how much power you’re using, and how quickly it’s charging. I also like that there are plenty of ports, so I can plug in multiple devices without having to swap things around. The only real downside is the weight. At nearly 53 pounds, it’s a little cumbersome to move around, especially if you’re hauling it to a campsite or lugging other gear.

What stood out to me during testing was how much the Yeti 1500 can handle at once. I can keep multiple devices plugged in without having to constantly unplug one thing to charge another, and the display makes it easy to see how much power I’m using. With 2,000 watts of continuous output, it has enough capacity for more than just phones and smaller electronics. We used it to power an electric cooler on an 8-hour road trip to the beach this summer, and it worked like a dream. I’d honestly feel comfortable keeping it on hand for backup power at home, too.

Battery life is one of the most important features of a power station, especially if you’re taking it camping or relying on it during an outage. With a 1,505Wh battery, the Yeti 1500 can keep your devices charged for a good while before you’ll need to recharge it. And when you do need to recharge it, I like how quickly it powers up, going from empty to full in just over an hour when plugged into a wall outlet. Bonus: If you’re using it off-grid or for camping, you can pair it with one of the compatible solar panels to recharge the generator without needing a power source.

The Goal Zero is worth every penny. Full stop. It’s easy to use, has plenty of power (and battery life) for camping trips and emergency backup, and recharges fast enough that you’re not waiting around all day to use it again. At $1,500, it’s definitely an investment, but if you spend a lot of time in the outdoors or want something reliable to have on hand when the power goes out, I think the performance and peace of mind justify the price.

For more than 125 years, Field & Stream has been providing readers with honest and authentic coverage of outdoor gear. Our writers and editors eat, sleep, and breathe the outdoors, and that passion comes through in our product reviews. You can count on F&S to keep you up to date on the best new gear. And when we write about a product—whether it’s a bass lure or a backpack—we cover the good and the bad, so you know exactly what to expect before you decide to make a purchase.

A portable power station lives or dies by one question: can you trust it when it matters? Running an electric cooler on an 8-hour road trip is a real-world test, not a spec sheet exercise, and the Yeti 1500 passed it without drama. What the testing here surfaces is a broader principle experienced campers already know: capacity headroom matters more than you think. A unit that can handle multiple devices simultaneously without compromise is the difference between convenience and frustration in the field. The solar compatibility extends that logic further, turning a capable camp accessory into a genuine off-grid tool.

Amanda came to Field & Stream in August 2022 from USA Today with nearly a decade of commerce and product testing experience. She’s passionate about the outdoors and spends as much time as she can shooting her bow, hunting with her husband at Hart-Miller Island, and hiking with their German shepherd. #8319. One Wrong Move Could Be Fatal. So Why Are These Climbers Competing at Free Soloing?

Michael Reese at the top of the First Flatiron in Boulder, Colorado (Photo: Courtesy of Michael Reese)

About our reporting: Climbing reporter Holly Chen interviewed three free soloists and one additional speed climber in Boulder, researched fatalities in Accidents in North American Climbing, and pulled from her own experience free soloing the Second Flatiron to answer questions about the world of competitive free soloing.

I stood waiting in front of a health food restaurant in south Boulder, Colorado. The Flatirons rose high above the building, their slabs of red sandstone jutting out of the mountainside like the spines of a prehistoric monster.

On September 3, 32-year-old climber Michael Reese broke the First Flatiron’s fastest known time (FKT) from the dirt at its base to the summit anchor, with no rope. He climbed the Direct Route (5.6,R; 1,000ft) of the East Face in 7 minutes 51 seconds, breaking what he believed would be the last minute barrier of this generation. The previous record was 8 minutes 33 seconds, set by Joe Kennedy in 2022.

Which one is Michael Reese? Everywhere I looked at the restaurant, less than a 10 minute drive from the Chautauqua trailhead, I saw La Sportiva and Scarpa running shoes, Salomon running vests, and folded ultralight running poles sticking out of ultralight backpacks. Any of these people could have just come off the climb.

The ease was the first thing I noticed about Reese. For someone who holds multiple FKTs in the Flatirons and one on Yellow Spur (5.8; 550ft) in Eldorado Canyon, I expected him to be cocky, confident, maybe a little elitist; he was anything but. Reese smiled easily, laughed easily, and spoke candidly, unperturbed by the recorder sitting between us. He was leaving for Yosemite the following day, and we exchanged stories of our experiences climbing in the Valley. When I joked about my personal best up the First Flatiron–somewhere shy of an hour, although I did not officially keep time–he congratulated me genuinely.

“You can do it,” Reese urged. “Get some racing shoes. Do some warmups … You’ll be going faster.”

As climbing has grown, it has increasingly legendized free soloing and going fast—but we’ve rarely seen these two disciplines combined and going without a rope. The Oscar-winning film Free Solo (2017) made the term so mainstream that it recently appeared in a Taylor Swift song, and speed climbing records have made headlines again and again. But these fantastical feats of risk and speed are usually in the hands of highly experienced climbers, such as Alex Honnold, the spectacular pendulum of Dean Potter, or Yosemite Search and Rescue members. Additionally, most of these races happen on cliffs that the average person can’t easily ascend, such as El Capitan.

Reese is a different kind of figure. A Boulder local, he is not sponsored, and not a professional. Reese started climbing at the University of Colorado (CU) Boulder in 2014. The first time he went up the First Flatiron, he said to himself, “If I get off this [alive], I’m never climbing again.” And the First Flatiron is far from inaccessible; with the base a 1.3-mile hike from the trailhead, for many people, the barrier to entry is only a pair of shoes.

The new FKT leaves me with an uneasy mix of admiration and doubt. A person’s risk is not entirely his own when he takes it in a busy place like Chautauqua Park, where hikers, runners, picnickers, and climbers share the same space. So is competitive free soloing on low fifth-class terrain something to celebrate or a toxic addiction to discourage? A fatal fall is always possible, and the barrier to entry is so low. In fact, anyone writing about it, including myself, is working on blurry ground where reporting and the glorification of risk are hard to tell apart. Does this recognition create a feedback loop that incentivizes more to partake in the risky sport?

To understand how competitive free soloing actually operates, I had to go back to the people who have been going fast on this rock for decades before Reese.

The history of speed records in the Flatirons runs through a small, unusual club called The Satan’s Minions Scrambling Club, which Bill Wright started in 2001. Three of its members told me they don’t “race” each other. Instead, they have “personal time trials,” to avoid the ire of the Parks & Open Space regulations, which prohibit races.

The club keeps books. Stefan Griebel, a longtime member, whom a mutual friend described to me as someone who holds “every record under the sun,” has a meticulously kept log book detailing every FKT on a Flatiron dating back to the 1980s. Today, members’ times are verified by Strava entries.

Griebel met Wright in 2003 and joined the club’s annual Flatiron scrambles, which have now run for about 22 years. Each one starts at a trailhead, free solos a Flatiron, and ends back in the parking lot. Buzz Burrell, a trail-running legend then 52, reset the trailhead-to-trailhead mark at 35 minutes and change. Griebel, who was half Burrell’s age at the time, couldn’t keep pace.

“[Buzz] just dropped every single person that day,” Griebel reminisced.

A year later, trail runner Dave Mackey took Burell’s trailhead-to-trailhead FKT down to 33:19. But being a trail runner, Griebel knew he would have the upper hand on rock. In 2010, Griebel closed the gap, and took the record to 33:05. The record changed hands to Mathias Messner in 2015 and Kyle Richardson in 2019.

In the spring of 2020, Reese returned to Boulder from a biotech master’s program at California Polytechnic State University. The COVID pandemic had canceled the triathlon nationals he’d spent months training for, and he had a season of fitness and nothing to spend it on. He decided to see how fast he could go on the Flatirons. It began as a text-message rivalry with Joe Mitchem, a friend from CU’s cross-country team, over Freeway (5.0; 600ft) on the Second Flatiron. Reese didn’t have Strava and didn’t know the records existed until the two of them realized they’d gone under the standing Freeway mark of about 6:20. That fall, he entered the club’s time trials and finished second.

Griebel remembers meeting Reese on the First Flatiron. The two soloed to the summit and trotted down together. “He can run uphill like nobody I’ve ever seen,” Griebel said.

The base-to-summit FKT, the one Reese prefers, was still Griebel’s in 2020, at 9:25. Reese told me the time stunned him. That summer, Reese broke it by seconds. Then Joe Kennedy, a California athlete, broke that in 2022 to 8:33. That sent Reese into harder training than he’d done in 2020 or 2021, and this September brought the record down to 7:51.

The club looks different today. It is still heavily male dominated; Griebel estimates eight men for every one woman participant. And membership is less casual. “We have some entrance requirements now,” Griebel said. “We don’t want to invite people into the club that aren’t okay with the risk and that are also very solid, obviously, on the rock.”

What the club shows is a culture more wary than toxic. It vets its members, keeps careful books, and wants to stay on good terms with the land managers. It also shows a feedback loop; each record pulled in the next challenger. Reese told me every broken record “ingrains it more as something to go for.” He felt inspired when he learned of Griebel’s record. Camaraderie and friendly competition keep people incentivized and returning. But this wariness only goes so far; while the Satan’s Minions can vet their members, they can’t actually stop others from trying competitive free soloing, too.

Reese said he has now climbed the First Flatiron 800 times. It taught him that the risk “is never zero,” but he believes it to be smaller than most people imagine.

Even inside the scene, no one agrees on what speed does to the odds of surviving a free solo. Griebel says that when he’s pushing hard, heart pounding and moving upward, he’s “less likely to make a mistake.” Kate Kelleghan, who holds the women’s Naked Edge (5.11b; 460ft) record with Laura Pineau, says free soloing only makes up about one percent of her climbing. “This is super high risk and low reward,” she told me. “I’ve always felt way safer and stronger on a rope.” John Alcorn, who holds the Diamond speed record, free soloing Casual Route (5.10a; 900ft), says going fast piles more risk onto something already dangerous. “You get one shot,” he told me, “and if you blow it, you’re dead.”

In his trip report, Alcorn wrote, “I accept the position that climbing without a rope is a pretty dumb thing to do, and I believe that it shouldn’t be glorified, normalized, or encouraged in any way.” When a friend’s wife called it “incredibly stupid” over dinner, he agreed.

Alcorn said the FKTs are “extremely competitive. We’re essentially all competing with each other. But all these guys are my friends.” He admitted that if someone took his Diamond time by a minute or two, “Oh, I’d be pissed.” Then he caught himself: “That’s just pure ego … one of the worst reasons to climb without a rope.”

According to Accidents in North American Climbing, there have been six fatalities in the Flatirons since 2016. All of them involved free soloists, although none of them involved speed climbers. That number puts the danger in soloing, not the speed.

Low fifth-class terrain pulls in runners, a demographic far larger than climbing. “The accessible, low-angle slabs of the Flatirons frequently lure inexperienced or ill-prepared scramblers,” wrote the ANAC editors in 2017.

Reese has noticed more crossover of hybrid athletes; people coming from a very high level running background. Alcorn saw the same shift from the trail running side: As running records multiply, people are “diversifying what counts as a goal,” and he finds it hard to say where running and scrambling stop and climbing begins. Griebel says the overlap between strong runners and people comfortable soloing is thin, and that overlap is the only reason he has ever held a record.

This summer Reese found a 20-year-old about 100 feet up at dusk, shaking, with no headlamp, his feet slipping. Reese guided him down a gully. By the time they reached the ground, it was too dark to see his own outstretched hand.

I have felt that same dread myself. In the summer of 2025, I took out-of-town friends up on a free solo of the second Flatiron. Near the top, three college-aged men were climbing without a rope, one in climbing shoes and two in running shoes. The leader, about fifteen feet above me, was shaking badly. I waved my friends to the left, afraid that if he fell, we would be in his path.

But inexperienced climbers aren’t always the ones to watch. In 2020, a man fell to his death on Freeway, even after he reportedly had climbed it “hundreds of times.”

The scrambling club’s precautions don’t reach the people who get in trouble because those people aren’t in the club. And just because one is solid on rock doesn’t mean they’ll never fall. Its members can be practiced and clear-eyed about the risk, but the rock belongs to everyone. “They don’t do it because they see somebody going fast,” said Griebel, referring to inexperienced scramblers. “They just see somebody soloing.”

The stereotype is that this is a content game. Climbers like Lincoln Knowles, who posts his free solos to a large and young following, make the impression that free soloing is about social media fame and monetization.

The record-holders I talked to disagree. Reese began timing himself in 2020 without Strava, unaware the records existed. “If there was no social media, no recognition of any kind, would you still do it?” I asked Reese. The answer was an unequivocal yes. “I’m more interested in doing the actual thing than the broadcasting of what I’ve done,” Reese said.

Alcorn never posted his Diamond record, a choice he called intentional. “I just don’t even want ego in the loop,” he said. Griebel’s Instagram account is private except to close friends. Reese’s posts reads more like a logbook than a boast.

Still, the pull of recognition isn’t zero. Reese allows that recognition probably motivates him now that it exists, but he still climbs for himself and not a like button. Alcorn admits that without a culture of records he probably wouldn’t have tried the Diamond record. Kelleghan sits in the middle. She has a following and has been paid, including for a watch ad, but says she has never climbed something just to post it.

Whatever these climbers are after, audiences both on and offline take their own lessons from the best in the sport.

On the Flatirons, free soloing and speed have become synonymous; on the Naked Edge, a short drive south, they still sit apart, for now. Some Boulder climbers are free soloing the Naked Edge already, Kelleghan said, and she knows at least one who has soloed it quickly, though not for a record. This climber, who Kelleghan refuses to name, believes the speed record will eventually belong to a free soloist. Kelleghan disagrees. A free soloist can’t push as hard, she argued, because “if you’re simul climbing, if you fall, it would be unpleasant, but you wouldn’t die.”

The people I spoke with showed that records have a way of recruiting. If someone does set a free solo speed record on the Naked Edge, will it stay an outlier, or become the standard, the way that free solo ascents became the standard on the Flatirons? Kelleghan is betting against it.

So for most people who hold these records, it isn’t a content game. But a motive doesn’t have to be public or monetized to be contagious. Each time a record falls, it tells the next climber what is possible. The risk the last person accepted becomes the new baseline.

For all the attention these records draw, free soloing mostly regulates itself. Most people look at the First Flatiron and never think of climbing it, let alone without a rope. Alcorn points to an innate fear of falling “baked into us” and doesn’t expect the number of people doing this to explode just because a few records have been broken.

Some people chase records, but does that make this a toxic culture? From what I saw, it doesn’t. The record-holders I met were generous rivals, wary of their own egos, more interested in doing the thing than in being seen doing it. But “not toxic” isn’t the same as “not influential.” We are not solitary creatures, we have family and friends who love us, so a risk taken is never entirely one’s own.

Reese was as easy at the end of our conversation as at the start. By the end of our meal, I had decided we were friends, so as we said goodbye, an uneasy feeling settled in my stomach.

Walking to my car, I looked up at the Flatirons. A friend of mine, Bailee Mulholland, still holds the female trailhead-to-trailhead speed record on the First. She belonged to the same scrambling club Reese does now. In 2023, she died free soloing a 5.4 route on Ypsilon Mountain (13,520ft) a few hours north. I remembered Mulholland’s unwavering bubbly personality; she smiled easily and laughed easily, too.

I don’t think the scene she came from is toxic. But I know what losing her did to the people who loved her. The risk may belong to the one who takes it. The grief never does.

#8318. Moultrie Edge 4 Pro Solar Trail Camera, Tested and Reviewed

The Moultrie Edge 4 Pro Solar is the top-tier option in Moultrie's Edge 4 lineup, built for hunters who want maximum image and video detail from a solar-powered cellular camera. It delivers 50MP photos, 4K video, and a .3-second trigger speed with reliable battery life in harsh conditions. Close-range nighttime images can be slightly blurry, so low-light performance at distance is where this camera excels.

This article was produced in partnership with Moultrie.

Moultrie’s Edge 4 Solar took Gold in our annual Best Cellular Trail Camera field test. The camera, with the included solar panel, is priced right ($169.99), and I ran a pair on my Colorado deer dirt for two months. I added Moultrie’s $50 (aftermarket) Power Mag II battery pack, and with the solar panel, battery life never dipped below 80 percent. The cameras stood up to powerful wind, heavy rain, marble-ball-sized hail, and hellishly hot temperatures. Neither cell cam produced many false triggers, and both delivered crisp, clear images and video to my smartphone.

Last year, Moultrie’s Edge 3 Pro and Edge Solar came on the heels of the Edge 3. True to form, Moultrie follows suit in 2026. Dubbed the Edge 4 Solar, Moultrie’s latest cellular trail camera comes with a rechargeable lithium battery pack, an integrated solar panel, and an easy-aim mount. Pleased with the Edge 4 Solar’s performance, I was excited to give the Pro model an in-field test drive.

When I see “Pro” added to a product, I assume it has features that put it in a class above the standard model. That’s the case with the Edge 4 Solar and Edge 4 Pro Solar. The Pro captures high-resolution, high-detailed 4K video and 50MP photos. I was highly impressed with the 1080p video and 40MP photos the Edge 4 Solar captured, and I’m excited to see the enhanced detail.

According to Moultrie, “detail” drove the Edge 4 Solar Pro. Moultrie’s continued growth largely comes from its ability to meet consumer expectations. Consumers asked for more detail, and the Edge 4 Pro Solar is Moultrie’s response.

The Edge 4 Solar Pro trumps the Edge 4 Solar’s trigger speed by .1 second. That’s not much, but when a buck is hot on the heels of a doe, rapid trigger speed is important.

Moultrie did an excellent job with its Edge 4 Series, and the Edge 4 Solar Pro looks to be the pinnacle. I’m a fan of Buck Shot. The Edge 4 Pro Solar uses Moultrie AI to detect big bucks. When the camera detects a big buck, it sends a tightly cropped, max-resolution image to your smartphone. This lets you immediately identify the buck and examine its headgear. And with the Pro model, Moultrie AI recognizes shooter bucks and switches the camera from photo mode to 4K video. Buck videos arrive immediately. Like the zoomed and cropped image, you don’t have to request or wait for the 4K video.

The Edge 4 Pro Solar comes with everything you need. The solar panel is connected, and the rechargeable lithium battery pack is inserted. Log into your Moultrie account, add a new camera, scan the QR code, and start tinkering with the camera’s many settings. As I noted in my review of the Edge 4 Solar, I like the new internal panel. The twist-and-turn dial ensures a positive on/off, and Moultrie left the battery-life indicator, which I appreciate. Once powered on, all three lights (Not Connected-red, Connecting-yellow, Connected-green) turn solid. Next, the Connecting light flashes slowly, and after about 45 seconds, the green Connected light turns solid green. At that point, you can close the push-button door. The camera connects to the strongest cellular signal in the area and starts transmitting photos immediately. Best of all, perhaps, is that you don’t need to insert an SD card. I hate SD cards. They are a pain. I love Moultrie’s included storage.

In a partnership with onX, Edge 4 cameras are instantly pinned the second they are placed. I have multiple trail cameras—cellular and conventional—spread across the West and Midwest. Too often, I get in a hurry and forget to drop a camera pin when I’m using trail cameras. However, if I’m using Moultrie, I can forget, and the map-pinning technology saves me.

My Edge 4 Solar withstood and continues to withstand rough conditions. We’ve had an extended monsoon season in my neck of the woods. Rain is one thing, but hail is another. All of my Edge 4 Solar cameras, including the new Pro, have zero damage to the housing or panels. Sadly, the Edge 4 Pro Solar did succumb to golf-ball-sized hail. The camera was facing straight into the storm. I’m not sure how many hailstones struck the photo lens cover, but one cracked it and some water got inside. The good news is that the camera is still functioning. The photos and video aren’t as clean and crisp as they were before the hail damage, but they are still solid. I called Moultrie and they are going to replace the camera. Moultrie has excellent customer service.

Moultrie Edge 4 cameras utilize waterproof IP67 waterproofing, and the housing and solar panel can take serious abuse. I was a little concerned that water would get into the removable solar-panel slot but that hasn’t happened and would have by now. If you want to remove the solar panel, push the unlock button on the back of the camera and pull the panel off.

As of this writing, my Edge 4 Pro Solar has been in the field for two weeks. The hail damage occurred 11 days into my field test. Until that point, the camera’s images and video were excellent. The detail and color, especially the video, was incredible. I couldn’t tell much difference between the 40MP and 50MP photos, but I could absolutely see the difference between the 1080p and 4K video.

After two weeks in the field, battery life is 94 percent. That percentage dips a bit when the panel isn’t getting sunlight, but as soon as the panel gets sun, it charges the camera quickly. I like the direct-to-housing panel attachment. The system eliminates wires that tangle and hang up everywhere.  Be sure to take advantage of the twist-and-lock solar panel direction and angle. Both are adjustable, allowing you to set your panel to absorb as much sunlight as possible.

I’ve had zero image delivery glitches; deer and other game animals are centered in the frame, and Moultrie lowballs the camera’s max detection range. Like the Edge 4 Pro, the Edge 4 Solar Pro captured deer beyond 100 feet. Moultrie brands the Edge Pro Solar trigger speed at .3 seconds, and my testing agrees. I set up an Edge 4 Solar and Edge 4 Pro Solar in my backyard, and the Pro proved quicker to trigger when I ran past the camera at 50 feet.

Like the Edge 4 Solar, the Pro model improves Moultrie’s nighttime image capture game. Moultrie used enhanced No Glow IR LEDs to illuminate every image evenly. The result is clearer edge-to-edge images. The only issue I’ve noticed the more I’ve tested Moultrie’s Edge 4 Solar models is the flash. The IR is almost too powerful. If the subject is close to the camera, the image gets a bit blown out. However, I’ve yet to have a deer spook from the Edge 4 Pro Solar, and I’ve run the camera on open ag fields and tight trail crossings.

Moultrie has once again raised the bar with the Edge 4 Solar and Edge 4 Pro Solar, both of which have proven to be exceptional in the field. The Edge 4 Solar, awarded Gold in our annual Best Cellular Trail Camera test, has consistently impressed with its performance, durability, and affordability. At $169.99, it offers outstanding value, especially when paired with the aftermarket Power Mag II battery pack. The solar panel and robust battery life combine to deliver a seamless experience in demanding conditions, from heavy rainfall to extreme heat.

The Edge 4 Pro Solar takes things a step further, delivering enhanced detail and high-resolution 4K video, perfect for capturing all the goings-on in your deer woods. Moultrie’s focus on user feedback has highlighted the importance of detailed imaging, and the Pro model reflects their commitment to customer satisfaction.

For setup, the straightforward interface and reliable battery performance let users maximize their time in the field. Both models have proven resilient in harsh weather, reinforcing Moultrie’s reputation for durability. If you’re looking for a dependable trail camera that excels in both performance and image quality, the Edge 4 Solar series is undoubtedly worth considering, and if you want Moultire’s cream of the crop, then go with the Edge 4 Pro Solar.

#8317. There Are Over 40 Resorts Planning To Open In November—Here’s Where Experts Say Conditions Will Be Best

Mammoth Mountain opening day 2025 (Photo: Courtesy of Mammoth Mountain)

Some folks may think skiing in November is crazy: the snow is rarely good, and the mere thrill of lifts spinning often attracts crowds larger than downhill capacity should allow.

It can be difficult to know where, if anywhere, it is worth skiing in November. While resorts are making snow around the clock, the decision to open boils down to weather.

For Colorado skiers, the weather may finally be on your side. According to Open Snow meteorologist Joel Gratz, November is set to start with a “bang.” He predicts a storm arriving Sunday will drop 6 to 12 inches on nearly all mountains, with some spots seeing up to 20. Did someone say powder day?!

Several Colorado resorts are opening their lifts before Halloween is over. Arapahoe Basin opened Oct. 28, Keystone follows on Oct. 30, and Wolf Creek on Oct. 31. Snow is thin at all three for now, but their high elevations should set them up for a stronger start to November.

Breckenridge and Copper Mountain are planning to open on Nov. 6, and if the snow comes in like Gratz is predicting, their opening days could feature more than just a white ribbon of death.

A little later into the month, Vail and Eldora are both planning Nov. 13 opening dates. It’s too early to tell if temperatures will preserve the snow from earlier storms, but as long as cold air remains, these are resorts to keep on your radar for potentially decent skiing.

Neighboring Utah resorts aren’t expected to receive as fruitful a snow bounty. They’ll see the same storm as Colorado, with the highest accumulations on Sunday, says Open Snow forecaster Evan Thayer. “Cooler air will eventually lower snow levels, with some decent accumulations possible up high.”

As of the time of publishing, Brian Head is planning on opening on Nov. 6. If Thayer’s prediction is accurate, the Southern Utah resort could see “decent accumulations” on its highest peaks. Alta, Park City, and Solitude are all planning on opening on Nov. 20. It’s too early to say how these resorts will fare, but cold temperatures will be the biggest asset.

California skiers will have to wait a bit longer. Open Snow forecaster Bryan Alleretto predicts the Tahoe region’s snowy start will likely come after Nov. 10, which could be good timing for Mammoth Mountain, set to open Nov. 20. Mammoth isn’t a Tahoe resort, but it tends to share weather patterns with those to the north.

The East Coast has had a warm fall, but that could change. There’s no official snow report yet, but Maine’s Sugarloaf plans to reopen Nov. 20, likely making it the region’s first resort to welcome skiers back. Vermont’s Sugarbush follows on Nov. 21, while nearby Killington, which often opens early, hasn’t announced a date as of press time.

#8316. Class 4 Terrain, Cozy Huts, Cold Beer: The Northern Alps Are Japan’s Best-Kept Secret

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Author and photographer Andy Cochrane spent months crafting this route from home in Bend, Oregon, consulting with multiple Japanese mountain guides, before flying to Tokyo to bring it to life. Along with four others, he ran this 100-mile technical traverse across the Northern Alps in a week, staying at mountain huts and soaking in Japanese hospitality along the way.

It’s not often that a local guide recommends helmets for a hut-to-hut trail running trip, but it’s always a sign of a good adventure if you ask me.

A couple of months before flying across the Pacific to Japan, I was on a mid-afternoon Zoom call—my third such conversation of the week—when my jaw hit the floor. I was meeting virtually with guides in the Northern Alps to learn more about the trails and huts of the range, hoping to suss out if a line I had plotted on a map was actually a feasible endeavor to run.

At the time, I wasn’t sure if anyone had run the route before us. There certainly weren’t any blogs, articles, or posts I could find about it. Hut owners on the trip later confirmed my suspicion that our 100-mile, seven-day itinerary was pretty far out of the box. Connecting the outdoor hub of Kamikochi at the southern end of the range to the Sea of Japan in the north along a single ridge line was an unheard of idea to everyone we spoke with. That made it a lot more exciting—and far from certain it would work out. If it did, however, we would get to experience all that the Northern Alps had to offer in a single push.

Because the route required a mix of trail running, boulder hopping, ladder climbing, and Class 4 scrambling, our local guide Tatsuro was adamant that we bring helmets, even if their use wouldn’t be required every day. TL;DR: he was right.

Before I get into specifics of the route and experience, let’s set the scene. The Northern Alps, or Hida Mountains, are Japan’s most primal terrain. Although lesser-known than the mountain ranges of Europe, South America, or mainland Asia, the Northern Alps are just as technical and challenging, if not more so. The range is a jagged, granite spine that defies the country’s reputation for manicured serenity. Trails in the Hida are riddled with boulders, ladders, roots, scrambling, and thick brush. Located just a few dozen miles off the Sea of Japan, the weather is incredibly fickle in the Hida, too.

Geographically, the Northern Alps lie just a few hours drive west of Tokyo on the main island and stretch across Nagano, Toyama, Gifu, and Niigata prefectures. Most of the range is inside Chubu-Sangaku National Park, which protects around 670 square miles from being absorbed by the urban centers that surround it. The Hida are widely regarded as Japan’s premier alpine terrain and feature the country’s most developed hut system, Yamagoya. These staffed huts offer hot meals, sleeping mats, water, snacks, and beer, allowing for multi-day runs and traverses with lightweight packs sans camping gear—perfect for a trip like ours.

Three years ago I ran across the Southern Alps on an ancient postal route called Nakasendo. While the Southern and Northern Alps offer remarkably different terrain and technicality, my first trip taught me much about Japanese culture and logistics that was helpful while preparing for my return.

Perhaps my biggest takeaway from that initial experience was that the language barrier is a major challenge—especially in rural places, where many people don’t speak a lick of English. While apps like Google Translate can help to order a quick meal or get assistance with navigation in a pinch, planning a trip and booking mountain huts requires someone not only fluent in Japanese, but who also understands the mountain culture. For us, that liaison was Kota.

I was connected with Kota at Japan Adventures Co. through a friend, and I honestly can’t say enough good things about him. He is an incredibly organized planner, a great communicator, and an avid hiker and trail runner. He even helped negotiate our stay with a few huts that didn’t believe our route was possible, ensuring the entire trip ran smoothly. Kota and his team lead a variety of hiking, food, and cultural trips around Japan, and are currently rolling out new trail running itineraries in the Northern Alps and elsewhere.

With help from Kota and advice from guides like Tatsuro and Paul from Nagano Adventures, I was able to refine our route to stay at unique huts, run the best trails, and find a balance between challenging and doable for each day. It’s important to note that mountain huts in Japan are warm and welcoming, but they run on rigid schedules. Breakfast is typically at 5 a.m. and dinner is around 5 p.m. If you don’t check in by 4 p.m., they will notify search and rescue, so it’s important to start early and keep an eye on your pace throughout the day.

My goal was to start in Kamikochi and end at the Seas of Japan, creating a single linkup by connecting a number of popular two- and three-day hiking routes—the Panorama Ginza Route, Mount Yari, Ura Ginza Panorama Route, the ridgeline from Mount Eboshi and Funakubo-dake, the Hachimine Kiretto, the Kaerazu no Ken (ridge of no return), and Tsugami Shindo. It’s a mouthful to say, but when drawn on a map, the routes piece together nicely, forming a (mostly) straight line running from north to south.

Getting to and from the Northern Alps isn’t terribly difficult. After landing in Tokyo (either HND or NRT), a bullet train, or Shinkansen, will take you to Matsumoto in just a few hours. From there you can take a smaller train, bus, or taxi into the mountains to begin your adventure. Returning to Tokyo is just as easy by hopping on a bullet train in a coastal city like Toyama. There are plenty of stations to choose from and you usually can find seats just a day or two in advance.

There are a few ways to shuttle your luggage from the start to the finish, but I recommend Yamato Transport. Other options include dropping bags at the post office, the front desk if you’re staying in a hotel, or even convenience stores like Lawson’s or 7-Eleven. Though this might seem risky at face value, it worked flawlessly for us. We walked into a convenience store around 10 p.m., spent a meager ten minutes filling out the paperwork, and walked out. Our bags arrived at our final hotel just after we arrived seven days later.

Despite plenty of challenges, the trip ran as smoothly as I could have imagined. We dealt with heavy rain, 50 mph winds, and thick mist for our first few days, which forced us to slow down on the scrambling sections, layer up to stay warm, and take plenty of breaks in huts along the way. Some days had tons of vert (often more than 1,000 feet per mile) and rocky trails that made running difficult, so we embraced the shuffle. On day four, when covering our most remote section, we didn’t see a single other person. Fortunately the trails are well marked, even where they are less frequented and overgrown.

The crux of the route, the Kaerazu no Ken, is a long and serpentine downclimb on Class 4 granite slabs, offering a chain for protection in some areas while others did not. This was one of the dozen or so sections that having a helmet was a welcomed addition to our kits. For those comfortable with alpine climbing, this will feel like a fun change of pace. For those afraid of exposure, it’ll be challenging. The huts themselves vary considerably from small ridgetop outposts like Funakubo to much larger and busier outfits like Hakuba Sanso. Regardless of size, every hut owner we met was incredibly kind. Japanese hospitality is something they take very seriously.

Overall, our experience in the Hida was more than we could have asked for. Steep and technical trails, unique and cozy huts, fickle yet fruitful weather, and no other Americans or Europeans along the way. It’s an undiscovered gem for anyone outside Japan. With the help of Kota, Tatsuro, and others, I’m already planning a return trip next year.

One of the lightest climbing helmets on the market, the Vapor was perfect for our trip. We frequently had sections of running between scrambles and wouldn’t leave it on because it breathes so well. The Vapor fits over a hat and under a rain jacket hood, making it great for wet days, too.

The latest from Garmin is designed for routes like ours with a solar-powered display that ran the full week on a single charge. The maps were critical on wet days when I didn’t want to use my phone, and the flashlight was perfect for early mornings trying to not wake up other guests.

The perfect size pack for a trip like ours, the Adventure was able to carry everything we needed—spare clothes, first aid, snacks, camera, and ditty—with ease, plus poles, flasks, and a phone in the external pockets. It can be adjusted on the fly to reduce bounce and chafing.

On a week-long trip you end up eating a ton of snacks—gummies, chips, gels, and whatever you can buy at the huts—but nothing hit home like GU stroops. Whether it was with morning tea, on the top of a big climb, or preventing a bonk, stroops played a big role in our success.

With major improvements from the previous version, the Speedgoat 7 was the perfect shoe for this trip, offering plenty of grip on technical scrambles and ladders, a comfortable and cushy ride for the long days, and a lay-flat tongue that kept most rocks and dirt out.

The perfect mid-layer for cool mornings or windy days, the Dawner breathes well and is quite comfortable next to skin. The exterior is stretchy and durable, which is great for running through brush and rubbing against rocks— an inevitability in terrain like the Northern Alps.

#8315. The Biggest Mule Deer Bucks of All Time, According to Boone & Crockett Records

The all-time top typical mule deer in Boone & Crockett records is the Doug Burris Jr. Buck, taken in Colorado's San Juan National Forest in 1972 with a score of 226 4/8 inches. To crack the top five in either category, a typical must measure at least 216 inches and a non-typical must surpass 324 inches.

The Boone & Crockett Club has been keeping meticulous records of the continent’s most impressive big game animals for more than a century. In that time, thousands of mulie bucks have made the books, but the top five spots for either the typical or non-typical category are rarely touched. One of the oldest entries dates to the turn of the century, for example, and the most recent top-five record book buck is still three decades old.

The minimum score for entry into the B&C books is 180 for a typical mule deer and 215 for a non-typical. But if you want to break into the top 5 you’ll need to bag a typical measuring at least 216—or a non-typical that surpasses the 324-inch mark . Good luck with that, but in the meantime you can at least read up on the current record book bucks below.

Doug Burris traveled from San Antonio, Texas to hunt mulies in Colorado’s San Juan National Forest in 1972 and ended up killing what is still the number one typical mule deer in the B&C books. According to lore, he rattled in six good bucks that day before stalking through a gambel oak thicket to shoot the 226 4/8 inch beauty pictured below. Today, the mount can be viewed at a Cabellas store in Delores County, Colorado.

Little is known about this buck or the hunter who shot it. But we do know that his name was Lars Svenson, and he harvested the iconic mulie buck with a .32 cailber rifle in 1948, somewhere near the Saskatchewan River. Lars apparently had no interest in getting it scored. Thankfully, his grandson did. The official B&C score is 214 4/6 inches. The rest is a mystery.

The Hoback Buck was killed in a Canyon south of Jackson Hole, Wyoming in 1925. B&C says that whoever shot it was a meat hunter, completely unconcerned with the massive antlers atop the buck’s head.

Thankfully, an unnamed ranch hand found and saved the buck’s discarded rack, which hung on the wall of a popular Jackson Hole saloon for years before B&C got ahold of it and issued it a score of 217 inches. That score stood as number one until the aforementioned Burris buck came along in 1972. Today, the Hoback Buck’s horns are hanging for all to see in the Jackson Hole Museum.

The most recent mule deer in our top-ten list wasn’t taken by a human hunter, and it’s the only Arizona mulie to ever make B&C’s top-ten typical list. The buck’s head was picked up in 1994 by Steven Stayner, who was searching for deer along the rimrock of Cococino County at the time. According to B&C, it was killed by a lion, but its rack was still in impeccable shape when Stayner found it. With an official score of 216 6/8, it is currently on display at Johnny Morris’ Wonders of Wildlife National Museum and Aquarium in Springfield, Missouri.

Idaho’s lone top-ten mulie was shot by the sheriff of Franklin County in 1961. Ray Talbot reportedly killed the buck near Worm Creek. Since then, it’s been showcased at an Idaho Fish and Game office in Boise, the Boone & Crockett headquarters in Cody, Wyoming, and at the Museum of Natural History in Washington, D.C.

Little is known about the Gary Alberston buck, except that it was killed in Uinta County, Wyoming one year before Talbot got his Idaho record. Both racks score exactly 215 5/8 inches.

Ed Broder shot his record-setting buck while hunting near Edmonton, Alberta in the fall of 1926. According to Boone & Crockett, he drove a Model T Ford to the terminus of a rural road and then hired a horse and sleigh to take him to a hunting camp on the south shore of Chip Lake.

He hiked out of the camp he was sharing with two friends at 1 o’clock in the afternoon, following deer tracks and toting a .32 Winchester Special. When he saw the buck pictured below, he trained the rifle on its spine and dropped it with a single shot.

Decades later, one of Broder’s sons sold the famous rack to an antler collector, unbeknownst to his siblings. The 355 2/8 inch rack brought six figures, but Don Broder spent six days in jail for selling it without permission from his fellow heirs.

Information about the hunt that took this incredible mulie buck is speculative at best. According to Boone & Crockett, the mount was given as a gift to a lieutenant governor of British Columbia who served from 1892 to 1897, and the buck might have been killed by a Native American hunter with a bow in the Okanagan Valley.

It wasn’t scored by B&C judges until 1955, after spending time on display at the International Hunting Exhibition in Vienna, Austria. With a combined 47 points (24 on the right side and 23 on the left), it’s the second-biggest non-typical mulie of all time.

Utah’s Hunsaker buck may sport the gnarliest and most unique set of antlers ever grown by a North American cervid. It was taken in 1943 in Box Elder, County by Alton Hunsaker, who was hunting from horseback in Baldhead Canyon near the state’s southwest corner. Like Ed Broder, Hunsaker took his B&C record with a trusty .32 Winchester Special. At 330 and 1/8 inches, it’s still the largest ever recorded in Beehive State history—and the number 3 non-typical mulie buck of all time.

Hunter Clifton Fauria shot this non-typical giant with a .270 in Nye County, Nevada in 1955, but he died a year later and it wasn’t measured by Boone & Crockett until 1991. All told, it has 46 scorable points—22 on one side and 24 on the other—which landed it a 325 1/8 inch score. It reportedly weighed in at 300 pounds after Fauria shot it in the Stoneberger Basin—which lies in Austin-Tonopah Ranger District near Austin, Nevada. It’s still the biggest mulie ever taken in Nevada.

Arizona’s Kaibab Plateau is a legendary mule deer destination, and the so-called Murphy buck only adds to the lore. In fact, five of the top 10 Arizona non-typicals were taken on the Kaibab. William L. Murphy shot his on November 14, 1943, and the massive rack stayed under the radar for 30 years before his son-in-law finally sent it in to B&C for scoring. The deer had an astonishing 43 and 4/8-inch inside spread and scored 324 and 1/8.

Travis is Field & Stream's full-time associate editor. He covers breaking outdoor news and pressing conservation issues.

#8314. The Best Survival Gear of 2026, According to a Preparedness Expert

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more

The world we live in is full of surprises, some of them not so pleasant. Whether it’s a natural disaster, getting lost on a deer hunt, or unexpected breakdowns in everyday systems, having the right survival gear could make the difference between thriving or just getting by. These days, being prepared isn’t about paranoia; it’s about practical foresight. A solid collection of survival gear—beyond just a trusty backpack—should include tools, shelter, fire starters, and medical supplies to help you stay safe when things go south.

Not all survival gear is created equal, though. The last thing you want in an emergency is for your equipment to fail when you need it most. Whether it’s a multi-tool that won’t rust, a fire starter that works even in the rain, or a med pouch that holds all you need, we’ve sifted through the countless options on the market to narrow down the essential items that can genuinely save your life in a pinch.

The Hill People Gear Umlindi stands out as a top-tier survival pack for those who value functionality, durability, and versatility. Built with rugged materials, this pack is designed to withstand the harshest conditions, whether navigating dense forests, scaling mountains, or trekking through unpredictable weather. Its 500D Cordura construction ensures it can take a beating without compromising performance, while the thoughtful design minimizes points of failure, such as weak zippers or seams. This level of durability makes it a reliable choice when you’re far from civilization and need a bug out bag you can count on.

Its innovative layout and modularity set the Umlindi apart from other packs. At 30 liters, it’s the perfect size for a range of survival situations—small enough to be portable and easy to carry yet large enough to store essential gear like shelter, water, food, and medical supplies. It integrates very well with other Hill People Gear pockets and add-ons, as well as third-party makers (see Tuff Possum Gear Med Pouch below).

One standout feature of the Hill People Gear Umlindi is its exceptionally stable carrying chassis. Combining the Umlindi’s delta straps and the optional belted system integrates the pack seamlessly with the wearer, making it feel like an extension of the body rather than just something you’re hauling. This design connects the pack to the wearer’s core and lower back, maximizing strength and stability and allowing for better control and comfort during long treks or challenging terrain.

The radio purists will not like this choice, but it still stands out as the best choice as a starter radio. With that said, I have used these walkie talkies for years without issue. The Baofeng UV-5R Pro 8W is a versatile and powerful handheld radio designed to meet various communication needs, whether outdoors, at home, or in the workplace. With its tri-power settings (8W/4W/1W), you can easily switch between high, medium, or low power depending on your situation, ensuring you can conserve battery life when necessary or extend your range when conditions demand it. The radio has a rechargeable 3800 mAh Li-ion battery with power-saving features to maximize usage time. A low-battery alarm conveniently reminds you when to recharge, ensuring you’re never caught without power. Additionally, this model supports keyboard and PC programming, allowing for complete customization and ease of use with CHIRP software, making it an ideal choice for beginners and experienced radio enthusiasts.

This upgraded version also includes an AT-771 High Gain Long Antenna and the standard antenna, allowing you to boost your range when needed, especially in remote or challenging environments. It also has valuable features, including VOX (voice-operated exchange), a built-in LED flashlight, scanning, monitoring, and an emergency alarm. With all of these functionalities, this handheld radio is reliable and adaptable, making it perfect for ham radio enthusiasts, outdoor adventurers, or anyone needing dependable communication equipment.

4Patriots emergency survival food in a mini tote is a top-tier option for ensuring you’re prepared when disaster strikes. In an emergency, your priority is food, and both FEMA and the Red Cross recommend having a supply of non-perishable food on hand. This compact kit makes it easy to build your survival stockpile, with 84 servings of delicious, easy-to-prepare meals providing around 1,320 calories per day—more than enough to sustain you through a crisis. Plus, it’s conveniently packaged in a mini tote, making it easy to store and discreet, a perfect addition to any preparedness plan or a thoughtful gift for loved ones. Our experts even dubbed it some of the best survival food of all the options we’ve tested.

This emergency food kit stands out because of its durability and long shelf life. Designed to last up to 25 years, the meals are packaged in “disaster-resistant” packaging that protects them from damage and spoilage, ensuring they’re ready whenever needed. Hand-packed in the USA, each kit comes with a 100% money-back satisfaction guarantee, giving you peace of mind with your purchase. And with free shipping and handling within the USA’s lower 48 states, it’s a hassle-free way to ensure you’re equipped with one of the most critical survival elements—food.

The Sawyer Squeeze System is an outstanding choice for anyone needing reliable access to clean water in the backcountry or while traveling. Whether hiking, camping, hunting, fishing, preparing for emergencies, or traveling abroad, this water filter covers you. Its 0.1-micron absolute filtration effectively removes 99.9% of harmful bacteria like salmonella and E. coli and 99.9% of protozoa such as giardia and cryptosporidium. Independent testing supports its effectiveness, making it a top choice for those who prioritize safety and health while adventuring.

What sets the Sawyer Squeeze apart is its ease of use. The system comes with a reusable pouch that you can fill up at any water source, screw the filter directly onto the pouch, and either drink straight from it or squeeze the water into another container. This versatility makes it ideal for different scenarios, whether on a day hike or setting up a multi-day camp. The compact design makes it easy to carry and lightweight enough not to weigh you down on the trail. Plus, the filter comes with a great warranty and is rigorously tested by Sawyer to ensure optimal performance, giving you peace of mind that it will work when needed.

Overall, the Sawyer Squeeze Water Filter is a top-tier solution for ensuring access to clean water in any situation. Its thorough filtration, ease of use, portability, and great warranty make it an excellent investment for anyone who spends time outdoors or wants to be prepared for emergencies.

The LT Wright Handcrafted Knives Genesis is a meticulously designed survival and bushcraft tool that excels in craftsmanship and functionality. With an overall length of 9 inches and a sharpened edge of 4.25 inches, this knife is the perfect size for a wide range of outdoor tasks, from feathering wood for a fire to more intricate carving work. Made from 1/8″ A2 steel, the Genesis boasts a high-polished Scandi grind and complex micro-buffed for a razor-sharp edge that ensures smooth, precise cuts with minimal drag. This knife is built to work and last, with every detail carefully crafted to meet the demands of bushcraft enthusiasts and survivalists alike.

One of the standout features of the Genesis is its durable Micarta handle, designed for comfort and long-term use even in harsh conditions. LT Wright goes the extra mile by ensuring that the epoxy adheres to the scales and completely seals the brass pins and lanyard holes, providing superior water resistance and longevity. Thumb scallops and a sharpened spine add to the knife’s versatility, allowing for comfortable grips and easy fire-starting with a ferro rod. With its matte finish and ergonomic design, the Genesis tool looks great and performs exceptionally well in the field.

Whether you’re an experienced outdoorsman or just starting to build your bushcraft kit, the Genesis is a reliable, high-quality survival knife that stands out in any collection. Its balance of size, strength, and detailed craftsmanship ensures it can handle whatever your next adventure throws.

The Gransfors Bruk Small Forest Axe strikes the perfect balance between portability and power, making it a versatile tool for backcountry adventurers and survivalists. With a larger head and more extended handle than the Wildlife Hatchet, this axe delivers significantly more chopping power while still being compact enough to fit into a rucksack. This makes it an ideal choice for those looking for a tool that can handle severe tasks like felling small trees and limbing but without the bulk of a full-sized axe. Its carefully designed weight distribution and sharp edge provide efficient cuts, reducing the effort required for chopping, even on hard wood like we have here in Kentucky.

Crafted by Gransfors Bruk, known for their high-quality, hand-forged tools, the Small Forest axe is built to last. The head is meticulously shaped to balance strength and precision, and the handle is designed for comfort during prolonged use. Whether building a shelter, prepping firewood, or clearing a trail, this axe provides the control and durability needed for various wilderness tasks. It has a protective sheath to keep the blade safe when not in use, ensuring that it remains sharp and ready for action when needed.

This bushcraft axe offers unmatched versatility for those needing a compact yet powerful tool. It’s small enough to be carried easily in your gear but powerful enough to handle demanding chopping tasks, making it an essential part of any kit. Whether deep in the woods or just preparing for a weekend camping trip, this axe delivers performance and reliability you can count on.

The Solkoa Fastfire cubes are some of today’s most reliable fire-starting tinders and kindling accelerants. Engineered to ignite quickly and burn fiercely, these cubes are ideal for anyone who spends time outdoors, whether you’re camping, hunting, or preparing for survival situations. Designed to perform in adverse conditions, the Fastfire tinders are hydrophobic, meaning they resist water and can produce a wind-resistant flame that burns even when wet. With a low flash point and the ability to sustain a 1,300-degree flame, these cubes provide peace of mind, knowing you’ll be able to get a fire started no matter how bad the conditions.

Each cube burns vigorously for 10-12 minutes, enough time to ignite more significant pieces of wood or other kindling. If you want to extend the burn time, you can divide the cube into eight smaller pieces, each capable of burning for 2-3 minutes, offering up to 16-24 minutes of flame in total. The compact size at just over an inch and light weight (0.2 ounces per cube) make them easy to carry in any survival kit or emergency pack, while the heavy-duty foil laminate wrap ensures long-term storage for at least 10 years.

The Bic Classic lighter will not have any awards for being the coolest or most alluring. One of our experts’ favorite camping lighters, it is a nostalgic and reliable tool for fire-starting that has been trusted by outdoor enthusiasts, survivalists, and everyday users for decades. It’s compact, lightweight, and easy to use, making it perfect for hiking, camping, or emergency preparedness. Its durable design allows it to withstand various conditions, and its consistent flame makes lighting a fire or starting a stove quick and straightforward. With a long lifespan, a single Bic lighter can provide hundreds of ignitions, ensuring you have access to fire whenever you need it most.

What sets the Bic lighter apart is its simplicity and dependability. The lightweight plastic body makes it easy to carry in a pocket, pack, or survival kit, while its child-resistant safety features ensure it’s safe to keep on hand. With no moving parts or complex mechanisms, the lighter provides a wind-resistant flame and performs reliably in most conditions. Whether you’re lighting a campfire or preparing for an emergency, the Bic lighter remains a convenient and efficient tool for fire-starting, earning its place as a staple in any gear collection.

We don’t just review gear—we put it to the test in the most challenging conditions. At my school, companies seek professional consultation on a wide range of survival gear because they know we put it all to a lot of use. In addition, over the years, thousands of students have brought every type of gear imaginable to our classes.  From budget-friendly to high-end, we’ve seen it all in action. Through real-world use and, in many cases, their outright abuse, we’ve learned firsthand which gear holds up under pressure and which falls short. This hands-on experience allows us to confidently recommend the tools and equipment that can truly stand up to survival challenges.

When selecting survival gear, several key factors can make all the difference. Durability is crucial—your equipment must withstand harsh environments and repeated use without failing when you need it most. At the same time, staying within your budget is essential; high-quality gear doesn’t always have to break the bank, and there are reliable options for every price range. Portability is another vital consideration—your gear should be lightweight and compact enough to carry easily without sacrificing functionality. Finally, integration matters—each item in your kit should work seamlessly with the rest, ensuring that your tools, shelter, and medical supplies complement one another for maximum efficiency and effectiveness in any emergency.

For more than 125 years, Field & Stream has been providing readers with honest and authentic coverage of outdoor gear. Our writers and editors eat, sleep, and breathe the outdoors, and that passion comes through in our product reviews. You can count on F&S to keep you up to date on the best new gear. And when we write about a product—whether it’s a bass lure or a backpack—we cover the good and the bad, so you know exactly what to expect before you decide to make a purchase.

Craig Caudill is the award-winning Director of Nature Reliance School. He has led backcountry, survival and leadership programs for the US Military, Corporate work groups and thousands of civilians. Highlights Education Caudill has a BBA from the University of Kentucky in Statistical Analysis. He is a Certified Master Naturalist from the University of Kentucky and a Level 2 Naturalist through the Kamana Naturalist Program. He has completed man-tracking coursework with Tyr Group, David Scott-Donelan Man-tracking, Hulls Tracking Services and Enhanced Tracking Applications. Experience Caudill is designated by the US Federal government as a subject matter expert on the topics of survival and man-tracking skills. He is the author of the following: Extreme Wilderness Survival, Ultimate Wilderness Gear, and The Secret Signs of Nature, and the co-author of Author of Essential Wilderness Navigation. Fun Fact Caudill has endured two different 30-day trips into a wilderness with only a knife. Notable Work

#8313. Why Québec is the Ultimate East Coast Ski Destination

Owl's Head Ski Resort at sunset. (Photo: Cantons-de-l'Est © Cantons-de-l'Est/BBT Productions)

Nope, it’s not too much to ask: You can get great snow, both natural and man-made, wild terrain, incredible food, historic architecture, and rich cultural immersion all with just a short drive and no time zone change. That’s right. In Québec, winter is so good it feels like it should be hard to get to, but it’s just across the border.

Let’s start with the snow. Canada’s French-speaking province boasts some of the nation’s highest annual snowfall, with up to 250 inches per year. And you’ll find it in every form: deep powder, groomed tracks, and perfect corduroy, spread across terrain that varies from steep and wild to mellow and peaceful. And all that snow comes with dozens of vibrant mountain towns and more than 70 ski resorts—all within a stone’s throw of the Lower 48. (Montréal is just a 90-minute flight or six-hour drive from Boston, and New Yorkers can reach Québec City in less than two hours by air.)

Next, enjoy the rewards of going wherever the path of adventure takes you. The size of the province means you have lots of choices, but rest assured you can’t go wrong: in Québec, skiable terrain unfolds in nearly every direction. The only question is what kind of ski experience you’re looking for. Here’s what you’ll find in the four ski regions featured here—plus which resorts to hit to make the most of it

Looking for spectacular scenery? Unbelievably long runs? Buttery maritime snowpack coming in off the St. Lawrence River? Northeast of Québec City, you’ll find all three in Charlevoix, where the steep slopes of Le Massif de Charlevoix hover over the water, serving up mountain-meets-river views that are totally unique, and plunging valleys and sweeping bowls attract skiers looking to test their skills amid the serene quiet of a Québécois winter. Le Massif serves up the biggest vertical drop east of the Canadian Rockies, while Mont Grand-Fonds offers a compact layout, laid-back atmosphere, and terrain for all ability levels.

Use Québec City as your base camp and you won’t have to choose between good skiing and vibrant arts and culture. The province’s capital is an enchanting maze of European architecture and historic neighborhoods. An evening walk downtown feels like a wander through a snow-draped fairytale. The food and bar scene reflects a similar blend between time-honored traditions and modern flair. And at just 30 minutes from Mont-Sainte-Anne, it’s close enough to the slopes that you can fully immerse yourself in the true Québecois lifestyle without cutting into your ski time.

Close to Montréal, the Laurentian Mountains are speckled with charming, Alps-style villages—complete with classy accommodations, spas, bistros, and microbreweries—that support a robust après-ski tradition. Mont Tremblant offers a stunning variety of terrain, including both gentle runs and enough steep-and-deep to challenge the experts. Meanwhile, Mont-Blanc and Sommet Saint-Sauveur boast quieter settings, family-friendly atmospheres, and five-star night skiing.

The lush, forested mountains southeast of Montréal are densely packed with ski areas, making this the perfect region for some serious resort-hopping. Even better: with the L’EST GO Pass, you can nab discounted lift tickets on four of the zone’s best hills. If you like night skiing, head to Bromont, a local favorite that opens more than 90 runs after sunset. Prefer the solitude of the deep woods? Head to nearby Mont Sutton for world-class tree skiing and a far wilder feel. Laid-back resorts like Owl’s Head cater to families, while Mont-Orford’s high elevation makes it a motherlode of high-quality snow.

Each of the four ski regions featured here has its own distinct personality. What connects them is Québec’s unmistakable joie de vivre: a love of local flavours, lively après-ski, and taking fun seriously. It’s what makes a ski getaway here so full of character.

Québec isn’t far from America’s East Coast, but it feels like another universe. The province boasts a unique culture defined by its French language, historic neighborhoods, local cuisine, and a dynamic craft beer scene. In its urban areas, you’ll find 17th-century colonial architecture, complete with narrow streets, turrets, and flagstone courtyards.

Leave the urban centers, and historic brick quickly gives way to winter’s snow-flocked evergreens and white-blanket pastures. Barns and silos dot the countryside, and just beyond, mountains rear into the skyline like 5,000-foot beacons calling skiers home.

Québec’s unique combination of proximity and novelty make it one of the most unique ski destinations in North America. And yet it’s not nearly as pricey as some of the other life-list destinations you might have on your list. With the American to Canadian Dollar exchange rate, accommodations and food in Québec tend to offer a strong value on a complete ski trip, especially for U.S. travelers. To make the most of that value, explore ski packages and resort offers across Québec on maneige.ski to find the right getaway for your next winter adventure.

Between its vast and varied terrain, deep snow, rich culture, easy access, and affordable prices, Québec has everything skiers need to squeeze more adventure out of winter. Whether you’re looking for more terrain, more culture, or more discovery, you’ll find it here.

Ready to take your ski adventure further? From breathtaking mountain views and exhilarating runs to vibrant après-ski and charming resort villages, Québec offers much more than great skiing. Explore the regions and plan your winter getaway with Bonjour Québec.

#8312. Christopher Wren, Climber and Legendary Reporter, Had a “Wry Sense of Humor”

Christopher Wren at basecamp during the 1974 Pamir Expedition. In this photo, he is using a typewriter to draft the New York Times story that revealed the deaths of American climber Gary Ullin and eight Soviet female climbers. (Photo: Courtesy of Jed Williamson)

Christopher Sale Wren served as The New York Times bureau chief in Moscow, Cairo, Beijing, Ottawa, and Johannesburg. His creative life was deeply intertwined with a respect for nature, big expeditions and the many people he met on assignment. He passed at his home in Vermont on February 15, 2026, at age 89.

Wren began climbing as a student at Dartmouth, where he sometimes felt out of place, according to his daughter, Celia. A scholarship student whose parents were actors, he had little interest in fraternity life. In the outdoors, he found a bigger sense of kinship. He learned to climb with the college’s mountaineering club, practicing on campus at Bartlett Tower and on the nearby cliffs of Orford and Owl’s Head. According to Samuel C. Silverstein’s memorial in The American Alpine Journal, he once ended a public-speaking assignment on mountaineering by rappelling out of the classroom’s third-floor window.

In 1962, Wren joined the six-man team that made the first ascent of Denali’s Southeast Spur (Alaska grade 4, 65-degree ice). The expedition became the subject of his first major article for Look magazine, merging his climbing with his reporting into a career he chased around the world.

Twelve years later, while stationed in Moscow for the Times, he joined an American expedition to the Pamirs. On Lenin Peak (23,406ft), Wren and fellow climbers Jock Glidden and Allen Steck encountered members of a Soviet women’s team who had died in a storm. His reporting brought their tragedy to the Times front page, breaking the news of deaths Soviet authorities had kept secret.

For Jed Williamson, who was also on the Pamirs expedition, Wren’s contribution to mountaineering extended to his ability to tell its stories. “What he really brought to the mountaineering scene was his ability to write about it and put it out there,” Williamson said. “He had a really good sense of humor. He could turn a situation that one might not think was so humorous into one that was humorous.”

Even when faced with tragedy, Wren found a way to bring levity to dangerous moments. Celia remembered one story her father told about provisioning the Pamirs expedition. The American climbers wanted peanut butter, which he couldn’t find in Soviet shops. Instead, he packed tins of caviar for protein. “His teammates thought it was disgusting,” she remembers. “But he was a Renaissance man with an incredible sense of humor.”

Wren played guitar and banjo and wrote songs, two of which Johnny Cash recorded: Jesus Was a Carpenter and Gospel Road. “It was a fun thing that he did, and he was good at it,” Williamson said. “But he was never a chest pounder about that kind of thing.”

At home, Wren’s appetite for being outside became part of family life. During the family’s years in the Soviet Union, Celia remembered her father heading out on skis, pulling her and her brother behind him on a sled. He penned numerous books, from a biography of Johnny Cash to Walking to Vermont, an account of his roughly 400-mile walk home from Manhattan after retiring from The New York Times.

Williamson remembers that despite the breadth of his traveling and range of his accomplishments, Wren was down-to-earth.  “He wasn’t aloof or standoffish or anything like that,” he said. “He was happy to share.”

Late into retirement, he continued to ski and ride his mountain bike around the nearby lake. Celia remembered his ability to keep moving ahead. When recalling difficult experiences, he would often say, “Well, you know, that’s all behind us now.”
