#8298. At This Resort, The Owner is Driving A Snowcat, Turning Wrenches, and Fixing Broken Fences

I’d never ridden a ski lift with the person who owns the mountain below us before, so I’m not sure if this is common.

But as we chugged from the Ski Santa Fe’s base toward its 11,075-foot peak, Ben Abruzzo noted a chairlift returning to the base that sounded squeaky, a groomer that needed tending, and an orange safety fence that had fallen over. Abruzzo—whose day was charged with showing this writer around the mountain his family has owned since the mid-1980s—interrupted his responses to any of my questions on more than a few occasions, apologizing before speaking into a small walkie-talkie mounted on his chest. He instructed this person or that to address the various tiny issues that must pop up a million times a day on a mountain, acting more like a manager than The Guy Who Owns the Mountain.

Over the course of a single lift ride, it became clear how much Abruzzo not only cared about the experience of the roughly 250,000 visitors who enjoy his family’s mountain every year but also about the mountain itself. It makes sense once you realize that Ski Santa Fe is, in a way, woven into the very fabric of the person Abruzzo is.

“It’s all I’ve ever known,” Ben said, as the lift neared Ski Santa Fe’s peak, the mountain he described as his “lifelong backyard.”

Owners and CEOs often love to say that their businesses are like a family. However, for the Abruzzos, Ski Santa Fe is not only their family business, but it’s their ancestral home.

Ben is the third-generation owner of Ski Santa Fe, following in the footsteps of his grandfather, his father, and two of his uncles, who finalized the purchase of the mountain in 1985. It was hardly a lark, as the elder Abruzzo purchased the Sandia Peak Ski Area in nearby Albuquerque in the late 1950s.

Their familial sensibility permeates much of Abruzzo’s staff. His grooming manager has worked at the mountain for thirty years. His operations manager as well. The mountain’s ticketing manager bests them both, with 32 years of service.

“I think it’s because we treat our folks right,” Abruzzo said, pointing out that when he says ‘we,’ he doesn’t just mean his father, his late grandfather, his uncles, and any other Abruzzo who’s spent time working the mountain. “Our mountain manager, our operations manager, all of our full-time staff; they’re all invested because they’re all part of this community.”

Abruzzo started working on the mountain when he was 12, at first building mountain bike trails in the summer and working in the rental shop during the season. After commissioning as an infantry officer in 2001, Abruzzo deployed to Afghanistan with the Army’s 101st Airborne Division during the height of the Global War on Terror. Abruzzo returned home in 2005, working as an area manager at Sandia Peak. He relocated to Ski Santa Fe in 2010, eventually taking over the mountain shortly before the Covid-19 pandemic.

And even though he owns the ski area, Ben still drives snowcats, still turns wrenches when chairlifts need tending. And he requires the same of all the mountain’s senior staff.

“We expect all of our managers to be well-versed in the blue-collar side of things,” he said. “And that includes me.”

Sitting high in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, Ski Santa Fe is about a thirty-minute drive from the heart of the famously artsy city in northern New Mexico. Of course, snowy days and weekends might impact that commute time, Abruzzo admits, despite the fact that the mountain has its own dedicated road crew charged with plowing the two-lane road leading up to Ski Santa Fe. Still, as Ski Santa Fe is the only ski area in the vicinity, it’s a drive that never feels out of reach for locals and visitors alike.

In a more corporate environment, that dearth of options could provide owners an excuse to rest on their proverbial laurels. However, Abruzzo sees that scarcity as an honor to uphold. If people only have one option, it’d better be a good one.

With 88 total trails, almost evenly split across blacks, blues, and greens, a trio of terrain parks, and 1,800 feet of vertical drop, all serviced by a double lift, two triple lifts, two quad lifts, two surface lifts, and a high-speed detachable lift, the mountain is far bigger and more diverse than you might think when you hear “family-owned ski area.”

But beyond all that, Ski Santa Fe is known by locals and regulars for two main reasons: first, its off-piste skiing. And second, its snowmaking capabilities.

On the day we spent together, snow fell from the sky in big, thick flakes. It was one of the 20 or so powder days Ski Santa Fe gets each season. The tops of tall pine trees, buried in some 200 inches of snow, poked out of the thick layers of powder. It was a relatively unfamiliar sensation to this lifelong East Coaster who is far better versed in riding ice than he is powder.

Still, Abruzzo assured, even when it’s human-made, Ski Santa Fe’s snow is some of the best and most consistent there is.

“We make very dry snow,” Abruzzo said, before pointing out how the mountain’s 42 snow guns and 5-million-gallon storage tank allow them to cover most of the mountain in snow throughout the season. “It’s dry to the point where we have had snow gun companies write us a custom setting. And what you get is a much nicer surface to ski on that stays nice longer.”

A little shy of halfway down one of our day’s runs, Abruzzo cut from one groomer to another and, suddenly, a rustic, two-story shack stood surrounded by a small sea of skiers and snowboarders, each of whom seemed to have a beer, a cocktail, or a hot chocolate in hand.

At 10,500 feet, Totemoff’s sits higher than the peaks of many ski areas in North America.

And while there was no entertainment beyond some music playing over the speakers, Abruzzo assured me that Totemoff’s often plays host to live music. Above the bar, apartments for Abruzzo’s family and staff really hammer home the idea of how deeply entwined the Abruzzo family is in this mountain.

As we sat chatting over a pair of light beers, the talk eventually came back to the Abruzzo family, their lifelong marriage to this mountain. I ask Ben what it’s been like having three generations of Abruzzos run a mountain together. He quickly corrects me.

“Both of my kids work here,” he said with a laugh. “So, it’s actually four generations.”

#8297. What Matters Most to Jimmy Chin? The Oscar-Winning Director on Fear, Parenting, and His New Book.

(Photo: National Geographic/Savannah Cummins)

When Jimmy Chin was in his twenties, living out of a 1989 Subaru Loyale somewhere between Yosemite and the Tetons, he kept trying to explain climbing to his father. His father, a librarian at Mankato State University in Minnesota, would listen, and then say: “Our language is 5,000 years old, and there is no word for what you do.”

Chin has spent the decades since building a vocabulary for it anyway, as a climber, a photographer, and the Oscar-winning director of Free Solo featuring Alex Honnold, and his latest film, Everest: The Other Side, which documents Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson’s attempt to climb and ski down the North Face of the world’s tallest mountain.

His new book, Rules to Live By (Celadon), presents other people’s words, but is also part memoir. It’s built from ten conversations with people who have lived on their own terms: Yvon Chouinard, Yo-Yo Ma, Simone Biles, Ridley Scott, Kelly Slater, Annette Bening, Lynsey Addario, Kris Tompkins, Alex Honnold, and Bill King, a retired command master chief of SEAL Team 6. He asks each of them some version of the same question: In the end, what really matters? And in the end, we learn what matters most to Jimmy Chin as well.

Earlier this month, I sat down with Chin onstage at the Bell House in Brooklyn. It was his first book event, and he confessed he hadn’t reread the book since turning it in. “There’s a reason I’m a filmmaker,” he told the crowd. “Writing is really, really difficult.” What followed covered violin practice, an undisclosed military base, and a missing sock. The conversation has been edited and condensed.

OUTSIDE: You write that you’re “the only son of an only son of an only son.” That sounds like a lot of pressure.

Jimmy Chin: I started violin when I was three, and it became two hours of practice a day. Then martial arts, two hours a day. Then homework. That was my weekdays, and it was all I knew. But I learned discipline, and there was a very high expectation for excellence. My dad always said, “If you’re going to do it, you might as well do it well.” I hated that. Sometimes I still struggle with it.

There’s a scene in the book where you’re practicing violin, staring out the window at the forest. When did the forest win?

Chin: Anytime I did well in school, my reward was running off into the woods. There were no rules out there. My parents were librarians, so I always had a lot of books, and later, when they asked how I ended up doing this, I said, “It’s your fault. You gave me all these books.” I found climbing in college, and it was the first thing that felt like a calling. Growing up, I literally thought there were three jobs: lawyer, doctor, or professor. So after graduation I told my parents I’d take one year off, get it out of my system, and then pursue my real career. Which was a total lie. From 21 to 28 I lived out of my car, or in a cave in Camp 4, or in a chicken coop in Jackson.

Chin: My sister, who went to Stanford and worked at Yale for 18 years, was my huge advocate. I’d ask her how Mom was doing, and she’d say, “Mom just keeps saying, ‘I raised a homeless man.” With my dad, I deeply wanted him to understand me. People see the films and photographs and ask about the greatest risk I’ve ever taken. It definitely wasn’t a mountain. It was being in my early twenties, full of doubt. There are a lot of storm days, sitting in a cave with water dripping, soaking wet, thinking, What am I doing here? Meanwhile your friends are going to grad school and starting careers.

And during this time, you were in a reggae band.

Chin: I dropped violin after high school and picked up the guitar. The furthest thing I could think of from a concerto in D minor was covering Bob Marley. The whole band was classically trained kids. Everybody was technically skilled, so we could play whatever we wanted.

How did you choose the ten people in the book?

Chin: My documentaries take four, five, six, seven years. You have to bleed for them. You can only make so many films in a lifetime, and there are so many people I admire who I’ll never make a film about. I wanted the book to be a constellation: totally different backgrounds, totally different careers. After these extraordinary lives, what have you discovered really matters? What did success look like when you started, and what does it look like now? I had just turned 50, so I was looking back at my life in phases and thinking about what was to come.

Chin: After Meru, producers kept asking what was next. I mentioned to my friend Evan Hayes, who became a producer on Free Solo, that I’d been thinking about a documentary about Alex. I hadn’t even finished his name before he said, “That’s it.” National Geographic green-lit it immediately. I hadn’t even made a pitch deck.

I’d been filming and photographing Alex for ten years. I’ve worked with some of the greatest adventure athletes of our time, people at the pinnacle of their sports. All of them were anomalies within their sport. In my mind, Alex was an anomaly among anomalies. Even athletes at that level were confounded by what he was doing.

So I called him: “Good news, the film’s green-lit.” He said, “Great, because I’m thinking about soloing El Cap.” I said, “No. Not making that film.” I literally called Evan and said, “I’m out. Done.”

Chin: Among his friends, none of us would even talk about that idea. We didn’t want to put it in the ether. We’d seen the trajectory. He soloed Moonlight Buttress, which was outrageous. Then he soloed Half Dome. We were talking about breaking speed records on Half Dome, not free soloing it. It wasn’t hard to see what came after that. We just didn’t want to say it out loud. And then he dropped it in my lap. My fear was obvious: What if filming him causes him to fall? That’s not something I could live with.

Chin: He was going to do it anyway. I knew Alex really well. I took him on his first international expedition, and we’d done so much together. And I trusted him. Alex was the most calculated person I’d ever met. He had instinct, he was extremely smart, and it was never about external validation. He’s also straightforward, to a fault. He’s been well trained by now, with all the awards. But when I first met him, he’d say things and we’d be like, “You can’t say that.” If he isn’t comfortable doing something, he’ll tell you, and tell you why it’s stupid.

So we moved forward, and I gave my crew three rules. They were almost all elite professional climbers, because that’s the only team you could have: a short list of people who are both. Number one, we’re his friends first. Second, we’re climbers; you think like a climber before you pull out the camera. Third, we’re filmmakers. The film’s needs can never supersede Alex’s needs.

People saw the brain scan in the film and decided Alex was superhuman. You write that he resents that.

Chin: Because it’s just not true. He says, “I feel fear. I’ve always felt fear.” One of the reasons he started soloing was that he was so shy he was too scared to ask people to climb with him. So he climbed by himself. His process was to step outside his comfort zone a little at a time, in a regimented, disciplined way, until the things that scared him were well within it. The film took almost four years. But he’d been training for that climb his entire career. We left the brain scan open to interpretation, but that’s his process.

In 2017 you were trying to dial down the risk in your life. Then Conrad Anker and Alex asked you to come to Antarctica, and you went. You argue in the book that children need parents who are alive, but also parents who feel alive inside. Is that an argument or a good excuse?

Chin: Those are really personal decisions. It’s impossible to justify to a child that their parent died in the mountains doing what I do. I don’t know if there’s a right answer. I’ve lost a lot of friends in the mountains, some of them parents. After my friend Hilaree Nelson died, Bill King wrote to me, and I wrote back: “The mountains give us so much life, yet they take so much life away. It never makes sense, but we understand.” He quoted that line in his retirement speech. So it’s not an excuse. I believe your kids want you alive physically, and alive as yourself. For better or worse, this is my calling.

How do you tell fear that’s protecting you from fear that’s psyching you out?

Chin: Fear can sharpen your senses or paralyze you. When things are going sideways, panic never serves you. So you break it down: How much of this is perceived risk, and how much is actual risk? That exercise alone brings you back into the present. You set the perceived risks aside, focus on what’s real, and mitigate it. Then you make a plan and execute.

I love how all Bill King wanted to know was why you turned around 100 meters from the summit of Meru.

Chin: I got a surprise call from SEAL Team 6 asking me to come talk at the base. They gave me a date, a time, and an airport. I got on a plane, they flew me to an undisclosed location, took my phone. I hadn’t been nervous speaking in years, but these guys roll in and size you up. Someone told me every member of Team 6 had watched Meru. When I finished, a guy in the back cut to the chase: “How did you decide to turn around 100 meters from the summit?” I knew the entire reason I was there was to answer that question. That was Bill.

When you’ve put years into an objective and it’s within sight, and things aren’t right, it takes extraordinary discipline to walk away. On Meru we had seven days of food and were on the wall for 19. We crossed so many of our own lines, deliberately. You set a line, reach it, evaluate, set another. The more you do that, the more invested you are, and the harder it is to turn around.

You and the SEALs share a no-asshole rule. Tell me about that.

Chin: I asked Bill what trait gets people through training. He didn’t flinch: “Humor.” If a guy is getting his ass handed to him and he’s still cracking jokes, they’re not worried about him. It’s the same in the mountains. Humor changes the environment and brings you back to good, rational decisions. My selection process isn’t as serious as theirs, but these are the people holding a rope for you. You can’t have people who only think about themselves. And you can feel it. In conversation, it’s “I, I, I, me.”

Yvon Chouinard is the closest thing you have to a guru. He tells you, “It’s so easy to complicate your life. It’s so much harder to simplify it.” Have you managed it?

Chin: On expeditions, yes. That’s part of why I love them: the best version of me comes out. We’re brutal about simplifying, because every ounce counts. Everything is about efficiency, even how much stress you allow, even your heart rate. I can stay really calm in the worst situations. But if I can’t find my matching sock at home, it’s all over. In the mountains, when things are going sideways, I’m like, oh, this is casual.

You have kids. Do you worry about whether the wild places you’ve spent your life in will still be there for them?

Chin: It’s what the last pages of the book are about. I think of it with Yvon on one end and Kris Tompkins on the other. They’ve both had a tremendous impact on my life, and I’ve talked with both of them about this a lot.

Yvon always says, “Everybody has different tools. Whatever tool you have in your toolbox, whatever you’re good at, that’s what you should contribute.” It’s not only activism. His example is that if you’re an accountant, there are a ton of grassroots organizations that need accountants. So you ask: What can I contribute? Contribute what you have.

Chin: Storytelling, and a platform. That’s why I made Wild Life after Free Solo. I had the chance to finance a film about conservationists, which I probably wouldn’t have had otherwise. It’s about Doug and Kris Tompkins, who preserved something like 17 million acres over a 25-year dream of creating national parks. I’ve brought my kids down there. Those are the things I hope will make a difference: telling these stories, and putting them in a book. What Yvon and Kris have to say is so much more compelling than what I have to say about it.

#8296. 5 DIY Climbing Projects to Get You Through the Long Winter

From garage-hammered pitons to swami-belt harnesses, climbers have been making their own equipment since the sport was in its infancy. Gear has come a long way since then. It’s also gotten a heck of a lot more expensive. While we can’t in good faith recommend you save money by making your own chocks and cams, there are still a number of things you can DIY for cheap.

Earlier this month, I went on a DIY kick and decided to hand-make a few pieces myself. Some were items I’d seen friends carry around at the crag. Other ideas came from online forums (and this magazine). With a single trip to the hardware store and a heap of old gear that’s been rotting in the trunk of my car, I was able to make five things—and saved $183 total. Here’s what I came up with, how much each item cost, and what I would do differently next time.

Usual cost: $39.95 for an Edelrid Spinner Leash on Backcountry

Dropped tools are no joke. At Colorado’s ice parks, losing one will typically earn you a swim in a very frigid creek. On multi-pitch ice, you could end up stranded. The trick is to clip your tools to your harness via a bungee system that’s elastic enough to preserve freedom of motion, but not so springy as to send your dropped tool boomeranging pick-first into your thigh

Purpose-made leashes are pricey. A DIY version is free if you have old tent poles lying around your house and only $5 if you need to purchase new shock-cord. I started by clipping the bar tack off an old piece of double-length tubular webbing. I then tied one end of the shock cord to a piece of wire, and shoved it through the tube (this took forever). Once I could access the shock cord from either end, I tied an overhand knot in the center to create a girth-hitchable loop for my harness. I then scrunched the webbing down as much as possible over the two legs of the shock cord, tied overhangs for both carabiners, and melted the edges to finish them.

(Note: For another $10, you can purchase a swivel from most hardware stores, putting the result on par with $80 swiveling leashes.)

Usual cost: $17 for a Personal Tool Tether on Gear Keeper

Some nut tools come with integrated leashes. These don’t add a ton of cost to the tool, but they are boring as all get out. Aftermarket versions from Gear Keeper, Amazon, and beyond aren’t much better. The answer: Make your own out of an old spring-coil keychain bracelet.

First, snip the bracelet in half and feed an electrical crimp onto either end. Next, fold one end of the coil around the inside edge of a nut tool, tuck the end into the nearest crimp, and squeeze the crimp shut with pliers or a crimper tool. Then do the same thing around a small accessory carabiner to complete the tether.

Usual cost: $94.95 for a Metolius Basic Stick Clip at REI

The cost of stick clips has always baffled me, especially since you can make one yourself with a tree branch, a small stick, and a bit of tape. However, I’ll concede that not everyone loves tramping around the crag looking for an appropriately sturdy stick. For those folks, try this trick.

You can buy a painter’s pole from just about any hardware store for relatively cheap. The ones at my local were $20 for 8 feet or $40 for 23. Once you’ve got that, use a couple of stainless steel hose clamps (basically big metal zip ties) to attach a small spring-loaded clamp. Voila!

Usual cost: $54.95 for a Panic Quickdraw on Kong

The internet said I could make one of these by stuffing a piece of webbing into a section of transparent vinyl tubing and tying carabiners to the ends. I tried this and found the result upsettingly floppy. Vinyl tubing is also much more expensive than heavy-duty housing wire, which you can purchase by the foot at Home Depot. Tubing has the added benefit of being foldable.

So, after my first attempt failed, I went back to an old Matt Samet recipe and shoved a section of wire into the hollow core of a length of tubular webbing. I then tied the ends with a water knot to make a continuous loop, and duct-taped a Mad Rock Trigger Wire Carabiner and a bent-gate carabiner to either end. It’s not quite as long as other purpose-made stiffy draws, but it does the trick at a fraction of the price.

Usual cost: $24.95 for a Trango Cord Trapper on Backcountry

I first saw a DIY rope tarp like this at the notoriously dusty Vail Amphitheatre. It’s incredibly lightweight and astonishingly cheap. All you have to do is cut a four-by-four section from a painter’s plastic drop sheet and affix loops to opposite corners. (Note: I used 1 mm-weight plastic, but it felt a little flimsy; 2 mm would be better and only costs $1 more. Tyvek House Wrap would also be superior, but it tends to be more expensive if you don’t happen to have a housing contractor in your life.)

I found that heavy duty plastic shipping tape (especially the kind designed for long-term storage) sticks better than just about anything else. Tape a loop to either corner, and add colored tape to distinguish the belay end from the climber’s end when the rope is stacked.

#8295. 4 Backcountry Field Repairs That Can Save Your Trip (When Duct Tape Isn’t Enough)

No matter how well you’ve prepared or how careful you are with your gear, at some point, whether by cactus spine or sheer volume of trail miles, you’re going to tear a piece of clothing. Or, if you’re me, you’re going to flop down on your sleeping pad, which is on top of your toiletry bag, which holds a pair of impossibly vertical tweezers, and punch an irreparable hole in your mat on the first night of a 225-mile backpacking trip.

You can’t fix every gear problem in the field—a melted down jacket is going to need professional attention or replacement—but with a few simple supplies and some know-how you can handle more of them than you think. Here are four field repairs beyond taping your down jacket you should know, along with a minimal repair kit to get you to the next road crossing.

The glue line that attaches the bottom package—the midsole and outsole—to the shoe upper is the most common structural failure in footwear. While you can manage a few days with a blown-out upper or worn-down outsole tread, the bottom of your shoe flapping in the breeze is a problem.

If you’re close enough to town or have a sense of humor, you can wear your Crocs as hiking shoes. For the rest of us, use a combination of lacing, zip ties, and duct tape to keep your kicks together long enough to get back to civilization. The most secure way to reattach the bottom of the shoe to the top is with an X pattern, similar to how you’d wrap a sprained ankle. If you have a spare set of laces or shock cord, begin at the front of the shoe and criss-cross over the bottom and top in a series of figure-eights until you reach the top of the laces. From here, you can cover the lacing with duct tape in the same pattern. If you brought zip ties, you can punch through the outsole/midsole (be sure to punch far enough in that it doesn’t wear through the side) and the edge of the upper where it won’t rub or cause blisters. Secure it tightly, then finish with the duct tape in a figure-8 pattern.

I typically don’t carry single-use items in my pack aside from the core components of my kit, but a tent pole splint is an exception. Tent poles carry high amounts of tension from taut pitches and are under even more strain in high winds, and the tape-a-stake-to-the-pole simply does not work. A tent pole splint (or sleeve) is a tube made from the same material as the pole, and simply slides over the bent or broken section to create an unbroken line.

Before you do anything else, straighten the bent pole as much as possible or line up the two broken sections as close as they can get. Once the sleeve is centered over the break, secure it with plenty of duct tape. The pole splints are typically not much wider than the pole itself, so it should hold in place fairly well until you can get a replacement pole section.

I’ve slapped plenty of patches onto my down jacket and sleeping pads, but tearing your fly is trickier because you’re relying on the material for waterproofing. I ripped a 10-inch hole in my Big Agnes Copper Spur tent a few years ago, and my attempt at a duct-tape repair held up for about six minutes before condensation separated it again. This is where the Tenacious Tape comes in handy, with its flexible nylon, vinyl, or ripstop material and aggressive adhesive backing. It sticks better than duct tape and can fend off a decent amount of moisture for a surprisingly long time.

Be sure to clean the area around the tear as thoroughly as possible (alcohol wipes come in handy here) and dry it thoroughly before applying the tape. GearAid also makes an incredibly waterproof Aquaseal adhesive compound that can act as a seam sealer or smooth on over raincoat tears.

I must be cursed with backpacking stoves, because I feel like my ignitor stops working after my first few trips. I try to remember a lighter for this very reason, but if you didn’t and the finicky ignitor stopped sparking, you can try repositioning the electrode tip. This works if you can hear the igniter clicking but not lighting the gas—the delicate metal electrode wire likely bent away from the port.

Use your multitool pliers here and position the tip five millimeters (just under 1/4 inch) from the center ring, which should be enough for the spark to jump. The wire on the popular MSR PocketRocket tends to slip out of its guide tube, and if you know what to look for, you can slide it back into the alignment sleeve to restore contact. This video demonstrates replacing the ignitor on a similar stove. (Alternatively, just remember your lighter.)

Some items, like load-bearing pack straps or buckles, will need to be tied together until you get to town, but there are a few things that are handy to take into the backcountry.

The short answer is tape, tape, tape, tape. I wrap a healthy dose of duct tape (bonus points for weird patterns) around my trekking poles or a prescription bottle to cobble together many repairs. I also bring a few inches of Tenacious Tape, designed to patch waterproof fabrics like rain jackets and tent flies, and a NoSo Patch, which works wonders for keeping the feathers inside a torn jacket or sleeping bag.

For thru-hikes or longer trips where I’m going to be way in the backcountry, I bring a tiny sewing kit, a lightweight knife with grippy pliers and a screwdriver end, a few zip ties for holding a backpack together, a tent pole splint, and several safety pins. Finally, your inflatable sleeping pad likely came with its own tiny repair kit, including an alcohol wipe and a matching repair patch with adhesive optimized for the pad material. This whole kit weighs three ounces and can help prevent some serious headaches.

#8294. Scarpa Golden Gate LT Review: Moderate Stack Is So Back

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Trail shoes with a moderate stack are becoming harder to find. New trail models either have inches of soft, bouncy foam underfoot (sometimes with a carbon plate), or they are minimalist models that let your feet feel every pebble. Fortunately, a few that balance protection and ground feel still exist. I’ve just discovered one: the Scarpa Golden Gate LT.

Scarpa is an Italian mountain brand based in the Dolomites. Specializing in mountain climbing footwear, elite mountaineers historically wore the brand’s lightweight mountain shoes to cross rugged terrain. Scarpa’s trail running shoes reflect that heritage; they’re known for their rugged protection and firm, surefooted ride. But many trail runners who don’t live in places like the Alps or the White Mountains don’t need an indestructible mountain running boot. Enter Scarpa’s new trail shoe line-up.

The Golden Gate LT is Scarpa’s lightweight “door-to-trail” shoe meant for a broader trail running audience who want a single functional trainer on runs that bridge varied terrain, from asphalt to gravel to rocky singletrack. I put the shoe’s prowess to the test across Los Angeles’s urban streets, steep horse trails, and sandy beaches.

Weight: 10.5oz (men’s 9, women’s 10) Stack Height: 30 – 24 mm Heel-to-Toe Drop: 6 mm

+ Handles road-to-trail transitions smoothly + Stable base + Excellent traction – Fit too narrow for wide feet – Slightly sluggish on quick turnover

The Golden Gate LT may be a departure from Scarpa’s roots in many ways, but not in style: I received a hot orange-white colorway that immediately reminded me of the Orange Crush soda can and blends right in with Scarpa’s line up of mountain running shoes and ski boots. Though the flashy look isn’t entirely my style, I’m just glad it’s not a monster truck of a trail shoe.

Most of my test runs were on the hilly, paved roads of my neighborhood. Cruising through the familiar streets, I was happy to find that while cushioned, my landings weren’t squishy at all. Instead, I noticed a small bounciness in the midsole — like I was running on a shallow trampoline. That’s likely because Scarpa blended 20% PEBAX into the EVA compound midsole to provide extra responsiveness for what I call the “road” side of the hybrid shoe’s performance.

Taking the shoes uphill, the rebound was still there but didn’t do the heavy lifting for me. That changed, however, when I picked up the pace. With some downhill momentum, my stride lengthened, and any feeling of a firm trail shoe was completely gone. At quicker paces, the bounce takes over and helps maintain speed, feeling like an uptempo road shoe. Normally I don’t like shoes with much cushioning, but the upper’s gentle TPU-reinforced support wrapped my feet so nicely that I felt confident running faster and farther.

Later, I took them out for a long run mostly on trails, connected by some roads, to see how they held up on different surfaces. On the trails, the midsole bounce was less noticeable, which I appreciated, as bouncing over unstable surfaces doesn’t make sense to me.

Compared to other trail models I’ve worn, the lugs are far more flexible, providing amazing traction across sand, dirt, and rocks. The flexibility of the outsole kept my stride smooth and stable on uneven trails and helped the shoe maintain its beginning-of-the-run feeling late into a 14-mile long run. Overall, the outsole’s efficiency felt more alive on the trails than on paved surfaces.

If you’re crazy, like me, and sprint down steep trails, you’ll appreciate the moderate, 24 mm stack under the forefoot, making toe-offs effortless, helping short, quick strides remain stable, and ensuring that tight cornering is no problem. The 30 mm heel stack, however, which contributed to the smooth cushioning on the road, could sometimes feel a bit sluggish on steep trail descents. I prefer 4 mm-drop shoes to keep my steps quick and agile and maximize the thrill of heading downhill with my hair on fire. But if you’re more sensible and take it easy on descents, then the 6 mm drop shouldn’t be a problem at all.

Back on the roads toward the end of my long run, I felt the same road-shoe ride I get on my neighborhood runs. Though my legs were more tired after battling the dusty, hilly terrain, the flexibility of the upper and the outsole encouraged me to keep my pace until the end of the run.

Durability seems mixed so far: After testing the shoe for a month of road and trail runs, the outsole has progressively felt more flexible under my feet and can take on rocks and tough objects on the trails. The edges of the lugs have retained their sharp definition from when it was new, while the upper and overall cushioning still feel just as comfortable. The midsole bounce, however, is much gentler than when it was new (for better or worse), and the bright Orange Crush splash has since faded.

Quality moderate-stack trail shoes are becoming harder to find. If your favorite model lost its way in the “space-age arms race of trail super shoes,” as our editor Cade Michael aptly put it, and you don’t like feeling every rock beneath your feet through a thin minimalist sole, this one’s for you.

Runners with narrow or medium-narrow feet who prefer a tight fit should appreciate this shoe. The heel and midfoot’s gentle padding hug my narrow feet quite tightly, and the toe box has some room for toe splay, though it’s not wide — it’s right in the middle. This close-fitting shape is useful for tight cornering and platform stability, but if you have wide feet and need breathing space for your toes, the M2C H1, an Altra, or a Topo trail shoe might be a better fit.

So, is this the lower-stacked hybrid shoe that we’ve been waiting for? With its dual personality, the Golden Gate LT certainly handles roads and trails like it’s built for both. You can also totally wear this exclusively as a trail shoe for runs of any length. Though difficult trails with demanding terrain may not be its greatest strength, this shoe provides a comfortable, energetic ride on all other terrain, achieving exactly what it’s designed for.

#8293. How to Car Camp in Your Subaru Crosstrek

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Jackery Explorer 1000 Portable Power Station

Exped MegaMat LuxeWool Auto Sleeping Pad Cover

I’ve always been jealous of people with a kitted-out Land Cruiser or a made-to-order Sprinter van. These #adventuremobiles not only look cool and bestow the driver with backcountry cred, but they also offer the freedom to roam without worrying about finding a place to pitch a tent. Behind the wheel of one, you can venture into the unknown and, when sleepiness starts making your eyelids heavy, pull off the road for some fully prone shut-eye without even stepping outside.

Even if you’re not pulling over at the last minute, these rigs serve as comfy, spacious home bases for drive-in campsites, getting rest before a big race, or road-tripping to a far-flung national park. The major problem? They can be prohibitively expensive, rarely work well as daily drivers, and can be tricky to keep running smoothly. Sleeping in my car comfortably always felt like a luxury I couldn’t afford—until this summer.

In June, I bought a car for the first time in years. Like many outdoor-minded folks, I gravitated toward a small, capable crossover that promised competence on dirt roads alongside decent city gas mileage. For me, that was a Subaru Crosstrek—a car I’ve wanted for nearly a decade. But it could have been an Outback, a Toyota RAV4, or any number of smaller utility vehicles. Since I’d be driving it daily in Los Angeles, the fuel economy and parkability made sense. But I also knew I could take it off the beaten path to road-trip to Mammoth or explore the American West. What I wasn’t sure of was whether I could turn it into my own adventuremobile and spend a comfortable night sleeping inside.

After some research and a few key car camping gear pick-ups, I can tell you that it is indeed possible to sleep in the back of my Crosstrek and fully stretch out my five-foot-ten frame—no scrunching or squishing necessary. In fact, two people could sleep back there quite easily, which I didn’t anticipate when I drove it off the lot. I’ve found car-specific sleeping pads, easy-access roof boxes, and numerous other bits and bobs that make sleeping in the back of a compact car genuinely comfortable.

Since June, I’ve dialed in a basic setup you can apply to just about any small vehicle. Read on for my car camping essentials, plus a few items I hope to pick up soon to make nights in my hatchback even more luxurious. Who needs a van? (Okay, I’d still love a van.)

If you buy only one thing to make sleeping in your car comfortable, make it the MegaMat Auto from Exped. The first time I slept on one was at a friend’s house; they used their original MegaMat as a guest bed. I was skeptical that a camping mattress could match a standard air mattress, but my skepticism was misplaced—it gave me one of the best nights of sleep I’ve ever had on an inflatable bed. When I saw Exped made a car-contoured version, I had to get one.

It fits snugly in my Crosstrek with both front seats pushed fully forward, providing plenty of width for one person and enough room for two to sleep as comfortably as they would in a two- or three-person tent. It inflates quickly—especially if you use the Mega Pump, which tops it off in under two minutes.

Plus, it doubles as a spare mattress for houseguests. For extra luxury, you can also add the MegaMat LuxeWool Auto cover.

I’ve never owned a roof box before, and it’s a total game-changer for car camping when square footage is at a premium. Sure, you could chuck everything from the trunk into the front seats while you sleep, but that leaves zero room for organization. With a cargo box, you can store your sleeping gear up top while driving, then swap it for your extra gear overnight.

The Thule Motion 3 looks sleek (especially in black) and opens smoothly from either side, which is handy on the Crosstrek since I can center the box on the roof and still access it from the driver or passenger side. The Large size fits perfectly on the roof length-wise. Locks and keys are included, and while it’s light enough for one person to hoist or remove, I recommend having a second set of hands. The mounting hardware clamps down without fuss. I pair it with the Thule WingBar Evo crossbars—a bit spendy, but versatile enough to keep on the roof year-round.

There are plenty of ways to manage car storage, but hard-sided crates solve one of car-sleeping’s biggest headaches: the rear footwells. While my back seats fold flat, there’s a wide gap between the folded seats and the front seats that needs support so your mattress doesn’t sag under your head.

My Sidio crate lives in the trunk loaded with car essentials—first-aid kit, blanket, towel, and miscellaneous gear. When it’s time to sleep, one of these crates slides into each footwell to create a sturdy platform. One crate isn’t quite tall enough on its own, so I usually stack a sturdy shoe box on top to level it out. Stacking a Quarter Size Crate on top of the Full Size Crate would likely hit the exact height needed for the Crosstrek.

You don’t strictly need a dedicated camping pillow, but keeping one in the car saves your everyday bed pillows from outdoor dirt. The Luno Packable Camping Pillow lives in my Sidio crate full-time. It doesn’t pack down microscopic, but it compresses enough to justify keeping it in the car 24/7, and the shredded memory foam fill is comfortable enough to use indoors. A zippered inner liner lets you add or remove filling to adjust the firmness.

Any standard blanket works, but a technical down quilt packs down small and adapts well to changing temperatures. I use the Therm-a-Rest Vesper (which doubles as my backpacking quilt), while the team at Backpacker rates the Neve Gear Waratah as a top choice. Choose based on the climate and temperatures you expect to encounter.

I’ve been using a compact Nestout Battery Pack to charge my phone, but a larger portable power station makes multi-day trips much easier. Compact stations like the Jackery Explorer or Goal Zero Yeti tuck away neatly while keeping cameras, headlamps, and laptops powered up.

To read or wind down without wearing a headlamp, interior lighting is a subtle upgrade. The BioLite Luci Solar String Lights add cozy ambient light across the cabin, while a compact lantern like the Big Agnes mtnGLO can easily hang from a grab handle or ceiling hook. The BioLite lights are rechargeable, and the Big Agnes light requires AAA batteries, so keep that in mind when adding accessories that require power.

#8292. I Hike With a Flip Phone. Here’s the Tiny Camera I’m Bringing Along.

Over the past few years, I’ve learned I’m much happier when I don’t have my smartphone on me—I’m not sure the human mind evolved to have 24-hour access to all of the Internet’s information on demand. In an effort to disconnect and be more present, I took a page from the Gen Z playbook and started carrying a flip phone instead. It’s been great—except for the camera.

A while ago, I started testing a potential solution in the Life Camera S168, a thumb-size digital camera built to compete with the Kodak Charmera. How did it actually perform on the trail? Check out this video to see what kind of photos and footage this $30 gadget is capable of turning out and read our full review for more.

A while ago, I swapped out my smartphone for a flip phone. I was getting tired of how distracted I was—doomscrolling, checking my emails—and I wanted to simplify things. This has really done the trick. On the trail it’s pretty much everything I need. It can send messages, make calls, if I need to get a hold of 911 in an emergency, it can do that. It has an MP3 player, so I can listen to podcasts at night, and it even has a rudimentary mapping app, although I’m not sure I’d trust it, I always bring a paper map and compass as backup.

However, it does have one big shortcoming: the camera on this thing really sucks. The pictures are grainy, blurry, and usually blown out. It’s not how I want to remember my trips. I often find myself hiking with my smartphone just so I can get better pictures and video. I’ve been looking for a solution, since that kind of defeats the purpose of ditching the smartphone, and I think I’ve found one.

This is the Life Camera S168. It’s part of a crop of new thumb-sized digital cameras that are designed to appeal to the retro crowd, they’re kind of like old digital cameras or old film cameras, you know, the disposable you used to take to summer camp with you. The most familiar one is the Kodak Charmera, you may have seen that in stores.

However, according to a lot of online reviews, the Life Camera’s photos and video quality is significantly better, and it has, from what I’ve seen, a fairly decent camera, you’re not going to confuse it with an iPhone or anything, but it may be enough for my purposes.

So, is the Life Camera a gimmick or a game changer? Well, that depends on you. If you’re like most hikers and you have your phone in your pocket most of the time, it’s definitely a gimmick. Your phone can do anything the Life Camera can do, and probably in better resolution.

If, however, you’re part of the small subset of hikers like me, who find they’re happier when their phone is off and in their pack, or if they’re just carrying a flip phone, you might give the Life Camera a try. No, the resolution isn’t anything to write home about, but it can capture your life on the trail in adequate detail, and if you don’t mind that retro vibe, it’s kind of fun. I’ll be carrying one on my next hike.

#8291. 9 of the Most Impressive Undercover Crushers in Climbing Right Now

Shanjean “SJ” Lee sending on the Liberty Bell massif. (Photo: Mikey Schaefer)

The climbing world may love its celebrities, but they also love their underdogs. Which is why we all seem to collectively lose our minds when an undercover crusher emerges from the undergrowth, sends some famous project, and then once again vaporizes into obscurity. The silent crusher archetype has been around since the beginning of climbing history, but in the days of climbing influencers and social media, they seem rarer than ever. To prove the paradigm isn’t dead, we decided to track down a handful and show them a little love.

The trick with finding undercover crushers is that many of them are, indeed, undercover. I initially put out a request for nominations on Instagram and watched the recs pour in. At that point, I figured writing this story would be easy. But many of the people recommended to me were impossible to find. Others were findable but declined to be mentioned. A few, I learned, were undercover because they had been canceled, and I decided that crafting their PR comeback was very much not my job. So, below you’ll find nine climbers who were recommended by one—if not several—of their friends, are in excellent social standing, and were kind enough to dip a toe into the spotlight for this story.

Here are nine of America’s most impressive undercover crushers.

This Bozeman-based young gun is responsible for establishing the hardest climb in Montana: Fox-Like Creature (5.15a), which has yet to see a repeat. But the 20-year-old says his proudest send to date is World Without End (5.14d). “It’s not my hardest route ever, but I think it took me the most effort, in terms of projecting as well as bolting,” he says. “It was also the first 9a [5.14d] route in Montana, which I’m proud of.” In between FAs, McIntosh works as a routesetter at local climbing gyms and spends his weekends cragging in Refrigerator Canyon. “I think it’s one of the best crags in the country and no one’s caught on yet,” he shares.

A lifelong climber based in Squamish, B.C., the 23-year-old Quinn Mason cut her teeth on the U.S. competition circuit before diverting her attention to outdoor pursuits. Last fall, she sent her hardest sport climb to date, Spirit Quest (5.14d), and this spring sent Squamish lines Tainted Love (5.13d R) and Free Dimensional (5.13d PG-13), both on gear. When she’s not climbing, Mason’s either plowing through her coursework for her filmmaking degree or coaching the local youth climbing team. She also does a bit of brand photography and has two sponsors—which means she might not be undercover for long.

One of the few Americans to send V16, Eli Perry learned to climb at a young age but didn’t get serious until he was 15 (he’s now 21). In that time, he started ticking through the grades at a frenetic pace, sending Pegasus (V15) in Joe’s Valley, Utah, and Grand Illusion (V16) in Little Cottonwood Canyon. “Both of them I spent a lot of sessions on and multiple seasons,” he says. In between sessions, he busses tables at an Italian restaurant, does ceramics, and reads. Perry is currently based in Salt Lake City, which he calls “definitely the best spot to be for climbing in the States.”

In between shifts as an orthopedic surgeon at the VA Medical Center in Reno, Nevada, Shanjean “SJ” Lee, 42, manages to send hard across multiple climbing disciplines. She’s redpointed sport routes up to 5.14, boulders up to V10, and is no stranger to Yosemite big walls: In 2021, she notched a free ascent of Free Rider (5.13a; 3,000ft). Lee is also a developer herself. “I put up a route on Liberty Bell in the Washington Pass area called The Dark Side of Liberty with my partner Mikey Schaefer [in 2020],” she says. The 10-pitch pump-fest clocks in at 5.13+, making it the formation’s hardest route to date. Liberty Bell was her local crag at the time, and the opportunity to add to its legacy was invaluable, she says. “It was really special to add a new testpiece route to a place that had given me so much.”

Tadros “Teddy” Eyob isn’t just a connoisseur of long finger cracks—he’s a master of them. The Squamish-based climber recently sent the Joshua Tree triple—Asteroid Crack (5.12d), Equinox (5.12c), and Acid Crack (5.12d)—a trio of stout finger cracks first freed by John Bachar. “I love lines that have finicky gear and keep you feeling like every piece you place is what’s keeping you from decking,” he says. “Something about the level of focus those lines demand really gets me excited.” Before that, he became the first Black climber to free El Cap (NBD), nabbing a proud, ground-up free ascent of Free Rider in early 2026. Now 31, Eyob has climbed all over the world, but his backyard crags remain his favorite place to climb. “The more I travel the world, the luckier I feel to get to call a place like Squamish home.”

Lani Chapko started climbing 12 years ago when her friends convinced her to take an outdoor adventure course for physical education credit in college. She fell in love with the sport right away, became a guide, and went on to establish big routes around North America, including La Sombra de Muerte, (5.12b; 1,500ft), which she and her partner recently authored in El Portrero Chico, Mexico. Chapko, 32, now lives in Index, WA, which remains her favorite place to climb. “There is always another 4-star route, a new way to get humbled, and something to learn from the climbing there,” she says.

Based in Truckee, California, the 33-year-old Sam Daulton is a modern-day Sierra legend. “I was incredibly psyched to make the first flash ascent of Grand Illusion (5.13c) in January 2026,” he says, referring to the finger crack corner near Lake Tahoe, CA. “Grand Illusion was the hardest climb in the world when Tony Yaniro made the first ascent in 1979.” He also bagged the second gear ascent of Tahoe’s Empath (5.14c/d). Daulton first learned to climb as a toddler and grew up training alongside future phenoms like Michaela Kiersch and Isabelle Faus. “At the time, I was a little punk, more interested in shenanigans than training, but after a hiatus in high school, I got back into it.” Now, Daulton works as a research scientist for Meta, a remote gig that allows him to maximize his time in Yosemite, the Sierra, and the French Alps.

Born and Raised in Durango, Colorado, and now a physics Ph.D. student at UC California, Berkeley, Liam Foster is one of the kindest (and most obsessive) rock climbers you’ll ever meet. His meticulous approach to training has served him well, propelling him to redpoints of Line Above the Sky (D16), the hardest drytooling route in the world at the time of the send; Dures Limites (5.14b) in Céüse, France; and The Arsonist (5.14d), a Connor Herson line on California’s Jailhouse Rock. As for what inspires him? “It doesn’t have to be aesthetic as long as the holds are cool and the movements are cool,” he says. “I think people get snooty about climbs, and only want to climb good climbs. But there are so many good bad climbs. It doesn’t have to be perfect to be worth a weekend out.”

West Virginia-based guidebook author Andrew Leich was on the verge of sending his project, Green Magic in the Hills (5.14c) at Seneca Rocks when a rattlesnake bite almost killed him. While he survived, a slow recovery forced him to start over, slowly building through the grades until he was back to authoring new 5.13s, his previous baseline. Then, in December 2025, he finally sent Green Magic, more than three years after bolting it with a friend and nearly two after his near-death snake encounter. Now 32, Leich works as a part-time climbing guide and is the author of two guidebooks: Cheat Canyon Bouldering and Cheat Canyon Rock.

#8289. A Love Letter to Flated’s Inflatable Truck Shell

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

For more than a decade, I’ve driven trucks, and always with a fiberglass hardshell topper. The cap transformed the bed of my pickup into a gear shed for all of my outdoor equipment and a tiny cabin for me to crash in on climbing trips and before alpine starts. But, as my hard shell weighed north of 150 pounds, I never—and I mean that literally—took it off.

That’s all fine and dandy for the dirtbag climber and runner, jaunting around New Mexico and Colorado without a care in the world in her twenties. But at this stage of life, as a mom of three kids with a house to maintain, a farm to care for, and loads of bikes and strollers to haul to and fro on the weekends, my truck needs to be a little more versatile.

As its name suggests, Flated shells are inflatable. I blew it up using the plug-in pump reserved for my SUP in just a few minutes. Installation required no further tools. At under 60 pounds, installation is not only simple, but easy to do by myself. I just inflate the cap and lift it onto my truck. Then, I attach it with a handful of tie-downs. In total, installation takes about 30 minutes, but I bet I’ll get faster with practice.

Flated doesn’t skimp on features, either. It’s fully waterproof with a rain skirt built in to repel water from the truck bed. There are two tinted windows, two screens on the side windows, and one rear window. The part of the topper that connects to the truck cab also features a pass-through window, so you can easily access the truck bed from the backseat. Sturdy zippers and Velcro secure window shades while you drive, and a couple of interior mesh pockets on the cab end help sort smaller gear and gadgets. I have yet to camp with the Flated Cap56, but when I do, that’s where I’ll stash my phone and headlamp for safekeeping.

At $1,600, it’s not cheap, but it does cost several thousand dollars less than a traditional hardshell.

I live at high elevation and full sun in northern New Mexico, so time will tell how the new topper stands up against the elements, but so far, I’ve driven it for about a month without any signs of wear.

Last weekend, I had it on for transporting bike gear and keeping it safe from the rain, but I pulled it off the next day to haul home some new trees from the local nursery. This, in a nutshell, is the beauty of the Flated Cap56: it’s versatile and goes with the flow of life, no matter how chaotic my days may get.

#8288. How I Got Benighted (Twice) on Yosemite’s ‘Lost Arrow Chimney’

In the first installment in our Benighted series, Shino Jomoto shares with Climbing the weird and spooky tale from her night in the chimney on September 17, 2023—and what all climbers can learn from her epic.

With over two decades of climbing experience, Jomoto specializes in epics, which she defines as getting sandbagged on adventure multi-pitch climbs and big walls that take far longer than anticipated. But her biggest epic of all occurred in the storied chimney route (5.10a) up Lost Arrow Spire in Yosemite.

Earlier this week, a Yosemite Climbing Association (YCA) newsletter detailed the history of the Lost Arrow Spire, including the chimney route. First ascensionist John Salathé himself bailed near the top in 1946. The next year, he came back “for an all-out effort” that took over five days. “Pushing through the claustrophobic shadows of the Lost Arrow Chimney, Salathé and [Anton] Nelson endured searing heat, dehydration, and brutal physical exertion,” the YCA shared. “They spent four bivouacs dangling from crude hammocks tied to pitons driven into the wall.”

The Lost Arrow Chimney is also believed to contain a human skeleton. On March 19, 1961, 17-year-old Irving Smith died in a rappelling accident from the top. An American Alpine Club trip report shared that Smiths’ body remains in the chimney: “While a ranger and volunteer rescue party was preparing to attempt the difficult and dangerous removal, Smith’s parents and Park authorities determined that no further life should be risked, and that the body should remain at rest where it lay.”

A comment on the Mountain Project page of Yosemite’s Lost Arrow Chimney (5.10a) foreshadowed what was to come: “Don’t let the moderate grade fool you. After pitch 7, you are halfway done.” The Lost Arrow Chimney is 10 pitches.

Poor fitness, dehydration, and sleep deprivation conspired, and by pitch eight we needed headlamps. Too tired to continue, we did the only sensible thing: slept inside the chimney.

I started climbing in 2005, mostly out of a hatred for my corporate job. That led to years living out of a station wagon, trying to figure out how to rock climb. Fast forward decades later, I’m in the business of going on epics—a lot.

Jim Herson said you could write an entire print edition on just my epics alone. I’ve had near-death epics like lightning and hypothermia on a big wall. But I’ll put it this way: I can climb El Cap faster than I can climb the Lost Arrow Chimney.

The reason why I wanted to share this is that nine out of ten climbers will have an epic on the Lost Arrow. You might be able to climb 5.13, but try to climb 10 pitches of old-school chimney—see if you can still call yourself a 5.10 climber. I think everyone goes in with the confidence of the grade. Then they just get gut-punched by the old-schoolness of the climb.

On my Lost Arrow Chimney epic, we weren’t in danger. We never called YOSAR (Yosemite Search and Rescue). You’re just humbled in a silly way because it’s such a silly grade.

Aside from the likes of Chuck Pratt or old-school climbers, I don’t know anyone who’s ever redone this route. When you do a climb, you usually redo it. You want a redpoint or you go back again. Nobody is dumb enough to redo this climb. We’ve done it three times, so it really goes to show either how incredibly stupid we are, or how memorable of an epic it was that we just needed to clear the record.

The lore that Jim Herson shared with me was he knew a guy who climbed the Lost Arrow Chimney and then never rock climbed again. The reality is he went to med school and gave up climbing. But that was his last-ever climb. It just embodies the spirit of the Lost Arrow Chimney.

The first time John and I did Lost Arrow Chimney in 26 hours on October 5, 2019 as a party of three, and we were actually in decent shape.

The time we slept in the chimney a few years later, we were a party of two. We thought we were fit. But we did all the classic gumby moves. We got up too late and got lost on the approach. To get back on route, we had to rappel. It’s obvious on a topo where you should go, but at four o’clock in the morning, you get lost. And we didn’t bring enough water.

On the climb, we started losing daylight. My boyfriend started dry heaving from dehydration and lack of fitness. He stopped mid-pitch in a chimney—he couldn’t go on.

There’s nothing you can really say in the dark. We’re not Rocky Talkie people. We have too much pride for that. So we just had to communicate with a rope. Finally, I was on belay. I went up to him. We were mid-chimney—this wasn’t even a belay station.

John was like, “I can’t. I can’t do this anymore.” And he’s a 10-times better climber than I am. So I was like, “All right, I’ll go.” He was like, “Are you sure?” I was like, “We can’t sleep here. We can sleep in a lot of places. This is not a place to sleep.”

It’s always scary when a very experienced person says, “I’m scared.” John rarely says he’s scared. It takes courage to say that. When you’re in the dark, there’s nothing you do. You can’t start yelling and placating, you know? You just realize in that moment like, it’s a serious climb. And you’re still having to reconcile that with 10a.

So I went questing and found this chimney that was adjacent to the climb. It wasn’t a chimney you go through on route, but everyone goes by it.

We were two pitches from the notch. Should we suffer for six hours, then rappel and call it a day? Or suffer through the whole night? You make those calculations. We decided we might as well stay put, rather than burden resources to call for YOSAR or any sort of search and rescue. I think that’s the number one thing: Can you self-rescue?

We had brought a salad that we thought we were going to eat at the base. So we ended up at the bivy with a salad, but no water. It’s kind of hard to eat a salad without water. So all of my swear words were salad- or foliage-related. It doesn’t matter if you have a whole buffet, if you have no water, you don’t want to eat anything. So we were just staring at this salad in the chimney. It’s one of those things with the Maslow’s hierarchy—if you don’t have water, you can’t do anything.

We laid out both climbing ropes so that we were a little bit insulated from the ground. We did the bivy dance. It was flatter than most bivy spots I have slept on. We were really depressed, just waiting for daylight.

Back sleeping was impossible, so we were relegated to side sleeping for the next six hours. There was no way to sleep besides big spoon, little spoon. The walls were very cold. I put a giant sad face in chalk where I was. Another group went and did it later and said, “We knew where you bivvied ’cause there was a giant sad face.”

But we were so thirsty, the epic wasn’t over. We could hear Yosemite Falls. Our brains went: Maybe we can just hike over there. Another lesson is you’re not rational when you’re having an epic. So we lost another half day going to the falls. We were sitting in a pool of water that we couldn’t drink. And we realized we couldn’t cut over. So we had to go back. A day and a half later, we got back to the car.

Finally, on June 2, 2024, we got our redemption. We did it in a day and tagged the summit where people do the Tyrolean. It still took us all day—and we didn’t even free it. We had to pull on gear. It makes you respect the history of the first ascensionists—the lineage of people who have tried it and who have bailed. There’s an insane amount of really, really old bail slings.

You’re in there and it’s a vortex. It’s spooky. I’m not a mystical person, but there are hexes that have been kind of swallowed by the rock. It’s a freaking spooky museum of gear. When you’re in there, you have an appreciation for who climbed this before you and the style in which they climbed it, because it is terrifying.

I feel like I’ve gotten my chimney badge in Yosemite. There should be a club for it: the Lost Arrow Chimney Support Group. If you can summit the whole climb and rappel in a day, I would have mad respect. More people climb the Nose than the Lost Arrow Chimney. Anyone who’s dumb enough and adventurous enough to sign up for that level of masochism will resonate more with me than if you’re C1ing a 30-pitch climb.

If you survive nine or ten pitches of chimneys with your partner, you will be bonded forever, for better or worse. They’ve done all these studies about reality TV shows, like for love matchmaking. You put people in intense situations and they confuse their endorphins as romance, but it’s really just adrenaline. Part of it is trauma bonding. Some couples are more willing to climb the Lost Arrow Chimney than go to couples therapy.

The beauty of epics is there are way more fun memories than sending. Every sending story is so ephemeral. But when you’ve been sucker-punched so hard by something scary, or that requires lack of sleep, or incredible amounts of suffering, you remember those experiences for decades.

If you don’t have some delusional optimism, you will never get off the ground. That delusion will catch up to you at some point. But you have to have a little bit of fuel. As long as it’s not over your head or dangerous for you and others. Can you live well and safely enough to live another day? Go do it.

Delusion meets reality at some point, like when you’re having an epic. Benighted is a subcategory of epics—it’s in the taxonomy. There has to be some darkness involved, generally speaking, but you don’t need to have slept.

The easy way to know is when you end up at the parking lot, you see your best friends, and they’re like, “How was it?” The face doesn’t lie. You actually don’t need to say words. They see your face and they’re like, “That was an epic.”

John and I have an epic grading scale. It’s the reverse GPA.

Every time we finish, we rate them. The Lost Arrow Chimney was like a 5.0.

As told to Maya Silver. This story has been edited for length, structure, and clarity.

#8287. Nearly Half of US Hikers Use Cannabis, And Other Strange Findings From the ‘Hiking While High’ Survey

Most hikers have experienced a natural high at some point in their outdoor adventures. Whether it’s the buzz of an athletic flow state or being straight-up stupefied by an amazing view, we’ve all been there. Endorphins fire, oxytocin floods the brain, and you’re overwhelmed with energy, good vibes, and a general sense of peace.

It’s also not news to anyone that some hikers use drugs in nature. People smoke weed on the trail, eat edibles, drink beer, and even take psychedelics. Every year it seems like we publish at least one story with a headline like, “Hikers Rescued After Mushroom Trip Goes Bad” or “Two Hikers Reported Their Friend Dead. It Turned Out They Were Just on Mushrooms.”

But how many hikers are actually hitting the trail under the influence? Those questions and several others led the team at Climbing Kilimanjaro, a Tanzanian guide company, to conduct its “Hiking While High” survey. It polled U.S. adults who hike to find out once and for all how many of them use cannabis, mushrooms, alcohol, and other substances, and importantly, in what circumstances.

The results surprised the folks at Climbing Kilimanjaro. Not just because of how many hikers admitted to using substances on the trail, but because those who do are “surprisingly disciplined about where and when,” Brian Raffio, Kilimanjaro consultant for Climbing Kilimanjaro, says.

“On one hand, we expected to get some respondents who were very into using substances while hiking, and others who were as sober as sober gets,” Raffio says. “What we ended up with was much more of a grey area.”

For the survey, Climbing Kilimanjaro polled 1,008 U.S. adults between September 1 and 3, 2026. The sample was 52 percent women and 46 percent men, all of whom counted hiking as a core interest or hobby. They also grouped respondents by experience level. Hikers self-reported as casual hikers (people who hike a few times a year), regular hikers (people who hike roughly monthly), or avid hikers (people who hike weekly or more).

Of the 1,008 U.S. hikers surveyed, 44 percent said they have hiked under the influence.

Cannabis is far and away the most popular trail substance. A notable 35 percent of respondents admitted to having used it while hiking. Of hikers who take anything, 80 percent said they are reaching for weed. Behind cannabis, alcohol was the second most popular, with 23 percent percent admitting to having drunk beer or liquor while hiking. In third were magic mushrooms, with 15 percent admitting use (and another 24 percent saying they are curious to try psychedelics in nature but never have).

However, a majority—56 percent of hikers—said they have never used any substances on the trail. And while 7 percent of hikers who enhance their hikes say they have felt judged for doing so, surprisingly more of the sober hikers (9 percent) said they have also felt judged, but for their choice to abstain.

“Hikers feeling judged for staying clear-headed rather than for using something was a bit of a head-scratcher for sure,” Raffio says. “Apparently ‘no thanks, I’m good’ raises a few eyebrows.”

What surprised the Climbing Kilimanjaro team even more wasn’t these reported use rates. Instead, it was the level of caution users claim to have when they’re hiking high. More than half (51 percent) said they seek out shorter, easier hikes, and would never try to hike under the influence at high altitude. And nine out of 10 who hiked under the influence said: “There’s at least one place they would never use a substance.”

“In the end, hikers seem to be a fairly self-policing bunch,” Raffio says. “The summit push is where folks want to stay sharp and have their senses fully alert. Whatever [substance] a hiker packs, the trail rewards you when you know the terrain, and you understand your limits.”

The final result that stuck out to Raffio was how many people use hiking to recover. Roughly half of the hikers surveyed said they hit the trail sometimes “to reset after drinking or a night out.”

According to the Outdoor Industry Association (OIA), there are roughly 63 million hikers in the U.S. That makes this sample size anything but definitive. The most obvious takeaway is that people like to enhance their hikes with substances—whether it’s cannabis, magic mushrooms, or something else.

Climbing Kilimanjaro’s results also suggest that hikers are fairly split when it comes to substance use on the trail. While the majority of the respondents had never used anything while hiking, a 56/44 split isn’t that wide of a margin.

For those who do partake, it’s clear (and unsurprising) that cannabis is hikers’ substance of choice—by a long shot.

The Hiking While High survey didn’t poll hikers on their feelings around the topic, and that was intentional. The guide company didn’t want to present opinionated data. It just wanted to open up an honest conversation around the rates of drug use on the trail.

“We asked ourselves: What if this was discussed more openly?” Raffio said. “We wanted to come from a place of curiosity, not judgement.”
